questions.e: Resuming continues a session with its history intact, which is what the returning customer needs. Forking creates an independent branch from the same history, and changes in the fork never flow back, which is what the supervisor needs. D matches both. B swaps the two. C lets the supervisor's experiment change the customer's conversation. A throws away most of the context and relies on one message to carry it.

questions.q: A nightly audit agent scans 40 repositories for security issues: a coordinator launches one scanner subagent per repository and then produces a morning report. Which execution pattern fits the scanning stage and the report stage?
o: Fan out the 40 scans in parallel, because they are independent, then run one merge step that builds the report from normalized results
Run several report writers in parallel and concatenate their outputs
Use one agent that scans all 40 repositories in a single context so it can spot cross-repository patterns
Scan sequentially so each scanner can learn from the previous one's findings, then write the report in parallel sections
questions.e: Independent work runs in parallel and dependent work runs in sequence, so the hybrid in A matches the data dependencies: the scans don't need each other, and the report needs all of them. D serializes independent work and slows the audit for no gain. C pushes 40 repositories into one context, which degrades attention and turns one failure into a total failure. B produces a report with no single view of the findings, which is what the merge step exists for.

questions.q: A nightly audit agent scans 40 repositories for security issues: a coordinator launches one scanner subagent per repository and then produces a morning report. Last night the audit crashed at repository 27. The rerun started again from repository 1 and opened duplicate tickets for findings already reported. Which TWO changes fix this? (Select TWO)
o: Checkpoint progress to a manifest file (completed repositories, pending repositories, results so far) and resume from it after a crash
Give the scanners larger context windows so they remember the previous run
Run the audit weekly instead of nightly
Make ticket creation idempotent, for example keyed by repository and finding id, so a replay can't create duplicates
Ask the coordinator at startup which repositories it already finished
questions.e: A manifest (A) lets the restarted coordinator continue from repository 27, and idempotent side effects (D) make any replayed step harmless; together they turn a crash into a delay. Context windows (B) don't survive a process crash, and the coordinator has no memory of the previous run to ask about (E), because the API is stateless. Running less often (C) leaves the failure in place.

questions.q: A nightly audit agent scans 40 repositories for security issues: a coordinator launches one scanner subagent per repository and then produces a morning report. An engineer proposes giving every scanner the full tool set, including `Write`, `Bash` and the ticketing tool, 'in case they need it.' What is the best response?
o: Replace the scanner tools with Bash alone, since Bash can do everything the other tools do
Give the scanners every tool and add a system-prompt rule forbidding writes
Keep each scanner on the read-only tools its job needs, and let only the coordinator open tickets from the merged findings
Accept the proposal, because more tools make the scanners more capable
questions.e: Least privilege scopes each agent to what its responsibility requires. C also keeps tool selection accurate and stops a misbehaving scanner from changing code or opening tickets. D widens the blast radius and adds selection noise for capabilities nobody uses. B relies on a probabilistic instruction to restrain a capability that should never be there. A hands the scanners the broadest tool of all.

questions.q: A nightly audit agent scans 40 repositories for security issues: a coordinator launches one scanner subagent per repository and then produces a morning report. The morning report said 'No critical issues found across all repositories.' The team later learns that six scanners hit their token budgets and skipped their largest files. What should the report format have required?
o: Nothing; the scanners needed a more capable model
A longer narrative summary from each scanner
A confidence score from each scanner
A coverage annotation from every scanner (files reviewed, files skipped with reasons, coverage counts) carried into the merged report
questions.e: Without explicit coverage, 'no issues found' can't be told apart from 'no issues found in the part that ran.' D makes the gap visible so the skipped files can be queued for a focused pass. Self-reported confidence (C) is poorly calibrated and says nothing about what was skipped. A longer summary (B) adds words without the counts. A stronger model (A) can still hit a budget, and the report would still hide it.

questions.q: After the first tool call, every follow-up request in your agent loop fails with a 400 error. Here is how the loop builds the next request. What is wrong? ```python response = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, tools=tools, messages=messages) if response.stop_reason == "tool_use": call = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use") result = run_tool(call.name, call.input) messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [{ "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id, "content": result, }]}) ```
o: The loop should set `tool_choice` to `any` after the first call
The assistant turn containing the `tool_use` block is never appended, so the `tool_result` refers to a call the next request doesn't contain
`tool_result` blocks belong in the system prompt
`max_tokens` is too low for a tool loop
questions.e: The API is stateless, so each request must carry the whole exchange: the assistant message with the `tool_use` block comes first, then the user message with the matching `tool_result` (B). Without it, the `tool_use_id` points at nothing. C misplaces tool results, which go in a user turn. D and A change settings that have nothing to do with a malformed history.

questions.q: Your research agent uses the server-side web search tool. Some responses come back with `stop_reason` `pause_turn`, and the loop treats them as finished, returning half-done research. What is the correct handling?
o: Send a follow-up request with the paused assistant response appended as-is, so Claude can continue the server-side work
Raise `max_tokens` and send the original request again
Run the web search locally and return a `tool_result` for it
questions.e: `pause_turn` means a server-side tool loop reached its iteration limit mid-task. The documented handling is A: return the response as the latest assistant turn, and Claude picks up where it stopped. C is the bug in the question. D treats a server tool like a client tool; there is no `tool_use` for your code to answer. B restarts the work and pays for it twice.

questions.q: A team answers one-line FAQ questions from a two-page policy with a six-subagent pipeline: retriever, reader, drafter, tone checker, fact checker and formatter. Answers take 25 seconds and cost far more than expected. What is the best change?
o: Collapse it to a single model call with the policy in context, plus a lightweight validation step if needed
Move every subagent to the most capable model to cut retries
Run the six subagents in parallel under a coordinator
questions.e: This is over-decomposition: the task is small, single-domain and fits in one context, so the subagents add orchestration cost without any isolation benefit, and A removes the overhead. Parallelizing (C) doesn't fit a chain where each step needs the previous step's output. B raises the cost of a design that shouldn't exist. D helps only with repeated identical questions and leaves the latency of the chain in place.

questions.q: A payments service's error rate spiked. The cause could be in code, configuration, infrastructure or a third-party API, and what to check next depends on what each check finds. How should the coordinator decompose the investigation?
o: One prompt asking Claude for the root cause
A fixed pipeline that runs the four checks in a set order
Dynamic decomposition: plan the next subtasks from each finding, with a token budget and iteration cap enforced in code as safety nets
Run every conceivable check in parallel with no coordinator
questions.e: Open-ended investigations, where the next step depends on what you just learned, call for dynamic decomposition. Because that pattern costs more and can wander, C pairs it with limits enforced outside the model. A fixed pipeline (B) suits workflows that are known in advance. D wastes effort and leaves nobody to connect the findings. A asks for an answer without giving the model any way to gather evidence.

questions.q: Long research tasks sometimes use ten times the expected tokens. Which TWO belong in a reliable token-budget design? (Select TWO)
o: Asking Claude each turn how many tokens it has used so far
A system-prompt instruction asking Claude to stay under 50,000 tokens
Track cumulative input and output tokens from each response's usage field inside the loop
Stop the loop in code when the budget is reached, with a wrap-up instruction injected at about 80% of the budget
questions.e: Budgets are enforced from outside the model: measure from the usage field (D) and act on the measurement with a soft warning and a hard stop (E). An instruction (C) and the model's own estimate (B) are probabilistic and unmeasured. A tiny `max_tokens` (A) truncates every response, so turns end at the cap before they finish.

questions.q: A team's MCP server should (1) let Claude create Jira tickets, (2) expose the team's API schema files so a user can attach them as context, and (3) provide a reusable 'triage this incident' template with the team's severity rubric. Which MCP primitives fit, in that order?
questions.e: Creating a ticket is an action, so it's a tool. Schema files are read-only data for the client to browse and attach, so they're a resource. The packaged triage template is a prompt. D matches action, data and know-how in that order. A turns data and a template into callable functions. B and C put the action in the wrong primitive.

questions.q: Every developer on a team should get the same internal MCP server in Claude Code, and the server needs an API token. Which TWO choices are correct? (Select TWO)
o: Put the token in `CLAUDE.md` so Claude can pass it to the server
Paste the raw token into `.mcp.json` so setup is a single step
Define the server in the project's `.mcp.json` and commit it to the repository
Reference the token in `.mcp.json` as `${INTERNAL_API_TOKEN}` and have each developer set that environment variable
Have each developer add the server with local scope by following a wiki page
questions.e: Project scope (C) is the configuration that reaches the whole team through version control, and environment variable expansion (D) keeps the secret out of the repository. B commits a credential. E relies on every developer repeating a manual step, and local scope never propagates. A puts a secret into the model's context, where it can leak through outputs or logs.

questions.q: When users ask to change their email address, Claude often calls `get_customer` instead of `update_customer`, then tells the user the change is done. Both tools exist. What is the first fix?
o: Add a system-prompt line telling Claude to use `update_customer` for updates
Rewrite both descriptions: what each tool does, when to use it, and when to use the other one instead, with `get_customer` described as read-only
questions.e: Claude selects tools mainly from their descriptions, so overlapping or vague descriptions are the first thing to fix (B), and the boundary statements ('to change a record, use `update_customer`') are what resolve this confusion. A rename (C) changes little while the descriptions stay vague. A system-prompt patch (A) is weaker than fixing the routing signal itself. Removing the read tool (D) breaks every legitimate lookup.

questions.q: Your team wants every file Claude edits to be formatted with Prettier immediately after each edit, for everyone working in the repository. Which configuration does that?
o: A `CLAUDE.md` line: 'Run Prettier after every edit'
A `PostToolUse` hook in the committed `.claude/settings.json`, matching `Edit|Write`, that runs Prettier on the edited file
A `PreToolUse` hook on `Edit` that runs Prettier
questions.e: Formatting has to run after the file changes, which is `PostToolUse`, and the committed project settings file shares the hook with the whole team, so C covers both requirements. D runs before the edit exists. B is guidance Claude may skip, while a hook runs every time. A works only for developers who set it up themselves.

questions.q: A team requires that Claude never ends its work while the test suite is failing. Which hook enforces this?
o: A `SessionEnd` hook that runs the tests
A `Stop` hook that runs the tests and exits with code 2, printing the failures to stderr, when any test fails
A `PostToolUse` hook that runs the tests after every file read
A `UserPromptSubmit` hook that runs the tests before each prompt
questions.e: Exit code 2 from a `Stop` hook prevents Claude from stopping and feeds the stderr text back, so Claude keeps working on the failures (B). `SessionEnd` (A) fires as the session closes and can't block anything. D tests before the work happens. C runs constantly at the wrong moment and can't stop Claude from finishing.

questions.q: A `PostToolUse` hook on `Write` scans each file Claude writes. It finds an API key in a file Claude just wrote and exits with code 2. What happens?
o: The file has already been written; Claude receives the hook's stderr message and can act on it, for example by removing the key
Claude Code shuts down the session
Nothing happens, because exit code 2 is ignored for `PostToolUse`
The write is cancelled and the file is never created
questions.e: `PostToolUse` fires after the tool has run, so it can't undo the write; exit code 2 shows its stderr to Claude (A). To stop the write itself, the check belongs in a `PreToolUse` hook, where exit code 2 blocks the call, which is the behavior D describes. B and C describe behaviors that don't exist.

questions.q: A developer asks Claude Code to migrate 40 files from a callback-based API client to async/await. The change touches shared types, and there are two reasonable migration strategies. What is the best way to start?
o: One prompt for the whole change, then review the final diff
Direct execution, file by file, fixing problems as they appear
Plan Mode: let Claude explore the codebase and propose a migration plan to review before any file changes
questions.e: Multi-file, cross-cutting changes with more than one valid approach are Plan Mode's case (D): the strategy gets agreed before 40 files move. B and A commit to an approach before anyone has compared the options, and a wrong choice is expensive to unwind. C states a preference without planning the migration.

questions.q: A team's dependency-audit skill prints thousands of lines of output, and teammates complain it floods the main conversation. Which frontmatter change fixes this?
o: `context: fork`, so the skill runs in an isolated subagent and returns its result
questions.e: `context: fork` (A) runs the skill in its own subagent context, so the verbose work stays out of the main conversation. B only stops Claude from invoking the skill automatically; the output still floods the conversation whenever someone runs it. C changes which tools are pre-approved and D changes the model, and neither moves the output.

questions.q: In a monorepo, files under `services/payments/` follow strict rules (all amounts in integer cents, no floats). The rules confuse Claude when it works on the frontend. Which TWO placements load these rules only when Claude works in the payments code? (Select TWO)
o: A section titled 'Payments only' in the root `CLAUDE.md`
A file in `.claude/rules/` with `paths: ["services/payments/**"]` in its frontmatter
questions.e: A path-scoped rule (C) loads when Claude reads or edits a matching file, and a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` (B) loads on demand when Claude works with files in that directory. The root `CLAUDE.md` (A) loads in every session, frontend work included. D is personal and reaches nobody else. E configures MCP servers and holds no instructions.

questions.q: A code-review prompt says 'Be thorough but avoid nitpicks.' Reviews flag style issues inconsistently and miss SQL injection. Which rewrite fixes the cause?
o: 'You are a world-class senior security engineer.'
'Be extremely thorough and never miss anything.'
'Report only these issues: SQL injection, XSS, authentication bypass and secrets in code. Report high or critical severity only. Do not comment on formatting or naming.'
questions.e: Vague instructions produce inconsistent behavior because the model has to guess the threshold. D names the categories, the severity floor and the exclusions, and anyone reading a review can check whether it followed them. B and C push the same vague guidance in two directions. A role line (A) without criteria leaves the same guesswork.

questions.q: A classifier should flag support tickets that mention a physical safety risk. In testing it flags every ticket containing the word 'fire', including 'firewall rules reset after update.' What is the best few-shot improvement?
o: An instruction: 'Don't be fooled by keywords.'
Two to four examples that include the firewall ticket labeled not-safety with a one-line reason, a genuine safety ticket, and an ambiguous case
Twenty examples of genuine safety tickets
questions.e: Few-shot examples teach reasoning and edge cases best when they include something the model should leave alone, so the tricky negative in B is the example that matters. C piles on positives and teaches nothing about the false positives. A is vague guidance. Temperature (D) changes randomness and leaves the misunderstanding in place.

questions.q: Your team plans to use structured outputs (a JSON schema in `output_config.format`) for invoice extraction. Which TWO statements about this feature are true? (Select TWO)
o: It guarantees the extracted values are correct for the source document
It works only when `tool_choice` forces a specific tool
It removes the need to validate business rules, such as totals matching line items
Constrained decoding makes the response valid JSON that matches the schema's structure and types
A refusal or a `max_tokens` cutoff can still produce output that doesn't match the schema, so check `stop_reason`
questions.e: Structured outputs guarantee format: valid, schema-compliant JSON (D), with the documented exceptions of refusals and truncation (E). Format says nothing about whether the values are right, so semantic checks such as totals and dates stay in your pipeline, which rules out A and C. B confuses the feature with forced tool use; structured outputs are requested through `output_config.format`.

questions.q: An extraction fails validation because `invoice_date` came back as 2026-04-31, a date that doesn't exist. What should the retry request contain?
o: The failed output and the words 'try again'
The original document again with no other changes
The original document, the failed output, and the specific error ('`invoice_date` 2026-04-31 is not a valid date'), with an instruction to correct only that field
The same request sent to a more capable model
questions.e: A useful retry tells the model exactly what failed and gives it the source to fix it against (C). B repeats the conditions that produced the error. A removes the source the model needs to correct the date. D changes the model without telling it what went wrong.

questions.q: A product team wants to move its live chat assistant to the Message Batches API to cut costs in half. What is the right assessment?
o: Reject it, because batch requests can't include a system prompt
Approve it: the same quality at half the price
Approve it, provided the app polls for results every second

Reject it: batches carry no latency guarantee (most finish within an hour, some take up to 24), so a waiting user can't be served; cut costs with prompt caching or by routing routine messages to a cheaper tier
questions.e: The batch discount comes with asynchronous processing and no latency guarantee, which rules it out for anyone waiting on an answer (D). B ignores the latency. Polling (C) doesn't speed up processing. A is false: batch requests take the same parameters as regular Messages requests.

questions.q: One prompt asks Claude to extract 30 fields from a contract, normalize every currency, classify the risk clauses and write an executive summary. Results vary from run to run, and errors are hard to trace. What is the best restructuring?
o: A chain of focused prompts (extract, validate, normalize, classify, summarize), each with its own instructions and checks
The same single prompt on a more capable model
Ask for the executive summary first, then the fields
The same single prompt with each requirement marked IMPORTANT
questions.e: Prompt chaining gives each stage one job and a validation point, so a failure shows up in the stage that caused it (A). Emphasis (D) doesn't reduce the number of jobs in one prompt. A stronger model (B) may help a little and leaves errors untraceable. Reordering (C) builds the summary on fields nobody has checked yet.

questions.q: A knowledge-base Q&A agent receives 40 retrieved passages per question. The passage with the answer usually lands near the middle, and answers often miss it. Which TWO changes address this? (Select TWO)
o: Re-rank the passages and pass only the most relevant few
Put the passages first and the question and instructions at the end of the prompt
Switch to a model with a larger context window
questions.e: Attention is weakest in the middle of long contexts, so the fixes shrink the middle and move what matters to the edges: fewer, better passages (B), and long material first with the question last, which Anthropic's long-context guidance recommends (D). A bigger window (E) and more passages (A) make the middle longer. Temperature (C) affects randomness and does nothing for attention.

questions.q: Two internal documents disagree about the warranty period: a 2024 policy says 12 months and a 2026 update says 24 months. What should the agent's answer do?
o: Decline to answer until someone fixes the documents
State 24 months without mentioning the conflict, because the newer document wins
Give the answer with attribution: both values, their documents and dates, the newer one identified as likely current, and the conflict flagged for review
Average the two and state 18 months
questions.e: Provenance keeps each claim tied to its source and surfaces conflicts instead of settling them silently (C). Silently picking one value (B) is the tested anti-pattern even when the choice happens to be right, because nobody learns that the documents disagree. D produces a number neither source supports. A withholds an answer the agent can give with a caveat.

questions.q: Your support agent loop calls `messages.create`, checks `response.stop_reason`, executes any tools, and sends back `tool_result` blocks. In production, the loop occasionally exits after Claude calls `lookup_order` but before calling `process_refund` or replying to the customer. Logs show `stop_reason: "end_turn"` on those turns. What is the most likely root cause?
o: The agent hit its `max_tokens` limit while composing the refund reasoning and silently truncated.
A `PostToolUse` hook is rewriting the tool result and blocking the next turn.
The agent loop is terminating correctly — `end_turn` means Claude produced a final natural-language answer for the user, so the model decided no further tool call was needed for that case.
`stop_reason: "end_turn"` indicates a server-side timeout and the request should be retried.
questions.e: `end_turn` is the normal stop reason meaning Claude reached a natural stopping point and is not requesting another tool call. If the agent answered the customer instead of processing the refund, the model chose that path — the loop is behaving correctly; the prompt or tool description, not the loop, is the issue. **Why A is Wrong:** `max_tokens` produces `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`, not `end_turn`; the two are distinct values and the logs show `end_turn`. **Why B is Wrong:** `PostToolUse` runs after tool execution and cannot change `stop_reason`; it can only append `additionalContext` to conversation state. **Why D is Wrong:** `end_turn` is a normal completion signal, not a timeout; Anthropic has no "retry end_turn" semantic.

questions.q: Your research coordinator spawns three subagents via the Task/Agent tool for a market-analysis query. The coordinator has already gathered a list of 12 target companies and stored them in its conversation. Subagent 1 returns findings about only 3 of those companies; when asked why, its logs show it only "knew about" companies it inferred from the short task prompt. What is the correct fix?
o: Serialize the full 12-company list into the `prompt` string passed to the Agent tool call, since subagents do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history.
Switch the subagent to Opus so it has a larger effective context window.
Increase the subagent's `maxTurns` so it can iterate longer and discover the remaining companies.
Add a `PostToolUse` hook on the Agent tool that attaches the coordinator's transcript to the subagent input.
questions.e: Per Anthropic's subagent docs, the only channel from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's `prompt` string. The subagent's context window starts fresh with no parent conversation; any data it needs (company list, file paths, prior decisions) must be explicitly included in that prompt. **Why B is Wrong:** Context window size is irrelevant when the parent history was never passed; a larger window stays empty. **Why C is Wrong:** More turns cannot reveal information the subagent never received; the constraint is missing input, not insufficient iteration. **Why D is Wrong:** `PostToolUse` fires after the tool (subagent) has already executed and cannot inject data into the subagent's starting prompt.

questions.q: Policy requires that `process_refund` never run for amounts above $500 without a manager-approval token. Currently the system prompt says "Never refund more than $500 without approval." A quarterly audit found 14 refunds of $500–$4,000 approved without tokens. Which change most reliably closes the gap?
o: Strengthen the system prompt with bold, capitalized warnings and add three few-shot examples of correct refusals.
Lower the agent's temperature to 0 to make refund decisions more deterministic.
Have a second Claude instance review every refund decision before it executes and veto if it disagrees.
Add a `PreToolUse` hook on `process_refund` that inspects `input.amount` and returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` when `amount > 500 && !input.approval_token`.
questions.e: Hard financial thresholds belong in programmatic gates, not prompts. A `PreToolUse` hook can deterministically deny tool calls (precedence: deny > ask > allow) based on structured input fields before the tool ever executes, making the policy enforceable rather than persuasive. **Why A is Wrong:** LLMs probabilistically violate prompt rules; strengthening prose cannot guarantee enforcement of a monetary policy. **Why B is Wrong:** Lower temperature biases toward likely tokens but does not enforce any specific rule; the model can still emit a $2,000 refund tool call confidently. **Why C is Wrong:** A reviewer LLM introduces its own error rate, doubles cost, and still relies on probabilistic judgment — the audit problem persists, only shifted.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline processes PDFs and calls `messages.create` with `tool_use` forced via `tool_choice`. Roughly 3% of requests return `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` mid-way through a `tool_use` block, producing invalid JSON and downstream parse errors. Which response is correct?
o: Treat `max_tokens` as equivalent to `end_turn` and parse whatever JSON was produced.
Catch the error, re-issue the request with a higher `max_tokens`, and if the partial tool_use is still present, continue the conversation with a `tool_result` marked `is_error: true`.
Delete the partial tool_use block from the assistant turn and retry with the same parameters.
Add a `PostToolUse` hook that repairs truncated JSON before it reaches the parser.
questions.e: `max_tokens` means output was truncated; the partial `tool_use` is invalid and cannot be executed. The correct handling is to raise `max_tokens` (or tighten the schema) and, if a malformed tool_use remains, satisfy the API requirement that every `tool_use` needs a matching `tool_result` — marked as an error — so the conversation stays valid. **Why A is Wrong:** `max_tokens` and `end_turn` are semantically different; treating them the same produces malformed outputs and silent data corruption. **Why C is Wrong:** If you retain the assistant turn with a `tool_use` block but do not follow it with a `tool_result`, the API rejects the next request with `invalid_request_error`. **Why D is Wrong:** `PostToolUse` fires after a tool executes; it cannot intercept an LLM output block that was truncated before a tool ever ran.

questions.q: A team shares a repo that defines two subagents via `.claude/agents/reviewer.md` and `.claude/agents/test-writer.md`. A developer created a different `~/.claude/agents/reviewer.md` on their laptop and wonders why teammates see different behavior. Which statement is correct?
o: `~/.claude/agents/` is user-level and never shared via git; teammates only see `.claude/agents/` in the repo.
User-level agents in `~/.claude/agents/` are automatically synced when the repo is cloned.
`.claude/agents/` is gitignored by default; agents must be placed at `~/.claude/agents/` to be shared.
Both locations are merged and the union is shared with teammates via Claude's cloud sync.
questions.e: Anthropic's settings hierarchy places `.claude/agents/` at the project level (checked into version control, shared with the team) and `~/.claude/agents/` at the user level (personal, per-machine, not shared). The developer's user-level override is invisible to teammates by design. **Why B is Wrong:** There is no automatic sync of `~/.claude/` across machines; that directory is private to each user. **Why C is Wrong:** `.claude/settings.local.json` is gitignored by default, but `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/agents/`, and `.claude/commands/` are the intended shared path. **Why D is Wrong:** Claude Code does not operate a cloud-sync service for agents; shared config flows through git only.

questions.q: The support agent has `allowedTools: ["get_customer", "lookup_order", "process_refund", "escalate_to_human"]`. A user writes: "Please escalate this to a human — I want a supervisor now." Claude responds by apologizing and offering a $20 credit instead. Which change is most aligned with best practice?
o: Add a system-prompt rule: "If the user requests escalation, call escalate_to_human immediately and do not offer alternatives."
Remove `process_refund` from `allowedTools` so Claude cannot offer credits.
Add a `PostToolUse` hook that rewrites credit offers into escalations.
questions.e: Explicit escalation criteria belong in the agent's system prompt (and reinforced by the `escalate_to_human` tool description). Honoring a direct user request to escalate is a policy rule the model must follow; a clear, unambiguous instruction is the correct first step before adding programmatic enforcement. **Why B is Wrong:** Removing `process_refund` breaks legitimate refund handling for every other case and does not teach the agent to escalate — it just narrows the menu. **Why C is Wrong:** Temperature 0 does not teach escalation behavior; the model can still deterministically pick "offer credit" if that is the highest-likelihood path. **Why D is Wrong:** `PostToolUse` cannot rewrite an assistant message that was never a tool call; credits here were conversational, not tool outputs.

questions.q: An architect designs an agent loop and insists the loop should also exit when `stop_reason == "pause_turn"`. In what situation is that stop reason emitted, and what is the correct handling?
o: `pause_turn` means the user paused the session; the agent should halt until resumed.

`pause_turn` is returned by server-executed tools (web_search, code_execution) when their internal iteration cap is hit; the client should resend the conversation including the paused assistant response to continue.
`pause_turn` indicates rate limiting; the client should back off exponentially.
`pause_turn` means Claude refused; treat it identically to `refusal`.
questions.e: `pause_turn` is specific to server-side tools like `web_search` and `code_execution`. When the internal server-side loop hits its step cap, the API emits `pause_turn`; the client continues by sending the conversation back (including the paused assistant turn) to resume execution. **Why A is Wrong:** There is no user-pause mechanic that surfaces as `pause_turn`; that is an API-level signal, not a UI state. **Why C is Wrong:** Rate limiting surfaces as HTTP 429 with retry headers, not as a `stop_reason`. **Why D is Wrong:** `refusal` is its own distinct stop reason with different semantics (safety); conflating them loses error fidelity.

questions.q: Your coordinator runs an 8-subagent research task. After all subagents return, the coordinator produces a final report. Average coordinator token usage is 180K tokens per run and the team wants to reduce it by 30%. Which approach preserves accuracy best?
o: Instruct subagents to return compressed, structured findings (key facts, citations, confidence) rather than raw search dumps.
Replace the coordinator model with Haiku to shrink the summary size.
Move the coordinator to the Batch API.
Run each subagent twice and majority-vote the outputs before returning to the coordinator.
questions.e: Per Anthropic's multi-agent research engineering post, subagents should return compressed findings rather than raw tool output to keep coordinator context manageable. This is the primary lever for coordinator token reduction without accuracy loss, because the coordinator only needs synthesized results to do its job. **Why B is Wrong:** Downgrading the coordinator model harms synthesis quality; the post notes coordinator capability is the single biggest predictor of final answer quality. **Why C is Wrong:** Batch API is for high-latency asynchronous jobs; a user-facing research task cannot tolerate 24-hour batch windows. **Why D is Wrong:** Duplicated subagent runs double token cost, the opposite of the goal, and consensus suppresses intermittent useful signal.

questions.q: A developer starts a debugging session at 9 AM, steps away, and resumes at 3 PM. She runs `claude --resume `. The session's conversation history refers to files that have since been edited by a teammate on a different branch. Which is the best practice?
o: Always resume; Claude tracks file state automatically and will detect mismatches.
Use `fork_session` to get a clean state while keeping the original history.
Resume only when the prior context is still valid; if the code has meaningfully diverged, start a fresh session to avoid stale assumptions poisoning the reasoning.
Run `--resume` with `--clear-context` to reset tool results while keeping messages.
questions.e: Sessions preserve the full transcript including prior tool results; if file contents have changed, the model's prior reasoning is built on stale data. A fresh session is appropriate when prior context is invalid, while `--resume` is for continuations where context remains accurate. **Why A is Wrong:** The SDK does not automatically re-verify file state against old tool results; stale reads remain in the transcript as if current. **Why B is Wrong:** `fork_session` copies existing state into a new session id; it does not clean stale file reads — it duplicates them. **Why D is Wrong:** There is no `--clear-context` flag that selectively drops tool results while retaining messages.

questions.q: A CI pipeline runs Claude Code non-interactively with `-p` to auto-fix lint warnings. The team wants to prevent Claude from ever writing to `node_modules/` or `.env*` files. Which configuration reliably enforces this?
o: A `PreToolUse` hook matching `Write|Edit` that inspects the target path and returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` for forbidden paths.
A system prompt directive: "Never edit node_modules or .env files."
A `Notification` hook that warns the user when forbidden paths are touched.
A `PermissionRequest` hook to pop up a confirmation dialog.
questions.e: `PreToolUse` hooks fire before the tool executes and can deterministically deny based on `updatedInput` inspection; deny precedence overrides allowlists. This is the correct programmatic gate for path-based access control in automated/non-interactive contexts. **Why B is Wrong:** Prompts cannot guarantee path-level enforcement against a probabilistic model, especially across thousands of CI runs. **Why C is Wrong:** `Notification` hooks are informational and fire after actions are taken; they do not block. **Why D is Wrong:** `PermissionRequest` hooks do not fire in non-interactive (`-p`) mode; Anthropic's docs explicitly direct users to `PreToolUse` for automated decisions.

questions.q: You define a subagent with `AgentDefinition` fields including `description` and `prompt`. Other developers notice Claude is not routing relevant queries to this subagent. Which field is most commonly the root cause?
o: `prompt` — it needs to be longer to give Claude more to work with.
`description` — it is used by the coordinator to auto-route to this subagent; vague or missing descriptions prevent delegation.
`tools` — subagents cannot be invoked unless `tools` is empty.
questions.e: The `description` field is the routing signal the orchestrator reads to decide "when to use this agent." If it is vague, missing, or overlaps with other agents, automatic delegation fails; explicit invocation ("use the X agent") can still work but auto-routing is description-driven. **Why A is Wrong:** `prompt` is the subagent's system prompt (internal instructions); it does not affect whether the coordinator chooses the subagent. **Why C is Wrong:** Empty `tools` is not required for invocation; it just restricts what the subagent can do once invoked. **Why D is Wrong:** `model` is optional; routing works fine with the default inherited model.

questions.q: You extract invoices into a schema with required fields `invoice_number`, `total`, `vendor_tax_id`. About 12% of source PDFs omit the tax ID. Current schema marks all three as required; Claude is fabricating plausible tax IDs when absent. Which fix is best?
o: Add a system prompt: "Do not hallucinate."
Re-run extractions that produce tax IDs through a second review agent.
Change the schema to make `vendor_tax_id` nullable and instruct the model to emit `null` when not present in the source.
Lower temperature to 0 so outputs become deterministic.
questions.e: Required fields with absent source data structurally push the model toward fabrication because the schema demands a value. Making the field nullable and instructing explicit `null`-on-absence aligns the schema with reality and eliminates the incentive to invent data. **Why A is Wrong:** Generic "do not hallucinate" prompts do not fix a structural contradiction where the schema demands a value the source lacks. **Why B is Wrong:** A reviewer agent cannot verify a tax ID it also cannot see in the source; it faces the same information gap. **Why D is Wrong:** Temperature 0 makes fabrication deterministic, not accurate; the model can consistently produce the same wrong tax ID.

questions.q: Your agent's `get_customer` MCP tool description reads: "Gets customer." The agent calls it unnecessarily (including for anonymous FAQ questions), driving up costs by 40%. What should you try first?
o: Add a classifier LLM in front of the agent to decide whether customer lookup is needed.

Rewrite the tool description to specify when to use it: "Retrieves authenticated customer record. Only call when the user has provided an order ID, email, or account number AND the task requires personal account data."
Remove `get_customer` from `allowedTools` and let the agent ask the user for details directly.
Reduce the main model from Sonnet to Haiku to make calls cheaper.
questions.e: Tool selection is primarily driven by the tool description. Rewriting it with crisp preconditions is the lowest-effort, highest-leverage fix and the first intervention Anthropic recommends before adding classifiers or new components. **Why A is Wrong:** A classifier LLM is an over-engineered addition that duplicates the LLM's native routing capability; descriptions are the correct lever. **Why C is Wrong:** Removing the tool breaks legitimate customer lookups; the problem is over-use, not existence. **Why D is Wrong:** Model downgrade may degrade quality across all tasks and does not address the misrouting cause.

questions.q: A developer is mid-refactor at turn 47 and wants to explore an alternative database choice without losing the current work. Which command supports this best?
o: `claude --new` to start fresh, then paste relevant context manually.
`claude --resume --fork-session` so the new session clones the transcript up to the current point, leaving the original session intact.
questions.e: `fork_session` combined with `--resume` clones the session state into a new session id so the developer can branch into the alternative database path while preserving the original session for continuation. This is the canonical "what if" branching pattern. **Why A is Wrong:** Resuming and editing modifies the single session history and loses the original path the team may want to keep. **Why B is Wrong:** Starting fresh loses prior reasoning and forces manual recovery, which risks omissions. **Why D is Wrong:** `--bypass-permissions` has nothing to do with branching; it disables permission checks.

questions.q: The team proposes giving subagents access to the `Agent` tool so they can spawn sub-subagents. What is the documented behavior and recommendation?
o: Recursive Agent spawning is supported and recommended for deep research trees.
Subagents can technically include `Agent` in `tools`, but Anthropic explicitly recommends against it; sub-subagent spawning is unsupported and can cause runaway token usage.
Subagents inherit the `Agent` tool by default; removing it requires `disallowedTools: ["Agent"]`.
Sub-subagents are allowed but inherit the root coordinator's conversation history.
questions.e: Per Anthropic's subagent documentation, subagents should not spawn their own subagents. Including `Agent` in a subagent's `tools` is discouraged because it enables uncontrolled fan-out, blows token budgets, and makes failure modes opaque. **Why A is Wrong:** Anthropic's docs explicitly caution against recursive spawning; the multi-agent research post describes a two-level hub-and-spoke, not arbitrary depth. **Why C is Wrong:** Subagents do not receive `Agent` in inherited tools when they have no way to spawn; the default for subagents excludes Agent to prevent recursion. **Why D is Wrong:** Even if spawning were allowed, sub-subagents would not inherit the root's history — the only channel is the prompt string.

questions.q: Aggregate agent resolution rate is 92%. Product leadership is happy until a segment analysis shows refund cases resolve at 63% while FAQ cases resolve at 98%. What is the correct architectural response?
o: Celebrate the 92% and move on — aggregate is acceptable.
Investigate the refund segment specifically; aggregate accuracy is masking a poorly performing subpath that likely needs its own tool, hook, or subagent.
Retrain the model on more FAQ data to further lift the easier segment.
Increase temperature to encourage more creative refund solutions.
questions.e: Aggregate metrics frequently mask segment-specific failure modes. A 35-point gap indicates a structural issue in the refund path (tool design, policy enforcement, decomposition) that requires targeted investigation, not aggregate optimism. **Why A is Wrong:** Ignoring segment gaps means refund users experience near-coin-flip support quality while leadership reports success. **Why C is Wrong:** Retraining on the strong segment widens the gap; it does not address the weak segment. **Why D is Wrong:** Higher temperature reduces determinism on a policy-heavy task, worsening refund accuracy.

questions.q: The coordinator returns its final report, but key numerical findings in the middle of the 12,000-token synthesis get dropped when downstream summarization runs. What is the most effective mitigation at the coordinator output stage?
o: Progressively summarize multiple times to tighten the report.
Use a larger-context model and let it summarize.
Position the most critical findings, numbers, and dates at the beginning and end of the report; avoid burying them in the middle to mitigate "lost in the middle" effects.
Encode the findings as base64 so the summarizer cannot drop them.
questions.e: The well-documented "lost in the middle" phenomenon means models attend less to content placed midway through long contexts. Front-loading and back-loading critical findings preserves them through downstream processing far more reliably than any encoding trick. **Why A is Wrong:** Progressive summarization degrades precision on numbers and dates with each pass; it compounds the problem. **Why B is Wrong:** Larger context does not improve attention quality in the middle; the failure mode persists regardless of window size. **Why D is Wrong:** Base64 obscures the content from the model entirely, preventing any useful summarization; it is not a serious mitigation.

questions.q: Your extraction agent occasionally emits dates in `MM/DD/YYYY` when source documents use ISO format and vice versa, producing 6% downstream parse failures. Which approach uses Agent SDK hooks most appropriately?
o: A `PostToolUse` hook on the extraction tool that normalizes all dates to ISO 8601 before the result enters downstream storage.
A `PreToolUse` hook that rewrites the user prompt.
A `Notification` hook that pings Slack on each inconsistency.
Add a system prompt saying "always use ISO format."
questions.e: `PostToolUse` is designed for data normalization and side-effects after tool execution; it can append normalized values or transform tool output into conversation-visible `additionalContext`. Deterministic normalization at that layer fixes format drift without re-prompting. **Why B is Wrong:** `PreToolUse` runs before execution and rewriting the user prompt does not deterministically normalize output format. **Why C is Wrong:** Notifying Slack records the problem but does not fix it; data still flows in mixed formats. **Why D is Wrong:** Prompt instructions for formatting are probabilistically followed; 6% deviation is consistent with that weakness.

questions.q: An agent loop receives `stop_reason: "refusal"`. Which handling is correct?
o: Retry the same prompt — refusals are usually transient.
Treat it as a terminal state: exit the loop and surface an appropriate message; do not resubmit tool results because there is no tool_use block to satisfy.
Continue the loop with an empty `tool_result`.
Escalate to a more capable model automatically.
questions.e: `refusal` indicates Claude declined to respond due to safety constraints. It is a terminal stop reason with no tool_use to satisfy; the correct handling is to exit, log, and surface a user-appropriate message (or route to a human/policy flow), not retry blindly. **Why A is Wrong:** Refusals are policy-driven, not transient; retrying the identical prompt typically yields the same result and wastes spend. **Why C is Wrong:** There is no `tool_use` block to match, so sending a `tool_result` produces `invalid_request_error`. **Why D is Wrong:** Automatic model-escalation on refusals is an attempt to evade safety controls; it is neither a recommended nor reliable pattern.

questions.q: A developer proposes consolidating four tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`) into a single `support_action` tool with a `type` parameter to "simplify" the tool list. What is the trade-off most relevant here?
o: Consolidation improves accuracy because Claude picks one tool name.
The Agent SDK requires at most three tools, so consolidation is mandatory.
Consolidation typically degrades tool-selection accuracy and hides preconditions better expressed in per-tool descriptions and schemas; four well-described tools are generally preferable.
Consolidation reduces latency proportional to the number of tools removed.
questions.e: Tool selection is description-driven; distinct tools with precise descriptions and schemas give Claude the clearest routing signal. Collapsing tools into a typed dispatcher erases description-level precision and schema validation per action, degrading selection accuracy and raising error rates. **Why A is Wrong:** Selection accuracy depends on description quality, not the number of tools on the menu; one vaguely described tool is worse than four precisely described ones. **Why B is Wrong:** There is no such limit; Claude regularly uses dozens of tools. **Why D is Wrong:** Latency is driven by turns and token count; tool count is not a major factor.

questions.q: Your coordinator spawns a synthesis subagent whose job is to combine earlier subagent outputs and produce a final report. The coordinator currently asks that same synthesis subagent to also self-review its report for accuracy. Quality is mediocre. Which change is most effective?
o: Delegate the review to an independent, separately-instantiated reviewer subagent rather than having the author self-review.
Tell the synthesis agent to "be more critical."
Run the synthesis subagent three times and majority-vote the outputs.
Have the coordinator review by reading the report aloud in its response.
questions.e: Self-review by the same instance tends to reinforce the author's assumptions rather than catch them. An independent reviewer subagent with a distinct system prompt provides adversarial critique and catches errors the author is biased against seeing. **Why B is Wrong:** "Be more critical" is a prompt tweak that does not overcome the structural bias of same-instance self-review. **Why C is Wrong:** Majority voting on the same model/prompt suppresses intermittent but correct minority signals; it masks rare bugs rather than revealing them. **Why D is Wrong:** The coordinator reading text aloud adds no evaluative capability and does not constitute independent review.

questions.q: A CI job runs Claude Code to triage failing tests. The team wants runtime limits: no more than 25 turns per job. Where should this be enforced?
o: Include the limit in the system prompt.
Configure a `Stop` hook that counts turns internally.
Manually abort after 25 turns via a shell timer.
Set `maxTurns` in the `ClaudeAgentOptions` (or `AgentDefinition` if run as a subagent) so the loop terminates automatically at the programmatic boundary.
questions.e: `maxTurns` is a first-class SDK option that bounds the agent loop deterministically. It is the correct programmatic lever for turn limits and does not depend on prompt adherence or external timing races. **Why A is Wrong:** Prompt-level turn limits are not enforced; the model does not track turns reliably. **Why B is Wrong:** `Stop` hooks fire when a turn ends; they do not provide a cleaner mechanism than the built-in `maxTurns` option. **Why C is Wrong:** A shell timer on wall-clock time is a crude proxy; a slow single turn can burn the budget while a fast 30-turn job runs fine.

questions.q: Your agent handles refunds. After refund processing, the workflow must also (a) send a confirmation email and (b) update CRM. Currently the system prompt instructs Claude to "remember to always send email and update CRM after a refund." In production, one of these steps is missed in 9% of cases. Which is the best fix?
o: Add the two steps as bullet points to the system prompt in bold.

Implement a structured handoff: make `process_refund` return a `next_actions` array, and enforce via a `PostToolUse` hook that queues required follow-ups (`send_confirmation_email`, `update_crm`) or blocks finalization until they complete.
Have the agent apologize to the user and retry.
Deploy a second Claude agent to audit completed refunds weekly.
questions.e: Multi-step workflow enforcement needs programmatic prerequisites and structured handoff, not prompt reminders. Encoding the follow-up obligations into tool output contracts and gate hooks makes completion verifiable rather than hoped-for. **Why A is Wrong:** Bullet points and bolding do not make a rule programmatically enforceable; 9% drift is consistent with prompt-only controls. **Why C is Wrong:** Apologies do not prevent the next omission; they convert a reliability issue into a customer-experience issue. **Why D is Wrong:** Weekly audits catch problems after the fact and do not prevent missed steps in the moment.

questions.q: A colleague proposes an "orchestrator-workers" multi-agent design for a coding task that requires editing three tightly-coupled files across the repo. Anthropic's own guidance on this pattern suggests:
o: Orchestrator-workers is ideal because each file can be edited in parallel.
Use three independent sessions and manually merge.

Multi-agent architectures are poorly suited to tasks requiring shared context or tight inter-agent dependencies, such as most coding tasks with cross-file coupling; a single agent is usually preferable.
questions.e: Anthropic's multi-agent research engineering post explicitly notes that multi-agent systems are poorly suited to tasks requiring shared context or tight dependencies, and that most coding tasks fall into this category. A single agent retains holistic view of cross-file coupling. **Why A is Wrong:** Parallel edits across tightly-coupled files produce merge conflicts and inconsistent changes; parallelism is inappropriate where dependencies are tight. **Why B is Wrong:** Independent sessions plus manual merge is the exact anti-pattern the pattern guidance warns against. **Why C is Wrong:** The ~90% figure is specific to breadth-first research queries on Anthropic's internal eval, not a universal result; it does not apply to coding.

questions.q: Two `PreToolUse` hooks are registered on `Write`. Hook A always returns `{permissionDecision: "allow", updatedInput: {...pathA}}`; Hook B returns `{permissionDecision: "allow", updatedInput: {...pathB}}`. Which statement best describes SDK behavior?
o: Hooks run sequentially in registration order and the first result wins.
Conflicts cause the tool call to be denied automatically.
Hooks run in parallel; when multiple return `updatedInput`, the last one to finish wins and order is non-deterministic. Avoid multiple writers to the same field.
questions.e: Per Anthropic's hook docs, `PreToolUse` hooks execute in parallel; when several return `updatedInput`, the last to complete wins, which is non-deterministic. The documented guidance is to avoid having multiple hooks write the same input fields. **Why A is Wrong:** Registration order is not preserved; parallel execution means "first" is meaningless in the sequential sense. **Why B is Wrong:** There is no automatic conflict-deny; only an explicit `deny` decision blocks the call, and deny beats allow. **Why C is Wrong:** The SDK does not do field-wise merging of `updatedInput`; last-writer-wins is a whole-object overwrite.

questions.q: A developer wants a pre-commit guardrail: before Claude runs `git commit`, a Python script should validate that no `console.log` statements were added. Which mechanism is most appropriate?
o: A `PreToolUse` hook matching `Bash` with a command hook that inspects the pending command and greps the staged diff, denying if a `console.log` is found.
A `PostToolUse` hook that warns after the commit completes.
A system prompt rule that says "do not commit console.log statements."
Turn off the `Bash` tool and require the developer to commit manually.
questions.e: Pre-commit validation is a classic `PreToolUse` use case: intercept before the tool runs, inspect arguments and repo state, return `deny` if the policy fails. Matching on the `Bash` tool name and running a shell command hook is the canonical pattern in Anthropic's hook guide. **Why B is Wrong:** `PostToolUse` cannot block the commit; it only sees results after execution and cannot undo them. **Why C is Wrong:** Prompt rules are probabilistic and do not enforce deterministic pre-commit gates. **Why D is Wrong:** Disabling Bash removes useful functionality broadly instead of narrowly enforcing the specific rule.

questions.q: The agent reports `confidence: 0.94` in its final message when resolving refund cases. Correlating with audit outcomes, refunds labeled "high confidence" have only a 71% correctness rate while low-confidence refunds have 68%. The team wants to use the confidence score to auto-approve. What is the best assessment?
o: Use a second LLM to re-grade the confidence score before using it as a gate.
The issue is a temperature problem; setting temperature to 0 will fix calibration.

LLM self-reported confidence is typically poorly calibrated. The near-identical correctness across bands indicates the signal has limited discriminative value; do not use it as a gating threshold without calibration and independent validation.
questions.e: Self-reported confidence from LLMs is a well-documented calibration failure mode. The 71% vs 68% split shows the score is not meaningfully predictive of correctness; using it as an auto-approval gate would produce incorrect approvals near the claimed "high confidence" rate. **Why A is Wrong:** The empirical data contradicts the assumption; 71% correctness is not acceptable for auto-approval of refunds. **Why B is Wrong:** A second LLM inherits the same calibration weakness; stacking self-reports does not produce a well-calibrated number. **Why C is Wrong:** Temperature affects output variability, not the calibration of a model's self-reported score; the miscalibration would persist.

questions.q: Your coordinator invokes a `web_researcher` subagent with only the prompt "Research recent trends." The subagent returns generic, unfocused findings. Which decomposition improvement is most impactful?
o: Provide a detailed subagent brief in the prompt: objective, output format, tool/source guidance, scope boundaries, and success criteria — per Anthropic's multi-agent research system guidance.
Add two more web-search subagents in parallel.
questions.e: Anthropic's engineering post on multi-agent research emphasizes that detailed delegation instructions — clear objective, output format, tool/source guidance, and task boundaries — are the single highest-leverage lever for subagent quality. Vague prompts produce vague work regardless of model or parallelism. **Why A is Wrong:** Opus cannot infer the missing brief; the model upgrade pays for capability on a mis-specified task. **Why C is Wrong:** More turns expand generic output without improving direction. **Why D is Wrong:** Adding parallel subagents with the same vague brief multiplies the cost of generic output.

questions.q: Two tools are currently separated by role: `get_customer_basic` for agents and `get_customer_full` for managers. About 80% of refund cases require only name + order history, which is in `basic`. However, some legitimate refund flows need `full`. The team debates least-privilege design. Which option best balances security and functionality?
o: Give all agents `get_customer_full` and rely on prompts to restrict use.
Remove `get_customer_full` entirely; agents should ask managers manually for every case.

Keep `get_customer_basic` as the default for agents with a scoped, purpose-restricted `get_customer_full` callable only via a tool whose `PreToolUse` hook enforces justification capture and refund-case verification.
Merge both tools into one and let Claude decide which fields to request.
questions.e: Least privilege with a scoped cross-role tool for legitimate exceptions is the canonical pattern: default narrow access, provide a gated escalation path for real needs, enforce via programmatic hook rather than trust. This preserves security without breaking the 20% of legitimate flows. **Why A is Wrong:** Prompts cannot guarantee restriction; exposing full data broadly violates least privilege and creates compliance risk. **Why B is Wrong:** Blanket removal blocks 20% of legitimate work and forces human bottlenecks on routine cases. **Why D is Wrong:** Collapsing tools removes the enforcement seam; Claude's "decision" is not a security boundary.

questions.q: A required field `ein` (US Employer Identification Number) is absent from 40% of source invoices. The team tries retrying the extraction up to 3 times hoping to get a valid EIN. After retry logic went live, the EIN population rate rose to 97%. A sample audit shows most of the newly-populated EINs are fabricated. What went wrong?
o: The retry count is insufficient; 5 retries would produce cleaner outputs.
The temperature is too low; raise it to encourage diverse retry outputs.

Retrying does not help when the information is absent from the source; the field should be made nullable and schema/prompt explicitly instructed to return `null` when absent. The rising "success rate" is a hallucination indicator, not improvement.
The extractor should pull EINs from an external database automatically.
questions.e: When source data is absent, no amount of retrying can recover the missing value; what it does produce is increasingly confident fabrication across retries. Making the schema nullable and explicitly instructing `null`-on-absence is the correct structural fix. **Why A is Wrong:** More retries amplify fabrication, making the audit failure worse; population rate is a misleading success metric. **Why B is Wrong:** Higher temperature increases fabrication variability, not accuracy; it makes the problem worse. **Why D is Wrong:** Silent automatic external enrichment is a material scope change that introduces its own correctness and privacy issues; it is not a fix to the extraction itself.

questions.q: A developer designs a long-running refactor agent and wants to handle crashes gracefully. Which session strategy best supports reliable recovery?
o: Persist the `session_id` returned in the SDK's init message; on crash, invoke `--resume ` to reload the full transcript and continue from the last state.
Serialize the entire conversation to a local JSON file and rebuild it manually on recovery.
Rely on memory-only sessions and re-prompt on crash.
Always start a fresh session after any crash to avoid stale state.
questions.e: Sessions persist to `~/.claude/projects//*.jsonl` automatically; `--resume ` reloads the full transcript including prior tool results, enabling clean recovery. Capturing the `session_id` from `system:init` is the canonical recovery pattern. **Why B is Wrong:** Manual JSON serialization duplicates what the SDK already does automatically and risks schema drift. **Why C is Wrong:** Memory-only sessions lose all context on crash, forcing expensive re-prompting and rework. **Why D is Wrong:** Starting fresh throws away valid context; resume is the correct default when the prior context is still valid.

questions.q: Your agent's `allowedTools` includes MCP-namespaced tools like `mcp__billing__process_refund`. A `PreToolUse` hook is configured with `matcher: "process_refund"`. It never fires. Why?
o: Hooks must be registered before the MCP server starts.
The matcher is a regex against the full tool name, which is `mcp__billing__process_refund`; use a pattern like `mcp__billing__process_refund` or `.*process_refund.*` to match MCP-namespaced names.
questions.e: Hook matchers are regex strings applied to the full tool name. MCP tools have names in the form `mcp____`, so a bare `process_refund` pattern does not match. Using the full prefixed name or a wildcard pattern works. **Why A is Wrong:** MCP tools are absolutely hookable; only the matcher pattern is at fault. **Why B is Wrong:** There is no ordering requirement between hook registration and MCP server startup; the SDK handles tool discovery. **Why D is Wrong:** `PreToolUse` works uniformly across built-in and MCP tools.

questions.q: A coordinator synthesizes four subagent outputs. To keep the final context small, the developer recursively summarizes the synthesis three times before presenting to the user. Leadership complains key numbers have shifted: a "$2.3M savings" reported by a subagent appears as "~$2M" in the final output. What is happening?
o: The subagent reported the wrong number originally.

Progressive (iterative) summarization is a known risk: each pass loses precision on numbers and dates. Preserve numeric precision by carrying through verbatim quotes or structured fields rather than re-summarizing.
Temperature is too high; setting it to 0 will preserve numbers.
questions.e: Progressive summarization compounds precision loss; numbers and dates drift under repeated compression because the model rounds or abstracts them for readability. Preservation requires carrying specific facts through as structured data or verbatim quotes, not re-summarizing. **Why A is Wrong:** The subagent's original number ($2.3M) was correct; the loss happened at the synthesis compression stage. **Why B is Wrong:** `PostToolUse` is not automatically truncating numbers; this is a prompt-side summarization artifact. **Why D is Wrong:** Temperature 0 does not prevent summarization-induced rounding; the model still abstracts during compression.

questions.q: A developer defines an agent with no `allowedTools`. They try to delegate via the Agent (Task) tool and find that subagents never spawn. What is the fix?
o: `Agent` (or `Task`) must be included in the parent's `allowedTools` to enable subagent spawning; without it, the tool is not available and delegation silently no-ops.
Subagents always spawn; the developer must be misreading logs.
Reduce `maxTurns` so the model runs out of room and is forced to delegate.
questions.e: Per Anthropic's subagent docs, the `Agent` tool (or its prior name `Task`) must appear in the parent session's `allowedTools` or the tool is not exposed to the model, so no delegation can occur. This is the most common silent-failure cause. **Why B is Wrong:** Delegation can silently fail without any error when the Agent tool is omitted; logs will simply show no `tool_use: Agent` blocks. **Why C is Wrong:** `maxTurns` does not affect tool availability; running out of turns terminates the loop without enabling missing tools. **Why D is Wrong:** Relocating the agent file does not solve the allowedTools omission; the parent still cannot emit the Agent tool call.

questions.q: The team asks: should the main Sonnet-based support agent also perform nightly data summarization of closed tickets? Nightly summarization is offline, tolerant of latency, and batchable. Which architecture recommendation fits?
o: Run nightly summarization in the live support agent loop to reuse infrastructure.
Route nightly summarization through a Claude Code CLI for developer-style task management.
Skip summarization; tickets are already logged.
Run nightly summarization through the Anthropic Batch API since the workload is asynchronous, latency-tolerant, and cost-sensitive; reserve the live agent for user-facing, blocking flows.
questions.e: Batch API is designed for asynchronous, high-volume, latency-tolerant jobs at reduced cost. Nightly ticket summarization is a textbook fit: it does not block a user, can run with hours of latency, and benefits from batch cost economics. The live agent stays focused on real-time blocking flows. **Why A is Wrong:** Interleaving nightly bulk work into the live agent risks latency spikes for real users and conflates very different SLOs. **Why B is Wrong:** Claude Code CLI is optimized for developer-interactive coding workflows, not scheduled bulk summarization. **Why C is Wrong:** Skipping summarization loses analytical value leadership requested; logs are raw, not insight.

questions.q: An architect observes a pattern across agent failures: whenever subagent output passes through the coordinator, specific structured facts (order IDs, amounts, timestamps) are sometimes dropped. Several fixes are proposed. Which is the best durable architecture for preserving structured facts end-to-end?
o: Increase coordinator context window to 1M tokens.
Ask the coordinator to "double-check" all numbers in its prose output.
Add a `PreToolUse` hook that rewrites coordinator prose.

Have subagents return structured JSON (not prose) to the coordinator, and have the coordinator treat those fields as immutable pass-through values in the final report rather than re-describing them in prose.
questions.e: Structured JSON handoff between subagents and coordinator preserves precise facts by construction; treating those fields as immutable pass-through data in the final output prevents prose-layer re-description from drifting numbers or losing IDs. This is the canonical structured-handoff pattern. **Why A is Wrong:** A larger context window does not address "lost in the middle" attention quality or progressive-summarization drift; more room is not more precision. **Why B is Wrong:** Asking the coordinator to self-check prose is weak self-review and does not prevent drift deterministically. **Why C is Wrong:** `PreToolUse` fires on tool calls, not on coordinator prose generation; there is no tool call to intercept at that stage.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline calls a `record_invoice` tool to return parsed invoice data. When an invoice field like `po_number` is absent from the source document, the tool schema marks it `required`, and Claude fabricates a plausible-looking PO number about 8% of the time. What is the correct fix?
o: Increase the temperature to 0 so the model stops hallucinating values.
Add a post-hoc validator that cross-checks the PO number against a database and retries on mismatch.
Make `po_number` nullable in the schema and instruct the description to return `null` when the field is not present in the source.
Add `"strict": true` to the tool definition so the API rejects invalid inputs.
questions.e: When a field is declared `required` but the source lacks the data, the model is pushed to invent a value to satisfy the schema. Making the field nullable and explicitly documenting that absence should produce `null` aligns the schema with reality and removes the fabrication pressure. **Why A is Wrong:** Temperature 0 reduces randomness but does not change the model's incentive to fill required fields; it often produces the same fabricated value deterministically. **Why B is Wrong:** Retry-on-mismatch only helps if a correct value exists somewhere to retrieve; when the source truly lacks the PO, retries produce the same fabrication or a new one. **Why D is Wrong:** `strict: true` validates Claude's output against the schema but does not make a required-but-absent field nullable — it would in fact enforce the fabrication.

questions.q: A developer asks Claude Code to rename a function across a TypeScript monorepo with ~4,200 files. Which sequence best reflects Anthropic's recommended incremental-exploration pattern?
o: `Glob("**/*.ts")` → `Read` every file → `Write` each file back with the rename applied.
`Agent(subagent)` where the subagent spawns another subagent per directory to parallelize.
questions.e: Anthropic's published Claude Code system prompt instructs the model to prefer `Glob` over `find`, `Grep` over bash-grep, `Read` over `cat`, and `Edit` over `sed`. The Glob→Grep→Read→Edit progression narrows the search space efficiently, preserves line-numbered context for accurate edits, and uses the permission cache. **Why A is Wrong:** Anthropic explicitly instructs Claude Code to avoid `grep` and `sed` via Bash; heredoc-style commands bypass permission caching and skip the safety property that `Edit` fails fast when `old_string` is not found. **Why B is Wrong:** Reading and rewriting thousands of files is wasteful — Edit sends ~2 lines versus Write sending the whole file, and Glob alone does not narrow to files that actually contain `oldName`. **Why C is Wrong:** Subagents in Claude Code cannot spawn other subagents (no nested delegation via the Agent tool), and parallelizing before narrowing with Grep front-loads cost.

questions.q: A coordinator agent delegates to four specialized subagents (web_search, document_analysis, synthesis, report). The report subagent produces summaries that reference statistics the coordinator discussed earlier in its own conversation but never passed in the subagent's prompt. What is happening?
o: The subagent is inheriting the coordinator's context window and the statistics are stale.
The subagent receives a fresh context by default and is fabricating plausible-sounding statistics because the coordinator did not pass them in the subagent's prompt.
The Anthropic API is auto-merging parallel subagent contexts after the last tool call completes.
The report subagent's `tool_choice` is set to `any`, which causes it to invent statistics to justify a tool call.
questions.e: By default, each Claude Code subagent starts with a fresh/blank context and receives only what the coordinator writes into its prompt — it does not inherit the parent's conversation history. When the coordinator omits the numeric facts, the subagent has no grounding and fabricates. **Why A is Wrong:** Default subagents do not inherit context; the coordinator must explicitly pass any facts the subagent needs. **Why C is Wrong:** There is no cross-subagent context merging; each subagent returns only its final result to the parent. **Why D is Wrong:** `tool_choice: any` forces tool selection but does not cause data fabrication on its own — the absence of grounding data does.

questions.q: The `process_refund` MCP tool sometimes returns a transient 503 from an upstream payments API. Ops wants Claude to retry automatically but not on validation errors (like invalid amount). How should the MCP server signal this distinction?
o: Return `isError: true` in both cases, with structured details in the result content (an error category such as transient vs. validation, an `isRetryable` flag and a readable description) so the model can decide whether to retry or self-correct.
Return a JSON-RPC protocol error with code `-32603` for transient issues and `-32602` for validation errors.
Return `isError: false` for transient errors (so Claude keeps going) and `isError: true` for validation errors.
Return `isError: false` with a top-level custom `retry` field outside the result content and rely on every client to honor it.
questions.e: The MCP spec defines two error mechanisms: JSON-RPC protocol errors (structural problems the model cannot fix) and tool-execution errors reported with `isError: true`. Tool-execution errors are meant to give actionable feedback the model can use, and the guide's pattern is to include structured metadata (error category, `isRetryable`, description) in the result so transient failures are retried and validation errors are not. B is wrong because protocol errors bypass the model's reasoning. C is wrong because reporting a real failure as `isError: false` makes the model treat it as success. D is wrong because a custom field outside the content, with success flagged, relies on clients that are not required to handle it.

questions.q: A team wants every developer on the repo to automatically get access to the same set of MCP servers (GitHub, Postgres, internal docs) when they run Claude Code. Where should the configuration live?
o: `~/.claude.json` committed to a shared dotfiles repo each developer clones.
`.mcp.json` at the project root, checked into the repository.
questions.e: `.mcp.json` is the project-scope MCP config explicitly designed to be committed to the repo and shared across the team. Claude Code picks it up automatically from the project root and requires user approval before first use as a security gate. **Why A is Wrong:** `~/.claude.json` is the user-level file scoped to a single developer's machine and is not intended to be shared; it stores per-user, cross-project MCP server entries. **Why B is Wrong:** `.claude/settings.local.json` is meant for per-checkout overrides and is conventionally git-ignored; using it would defeat the "shared across team" requirement. **Why C is Wrong:** `managed-mcp.json` is for enterprise/IT-deployed lockdown policies and takes exclusive control when present — it is the wrong mechanism for normal team sharing and would block users from adding personal servers.

questions.q: The research coordinator currently exposes 34 MCP tools to every subagent so they can "do whatever they need." Tool-selection accuracy on the web_search subagent has dropped from 94% to 71% since 12 new tools were added. What is the best architectural fix?
o: Tell each subagent in its system prompt which tools to prefer, leaving all 34 loaded.
Use `tool_choice: {"type":"any"}` so subagents are forced to choose quickly.
Scope each subagent's `tools:` allowlist to only the 3–6 tools relevant to its role.
Switch all subagents to a model with a larger context window so all 34 tool definitions fit without degradation.
questions.e: Per-subagent `tools:` allowlists are Anthropic's stated pattern for scoped, least-privilege tool access. Reducing the tool surface to what each role actually needs directly mitigates selection degradation — the documented motivation behind the Tool Search Tool is precisely that loading many definitions into context upfront hurts performance. **Why A is Wrong:** System-prompt preference instructions are secondary to the tool descriptions themselves and do not remove the attention cost of 34 definitions sitting in context. **Why B is Wrong:** `any` forces a tool call but does not improve which tool is chosen; the selection is still made against 34 candidates. **Why D is Wrong:** A larger context window does not fix attention quality — the "lost in the middle" phenomenon and selection degradation persist regardless of window size.

questions.q: A GitHub Action runs Claude Code with `claude -p "review this PR"`. The `.mcp.json` at the repo root references `"headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}"}`. On the runner, the job fails with a config parse error. What is the most likely cause?
o: `.mcp.json` does not support environment variable expansion in `headers`.
`${GITHUB_TOKEN}` is unset in the runner's shell because the secret was not exported as an env var to the Claude Code step.
`-p` mode ignores `.mcp.json` entirely; you must pass `--mcp-config` explicitly.
GitHub Actions masks secrets, which breaks the expansion step.
questions.e: Claude Code's `.mcp.json` supports `${VAR}` expansion in `command`, `args`, `env`, `url`, and `headers`. If the required variable is unset and no `${VAR:-default}` fallback is provided, Claude Code fails to parse the config.
