The key lesson is that **prompt refinement must happen before batch submission** because async validation gives no mid-flight feedback. **Why B is Wrong:** No batch update/PATCH endpoint exists in the Anthropic API; this option fabricates a capability that does not exist. **Why C is Wrong:** Submitting a parallel batch doubles cost and consumes rate-limit capacity for a batch whose results will be discarded. **Why D is Wrong:** Anthropic Support cannot modify the contents of an in-flight batch — this is a structural API limitation, not a permissions issue.

questions.q: A research orchestrator dispatches sub-tasks to specialist agents and parses their natural-language responses with regex to populate a planning data structure. Parse failures (~14%) cause cascading task-graph corruption. The team is debating fixes. What is the most reliable approach?
o: Add stricter regex with more fallback patterns to handle the 14% of edge cases.

Define each sub-task response as a JSON tool with a typed schema (`findings`, `confidence`, `next_steps`, `unresolved_questions`) and call it with `tool_choice: "any"` so every specialist returns schema-compliant structured output the orchestrator can consume directly.
Add a second LLM pass that converts the natural-language response to JSON, with retries on parse failure.
Increase the specialist agents' `max_tokens` so their responses are more complete and parseable.
questions.e: Tool-use with a JSON schema and `tool_choice: "any"` is Anthropic's most reliable mechanism for guaranteed schema-compliant output — the model is trained on the tool-use contract and the output is constrained at the decoder level. Eliminating the natural-language → regex layer entirely removes the 14% failure mode rather than patching it. **Why A is Wrong:** Regex fragility against open-ended LLM output is the root cause; more regex compounds the problem. **Why C is Wrong:** A second LLM pass to convert NL → JSON adds latency, cost, and a new failure mode while not eliminating the original brittleness. **Why D is Wrong:** Token budget doesn't make natural language deterministically parseable; longer responses can be *less* parseable.

questions.q: A team is designing a tool definition for medical-claim extraction. They've drafted a one-sentence description: "Extracts diagnosis codes from clinical notes." The tool is occasionally called when a billing tool would be correct, and it occasionally fabricates ICD-10 codes for vague symptoms. What is Anthropic's recommended fix?
o: Add few-shot routing examples to the system prompt so the model learns when to call this tool vs. the billing tool.
Add a regex post-validator that rejects fabricated ICD-10 codes.
Lower temperature to 0 to reduce fabrication.

Expand the tool description to 3–4+ sentences covering what the tool does, when it should be used, when it should NOT be used, what each parameter means, and important caveats including "return an empty array if no confirmed diagnosis is documented."
questions.e: Anthropic's tool-use best practices state that the **tool description is by far the most important factor** in tool performance — recommended length is at least 3–4 sentences covering purpose, scope, exclusions, parameter semantics, and caveats. The description (not surrounding prompts or routing examples) is what the model uses to disambiguate similar tools and constrain fabrication. **Why A is Wrong:** Few-shot routing examples paper over a tool-description problem; Anthropic's guidance is to fix descriptions first because examples consume tokens and cannot disambiguate inherently overlapping tools. **Why B is Wrong:** Post-validation catches malformed codes but cannot tell whether a syntactically valid code was actually documented in the note. **Why C is Wrong:** Temperature reduces sampling variance, not the model's choice of whether to invent an ICD-10 from vague text.

questions.q: A code-review architecture analyzes each file in isolation, then aggregates findings. A recent bug — a parameter renamed in one file but still referenced under the old name in three caller files — was missed by every per-file reviewer. Each reviewer's local analysis was correct in isolation. What architectural change closes this gap?
o: Add a "shared blind spot" verification agent whose only job is to check the per-file findings against each other.
Increase the per-file reviewers' `max_tokens` so they consider more context.

Add a cross-file integration pass: an agent receives the union of related files in its context window and looks for problems visible only across files (renamed parameters, unused arguments, type mismatches between caller and callee).
Run five identical reviewers per file and require unanimous agreement before flagging.
questions.e: Per-file passes find local bugs cheaply and in parallel, but cross-file issues like renamed parameters, type mismatches at call sites, and silent semantic drift are visible **only when multiple files share a context window**. The documented architecture pairs per-file local analysis with a cross-file integration pass. **Why A is Wrong:** A meta-reviewer of per-file findings still has only the per-file findings as input — it cannot detect issues that no per-file reviewer surfaced. **Why B is Wrong:** More tokens per file doesn't bring other files into context; the issue is which files are in scope, not how much room each gets. **Why D is Wrong:** N copies of the same per-file reviewer share the per-file blind spot — consensus on file-local context cannot manifest cross-file information.

questions.q: A pipeline extracts shipment data into a schema with 22 fields. Three fields (`hazmat_class`, `customs_value`, `consignee_tax_id`) are present in only ~30% of source documents. The current schema marks them all `required: true`. The model is fabricating values for these fields when they're absent. What is the best schema redesign?
o: Remove the three sparse fields from `required` and from the schema entirely; consumers can derive them downstream.

Keep them in the schema but remove from `required`, and change types to `["string", "null"]` (or appropriate type union with null), with descriptions instructing the model to return null when not documented and never to infer or estimate.
Add a `missing_fields: array` and require the model to list any field it couldn't extract.
Run extraction twice and accept only fields that match across both runs.
questions.e: Nullable typing combined with explicit "return null if not documented" descriptions gives the model a structurally honest path for absent data — the field remains documented and consistently shaped for downstream consumers, but the model is no longer cornered into fabrication. **Why A is Wrong:** Removing the fields entirely loses signal when they *are* present and pushes the absence-handling problem to consumers without solving it. **Why C is Wrong:** A side-channel `missing_fields` array is unstructured and doesn't prevent fabrication in the primary fields when the model "thinks" it found something. **Why D is Wrong:** Duplicate extraction doubles cost and latency for a problem the schema can solve cleanly; Best-of-N is a verification pattern, not a replacement for nullable design.

questions.q: A team enables `extended thinking` on a Claude review agent with `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "submit_review"}` to force structured output. The API call returns an error. What is the correct interpretation?
o: Forced tool selection (`tool_choice: "any"` or `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", ...}`) is incompatible with extended thinking; only `auto` and `none` are supported. Switch to `tool_choice: "auto"` and instruct the model in a user message to call `submit_review`.
Extended thinking requires `temperature: 1`; setting it to 0 (the team's default) caused the error.
Extended thinking requires the tool name to be prefixed with `thinking_`.
The error is a transient API issue — retry with exponential backoff.
questions.e: Anthropic's documentation explicitly lists this incompatibility: extended thinking works only with `tool_choice: "auto"` and `tool_choice: "none"`. The documented workaround is to use `auto` and place a user-message instruction directing the model to call the desired tool — the model will comply in practice and you retain extended thinking. **Why B is Wrong:** Temperature requirements for extended thinking concern values, not the choice of `tool_choice` mode; the error here is structural. **Why C is Wrong:** No naming convention requirement exists in the API; the option is fabricated. **Why D is Wrong:** This is a deterministic configuration error, not a transient one — retries will fail identically.

questions.q: A team is benchmarking three approaches to producing JSON output from Claude for a contract-review tool: (1) prompt-only ("Respond with JSON matching this schema..."), (2) tool use with `strict: true` and `tool_choice: "any"`, (3) tool use with `strict: false`. Schema-validity rates over 10,000 calls are 94.1%, 100%, and 99.4% respectively. The team wants to choose option 1 because it's "simpler". What is the right rebuttal?
o: Prompt-only achieves 94.1% which is sufficient; the 5.9% can be retried.
Tool use with `strict: false` at 99.4% is the best balance because strict mode adds latency.
Switch to prompt-only with `temperature: 0` — it will reach 100% validity.

Tool use with strict schemas + `tool_choice: "any"` is Anthropic's most reliable structured-output mechanism, with constrained decoding mathematically guaranteeing schema compliance; the simplicity argument is false economy because the 5.9% syntactic failure rate creates downstream fragility that exceeds the integration overhead of tool use.
questions.e: Anthropic explicitly documents tool use with strict schemas as the most reliable approach. Constrained decoding makes syntactic compliance a mathematical guarantee, not a probability — eliminating the entire class of malformed-JSON errors. A 5.9% failure rate at 10,000 calls is 590 broken integrations per run. **Why A is Wrong:** A 5.9% failure rate at 10,000 calls is 590 broken integrations per run — not a tail-risk to be papered over with retries. **Why B is Wrong:** Strict mode does not measurably increase latency; the 0.6% gap represents real production failures, and `strict: true` is the recommended default. **Why C is Wrong:** `temperature: 0` reduces variance but does not guarantee schema compliance — that requires constrained decoding, which only the tool-use path provides.

questions.q: A team's PR-review system is showing a pattern: on long PRs (>800 lines changed), the model frequently dismisses real issues in the *middle* of the diff as "intentional" while flagging issues at the start and end accurately. They've tried adding "review every line equally carefully" to the prompt with no effect. What is the most effective architectural fix?
o: Add a `detected_pattern` field to the output schema for the model to self-report dismissal patterns.
Increase `max_tokens` so the model has more room to discuss middle-of-diff issues.

Split long diffs into smaller chunks (per-file or per-hunk) reviewed by independent per-file agents, then a cross-file integration pass — addressing the lost-in-the-middle effect through architecture rather than prompt instructions.
Switch to a model with a larger context window and include the entire repository.
questions.e: Lost-in-the-middle is a documented attention-distribution effect that prompt instructions cannot reliably correct; the architectural remedy is to keep each pass's scope small enough that no content lands in the under-attended middle. Independent per-file agents plus a cross-file integration pass is Anthropic's documented pattern for exactly this regime. **Why A is Wrong:** A `detected_pattern` field is a useful logging idiom for offline analysis but doesn't change the within-call attention distribution that caused the dismissals. **Why B is Wrong:** More output tokens don't redistribute input attention; the bias is in how the model attends to the input, not how much output it can produce. **Why D is Wrong:** Larger context windows make the lost-in-the-middle effect *worse*, not better, by enlarging the under-attended region.

questions.q: A team wants to extract structured data from documents and is debating between (a) prompt-only with `"Respond in JSON"`, (b) tool use with `tool_choice: "auto"`, and (c) tool use with `tool_choice: "any"`. With option (b), they observe ~7% of responses contain natural-language preamble before the tool call or a text-only response. What's happening?
o: Tool definitions are missing required fields — fix the schema and the preambles will stop.

`tool_choice: "auto"` allows the model to either call a tool OR respond in text — this is documented behavior. To guarantee a tool call, use `tool_choice: "any"` or `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}`.
The 7% rate indicates a temperature that is too high; setting `temperature: 0` will eliminate it.
The tool descriptions are too short; expanding them will force tool use.
questions.e: `tool_choice: "auto"` is the default-with-tools and explicitly permits the model to either call a tool or respond in text — Anthropic's docs note Claude can be over-eager *or* under-eager about tool calls in this mode. To guarantee a tool call, use `"any"` (any of the provided tools) or a forced specific tool. **Why A is Wrong:** The behavior is the documented contract of `auto`, not a schema bug. **Why C is Wrong:** Temperature affects sampling variance, not the auto-vs-required choice axis controlled by `tool_choice`. **Why D is Wrong:** Tool descriptions are extremely important for *which* tool is called, but they don't override the `tool_choice: "auto"` permission to respond in text.

questions.q: A support agent escalates conversations to humans inconsistently. The system prompt says "Escalate when the customer is frustrated or the issue is complex." Sentiment-analysis logs show the model escalates 8% of conversations, but human auditors say the *correct* escalation rate should be ~22%. What is the most reliable fix?
o: Replace the vague criteria with explicit, observable triggers: "Escalate when ANY of: (1) customer has used a refund/cancel/lawsuit keyword; (2) the issue has been re-opened ≥2 times; (3) the resolution requires changes the available tools cannot perform; (4) customer explicitly requests a human." Provide 3 few-shot examples covering edge cases.
Lower the sentiment threshold for "frustrated" so more conversations meet the bar.
Add a confidence score to the escalate decision and escalate when confidence > 0.7.
Run a second Claude instance asking "Should this be escalated?" and OR the two decisions.
questions.e: "Frustrated" and "complex" are subjective adverbial criteria that the model maps to its own internal cutoff inconsistently. Anthropic's guidance is to replace them with explicit, observable, testable conditions. Concrete triggers plus a small set of few-shot examples for boundary cases convert subjective judgment into checkable rules. **Why B is Wrong:** Sentiment-classifier threshold tuning treats the symptom; the root cause is the criterion itself being vague, not its threshold. **Why C is Wrong:** Self-reported confidence from LLMs is poorly calibrated; this just adds another vague subjective scalar. **Why D is Wrong:** Two instances with the same vague criterion produce correlated errors, not independent confirmation; OR-ing decisions inflates false positives without fixing the criterion.

questions.q: An extraction system reports an aggregate accuracy of 96% across 50,000 invoices in a nightly batch. Finance flags that on the ~3,200 international invoices the accuracy is only 71%. The aggregate metric had been masking a domain-specific failure. What is the most appropriate response?
o: The 96% aggregate is acceptable; international invoices are an edge case.
Add `temperature: 0` to make extraction more deterministic across all invoices.
Switch to a more capable model for the entire pipeline.

Segment evaluation by document subtype (domestic vs. international, by country, by currency), build targeted few-shot examples for international cases, and re-evaluate the segment-level metrics; aggregate metrics mask domain-specific failure.
questions.e: Aggregate accuracy hides systematic failures on minority slices — a 96% global rate is consistent with disastrous performance on a 6% subset. The documented response pattern is segment-level evaluation, identification of the failing slice's specific characteristics, and targeted few-shot examples for the underrepresented case. **Why A is Wrong:** A 71% accuracy is unacceptably low for production finance data regardless of slice size; "edge case" reasoning normalizes systematic failures. **Why B is Wrong:** Determinism doesn't improve accuracy on a domain the model is mishandling; it locks in the wrong answer. **Why C is Wrong:** Upgrading the model for all 50,000 invoices is wasteful when 94% of the volume is already extracted correctly; targeted few-shot is the proportional fix.

questions.q: A team is designing a self-correction validation pattern for invoice extraction. They want the model to detect its own arithmetic inconsistencies. Which schema design best implements this?
o: Add a `confidence: number` field and reject any extraction with confidence < 0.9.

Add `stated_total` (verbatim from document) and `calculated_total` (model-computed from line items) plus a `conflict_detected: boolean` field the model must set to true when the values disagree; downstream code validates the boolean and triggers retry-with-feedback or human review when set.
Add a `notes: string` field where the model can mention any concerns it has.
Add an `extraction_quality: enum["high", "medium", "low"]` field and route low-quality extractions to humans.
questions.e: Anthropic's documented self-verification pattern is to **force the model to compare its own output against the source** and surface the comparison as structured fields. Dual-extraction (stated vs calculated) plus an explicit `conflict_detected` boolean creates an auditable invariant that downstream code can check; this is far more reliable than soft confidence fields because the comparison is mechanical, not subjective. **Why A is Wrong:** Self-reported confidence from LLMs is poorly calibrated; rejecting on confidence < 0.9 will simultaneously discard correct extractions and accept fabrications labeled "high confidence." **Why C is Wrong:** Free-text `notes` is unstructured and unparseable, so downstream code cannot mechanically act on it. **Why D is Wrong:** A 3-level qualitative enum is just confidence-binning under a different name and shares the same calibration problem.

questions.q: A research orchestrator runs three specialist agents in parallel and synthesizes their findings. The team observes that when all three agree, the synthesis is correct ~96% of the time, but when even one agent dissents the synthesis is correct only ~58% of the time. The team wants to use unanimous agreement as a green-light signal. What is the most accurate critique?
o: Three agents is too few; expand to seven to make consensus more reliable.
Unanimous agreement should override any dissent; the dissenter is the noise.

If all three agents share the same prompt and same model, unanimous agreement is *correlated* confirmation, not independent — when they share a blind spot, all three are wrong together. The 96% figure is calibrated against the kinds of cases where this prompt happens to work; deploy it as a heuristic for human-review triage, not as a correctness guarantee.
Unanimous agreement is fine; just track which agents disagree most often and remove them.
questions.e: N agents with the same prompt share the same training-data priors and the same blind spots, so their agreement is *correlated* error, not independent confirmation. The architectural fix is differentiated agents with non-overlapping mandates plus adversarial verification; consensus alone is a triage signal, not a proof. **Why A is Wrong:** More copies of correlated reviewers don't add independence; the marginal correlation of a 7th agent is near zero. **Why B is Wrong:** Dissent is often the *signal*, not the noise — minority-opinion findings frequently identify shared blind spots in the majority. **Why D is Wrong:** Removing the dissenter optimizes for echo chamber; this destroys the calibration value of disagreement.

questions.q: A team submits a 12,000-document batch. After it ends, `request_counts` shows 11,840 succeeded, 120 errored (`invalid_request_error`), 30 errored (server error), and 10 expired. The team's billing dashboard shows charges only for the 11,840 succeeded. What is the correct interpretation and recovery strategy?
o: Errored, canceled, and expired requests are not billed. For the 120 `invalid_request_error` cases, fix the request bodies (likely prompt or schema issues specific to those inputs) and resubmit by `custom_id`; for the 30 server errors, resubmit as-is; for the 10 expired requests, re-queue.
All 12,000 requests are billed because the batch was submitted; the dashboard is delayed.
Cancel any related in-flight batches because the error rate exceeded a 1% threshold.
Resubmit the entire 12,000-document batch with a new prompt to be safe.
questions.e: Anthropic's docs are explicit: only `succeeded` requests are billed within a batch; `errored`, `canceled`, and `expired` are not. The documented recovery pattern is per-state: invalid-request errors require fixing the request body before retry, server errors are retryable as-is, and expired requests need re-queueing — all driven by the `custom_id` join key. **Why B is Wrong:** Anthropic does not bill non-succeeded requests; the dashboard reflects actual billing accurately. **Why C is Wrong:** No 1% threshold exists in the API; 1.3% failure is well within normal operational variance. **Why D is Wrong:** Resubmitting all 12,000 wastes 11,840 successful and already-paid extractions and doubles cost for no benefit.

questions.q: A team builds a code-review architecture with one Claude agent that generates findings, then in the same conversation appends "Now act as a senior reviewer and disprove any finding you cannot defend." The disprove step removes ~3% of findings. They argue this is a low-cost adversarial review. What change would make this review step genuinely independent?
o: The 3% reduction is meaningful; this is a working adversarial pattern.

The same conversation retains generation context, so the "senior reviewer" persona is biased toward defending its own prior findings; 3% is the rate at which the model reverses *itself*, not the rate of incorrect findings.
Adversarial review only works with `extended thinking` enabled.

The disprove step should be applied as a separate API call with a fresh system prompt, fresh user message containing only the findings and the source code, and ideally a different model to break correlated biases.
questions.e: Independent review requires breaking context inheritance: a fresh API invocation with no prior assistant turns, ideally a different system prompt scoping it to disprove the prior findings, and where stakes warrant, a different model entirely to break correlated biases. Anthropic's Code Review architecture implements exactly this pattern. **Why A is Wrong:** A 3% self-reversal rate measures sycophantic editing tolerance, not correctness; it does not validate the architecture. **Why B is Wrong:** Diagnoses the problem correctly but stops short of the architectural fix; the question asks for the most accurate full evaluation including the remedy. **Why C is Wrong:** Extended thinking improves single-pass reasoning depth but still operates within the same instance and context — it is not a substitute for independent review.

questions.q: A team builds an extractor that must always return a JSON object matching a fixed schema. They set `tool_choice: "auto"` and provide one tool definition. They observe ~7% of calls return plain text instead of a tool call. The team is surprised because they assumed providing tools makes the model always call them. Which explanation is correct?
o: The model has a bug when only one tool is provided; use at least two tools.
The tool schema has an error causing the model to fall back to text.

`tool_choice: "auto"` explicitly allows the model to either call a tool OR respond in text; to guarantee a tool call use `tool_choice: "any"` or force a specific tool with `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}`.
The 7% represents rate-limited calls; add retry logic with exponential backoff.
questions.e: `tool_choice: "auto"` is Anthropic's documented default-with-tools behavior: the model may call a tool or respond in text. Guaranteeing a tool call requires `"any"` (must call one of the available tools) or a forced specific tool name. This is a configuration choice, not a bug. **Why A is Wrong:** Single-tool configurations work normally; the behavior is about `tool_choice` mode, not the number of tools. **Why B is Wrong:** A schema error would produce a different failure mode (validation error or malformed call), not a fallback to plain text. **Why D is Wrong:** Rate limiting returns HTTP 429 errors, not plain-text responses in place of tool calls.

questions.q: A team is preparing a 90,000-document overnight extraction batch. A pilot of 100 representative documents on the synchronous Messages API shows ~12% of outputs have a recurring error: line items missing their currency field. They have 3 hours until the batch must submit to meet SLA. What is the right action?
o: Refine the prompt and schema now (add an explicit "currency is required for every line item, infer from header if not specified per line" instruction plus 2–3 few-shot examples), re-pilot on the 100 documents, then submit the full 90,000-document batch — prompt iteration must happen *before* batch submission because there is no in-flight prompt update and validation is asynchronous.
Submit the batch as-is and fix the 12% with a follow-up batch.
Submit the batch and PATCH the prompt mid-flight when the issue manifests at scale.
Skip the pilot and submit directly; 12% is acceptable.
questions.e: The Batches API has no in-flight update endpoint and validates asynchronously; a known 12% defect rate on a 90,000-document batch yields ~10,800 broken extractions before any feedback signal arrives. Anthropic's documented best practice is to dry-run on the synchronous API to debug quality, iterate the prompt to convergence, and only then submit. **Why B is Wrong:** A follow-up batch doubles cost and adds another full processing window of latency for problems already known and fixable now. **Why C is Wrong:** No PATCH/update endpoint exists for in-flight batches; the option fabricates a capability. **Why D is Wrong:** A known 12% defect rate on 90,000 documents is 10,800 broken records; "acceptable" without remediation violates SLA quality requirements.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline retries failed schema validations. After analyzing 30 days of logs, the team finds that retries 1, 2, and 3 succeed at rates 73%, 41%, and 9% respectively for format errors, but 4%, 3%, and 2% for "field not found in source" errors. What is the most defensible retry policy?
o: Always retry 3 times — the marginal success rate is positive on every retry.
Retry up to 5 times because retry-with-feedback is Anthropic's recommended pattern.
Retry 0 times — retries add cost without solving real problems.

Cap retries at 2 for format errors (where marginal benefit is meaningful) and 0 for data-absence errors (where information is genuinely not in the source and retries produce fabrication); detect the error class via the validation message and route accordingly.
questions.e: Anthropic guidance distinguishes transient/format errors (retry with feedback works because the model has the information but produced a malformed shape) from data-absence errors (information is genuinely not in the source; additional attempts only generate more confident fabrications). A 2-3% "success rate" on data-absence retries is fabrication noise, not real recovery. **Why A is Wrong:** A 2-3% success rate on data-absence retries is fabrication noise, not real recovery; treating it as success poisons the dataset. **Why B is Wrong:** Anthropic's pattern recommends retries *with a maximum cap*, never unconditional retries, and explicitly distinguishes when retries are futile. **Why C is Wrong:** Discarding retries entirely sacrifices the 73% recovery on format errors — a real and well-calibrated benefit.

questions.q: A team's PR-review system uses a single Claude agent with a 12-page system prompt that lists every kind of issue to look for. Recall on critical bugs is 81%; the team wants 95%. They are debating between (a) further expanding the prompt to cover more issue types, (b) using extended thinking with `budget_tokens: 12000`, and (c) splitting the work across multiple specialized agents. Which approach is most aligned with Anthropic's documented Code Review architecture?
o: Option (a) — exhaustive prompts are the simplest approach and avoid orchestration overhead.
Option (b) — extended thinking provides the deepest single-pass analysis and is functionally equivalent to multi-agent review.

Option (c) — multiple specialized agents each scoped to a different failure mode (data-handling, off-by-one, API misuse, security) running in parallel, combined with a cross-file integration pass and an adversarial verification step, then aggregate by deduplicating and ranking by severity.
None of the above — recall above 81% is impossible without retraining the base model.
questions.e: Anthropic's Code Review blog documents this exact architecture: multiple specialized agents in parallel rather than one monolithic reviewer, each with a different failure-mode scope to reduce shared blind spots; a cross-file integration pass to surface issues invisible to per-file reviewers; an adversarial verification step where each agent attempts to disprove its own findings; and an aggregation step that deduplicates and ranks by severity. **Why A is Wrong:** A 12-page prompt is already showing diminishing returns; further expansion increases contradictions and hits attention-distribution limits without adding genuinely new perspectives. **Why B is Wrong:** Extended thinking improves single-pass reasoning depth but operates within the same instance, same prompt, and same blind spots — it is not equivalent to independent specialized review. **Why D is Wrong:** Anthropic's reported architecture demonstrably exceeds 81% recall on substantive findings without retraining; the option fabricates a ceiling.

questions.q: A support agent has been running for 47 turns with a customer disputing a charge. To stay under the context budget, the orchestration layer applies progressive summarization every 10 turns, replacing prior turns with a 200-token summary. On turn 48, the agent confidently tells the customer "we'll process your refund as discussed," but the most recent summary reads only "agent acknowledged dispute and discussed refund options with customer." The original turn-12 commitment was "refund of $147.83 to card ending 4412 within 3 business days." What is the most appropriate fix?
o: Raise the summarization interval from every 10 turns to every 20 turns so more raw context is retained between compactions.

Maintain a persistent "case facts" block (refund amount, card last-4, promised timeline, ticket ID) that is extracted on first mention and re-injected verbatim into every prompt, separate from the rolling summary.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so summarization is unnecessary for sessions under 100 turns.
Instruct the summarizer in its system prompt to "preserve all important details" before each compaction step.
questions.e: Progressive summarization reliably loses transactional specifics — exact amounts, dates, account identifiers, and explicit commitments — because summarizers compress toward semantic gist. Extracting transactional facts into a structured block that bypasses summarization preserves them losslessly across the entire session. **Why A is Wrong:** Less frequent summarization only delays the loss; once any summarization occurs, numerical specifics are still vulnerable. It also makes the eventual compaction more lossy because more must be condensed at once. **Why C is Wrong:** Larger context windows exhibit the same recall degradation ("context rot") and do not address the structural problem that summaries discard transactional detail. **Why D is Wrong:** A vague natural-language instruction like "preserve important details" is a prompt-only mitigation that fails unpredictably; the summarizer cannot reliably distinguish which numbers will matter on turn 48 when summarizing turn 12.

questions.q: A lead research agent receives reports from six subagents and concatenates them (in order of completion) into a 78,000-token aggregated input before producing the final synthesis. Evaluation shows the synthesis reliably reflects subagent #1 (early in the input) and subagent #6 (late in the input), but routinely omits findings from subagents #3 and #4 — the middle of the aggregate. Which change most directly addresses this failure mode?
o: Re-run the missing subagents to confirm their findings are reproducible before including them in the synthesis.
Reduce each subagent's report to a 500-token summary so the aggregate fits in 25,000 tokens total.
Have each subagent produce a structured "key findings" header (5–8 bullet claims with source IDs) and prepend all six headers to the top of the aggregated input, with full reports following.
Sort subagent reports alphabetically by topic so position is deterministic across runs.
questions.e: Models reliably attend to the beginning and end of long inputs but degrade in the middle. Hoisting compact key-findings headers to the top of the aggregate guarantees every subagent's claims occupy a high-recall position, while full reports remain available for grounding. **Why A is Wrong:** Reproducibility is not the issue — the findings exist in the input but are positionally disadvantaged. Re-running wastes tokens and budget without changing the geometry that caused the omission. **Why B is Wrong:** Aggressive compression risks dropping the same details the synthesis needs and does not eliminate the middle position; subagents #3 and #4 will still be middle in a smaller aggregate. **Why D is Wrong:** Alphabetical ordering makes position deterministic but does not place high-signal content at boundary positions. Whichever topics fall in the middle still get under-attended.

questions.q: A support agent uses an `order_lookup` tool that returns 43 fields per order (line items, tax breakdowns, fulfillment events, internal warehouse codes, marketing attribution). The agent typically only needs 5 fields (order ID, status, total, ship date, tracking number). After 8 lookups in a session, tool results consume 31% of the context window, and the agent begins missing earlier conversation details. What is the best first remediation?
o: Modify the tool wrapper to project only the 5 required fields by default, with a parameter to opt into the full schema when needed.
Increase the model's context window tier and accept the higher per-call cost as the price of reliability.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to "ignore irrelevant fields in tool results."
After each tool call, run a separate Claude call to summarize the tool output into 200 tokens before appending it to context.
questions.e: Tool-result accumulation is one of the largest sources of context bloat in agent systems. Trimming at the source — projecting only the relevant fields in the tool wrapper — eliminates the bloat deterministically before it ever enters context. This is a programmatic fix that scales linearly with calls. **Why B is Wrong:** A larger window delays the symptom but compounds cost, and recall still degrades over long sessions ("context rot"). It treats the symptom rather than the root cause of irrelevant tokens. **Why C is Wrong:** The model still pays attention cost on tokens it sees, regardless of instructions to ignore them. Prompt-only mitigations cannot reduce token consumption. **Why D is Wrong:** A per-call summarization step adds latency and another LLM dependency that can itself drop critical fields like the tracking number; the verbose data was unnecessary in the first place.

questions.q: A team building a chat agent on the Messages API observes that on the second user turn, the assistant frequently "forgets" facts established in turn 1. Inspection shows the client sends only the most recent user message in each `messages` array, relying on the model's "memory." Which statement correctly characterizes the problem and fix?
o: The Messages API maintains a hidden session cache keyed by API key; the team should pass a `session_id` header so prior turns are auto-loaded.
The team should use the prompt-caching feature, which causes the API to retain prior turns server-side between calls.
The model's context window is shared across recent calls from the same key, so adding a longer `system` prompt restating the facts will resolve the issue.
The Messages API is stateless; every request must include the full prior conversation (all user and assistant turns) in the `messages` array, or earlier facts are not available to the model.
questions.e: Anthropic's Messages API is stateless — the model only sees what is sent in the current request's `messages` array. The "memory" of a conversation is a client-side responsibility: the application must accumulate and resend prior turns. **Why A is Wrong:** There is no `session_id` mechanism on the Messages API and no hidden server-side conversation cache keyed by API key. This option fabricates a feature. **Why B is Wrong:** Prompt caching reduces cost and latency by caching token prefixes, but the client must still send those tokens in each request. Caching does not make the API stateful. **Why C is Wrong:** Restating facts in the system prompt could partly help but is brittle and does not address that assistant turns (decisions, commitments, tool results) are also lost. The structural fix is sending full conversation history.

questions.q: A customer writes: "This is the third time I've contacted you. I want to speak to a human agent now." The agent has full capability to issue the duplicate-shipment refund the customer is requesting and the policy clearly applies. What should the agent do?
o: Acknowledge the frustration, issue the refund immediately since policy permits it, and only escalate if the customer remains dissatisfied after the resolution.
Hand off to a human agent immediately, summarizing the case and the customer's explicit request, even though the agent could resolve it.
Ask one more clarifying question to confirm the refund details before deciding whether to escalate or resolve.
Issue the refund and send confirmation, noting in the ticket that the human-agent request was overridden because the issue was resolvable.
questions.e: An explicit customer request for a human agent is a hard escalation trigger that must be honored regardless of whether the agent could otherwise resolve the issue. Overriding an explicit request — even with a correct outcome — damages trust and violates a clear escalation criterion. **Why A is Wrong:** Resolving despite an explicit human-agent request ignores a hard trigger. The "offer to resolve" pattern applies when the customer is frustrated but has not explicitly requested escalation. **Why C is Wrong:** Asking another question delays handoff and ignores the explicit request, likely intensifying frustration. The trigger is unambiguous and a clarification is not warranted. **Why D is Wrong:** "Overriding" an explicit human-agent request is the worst pattern: it disregards the customer's stated preference and creates a paper trail of policy violation, even when the outcome is correct.

questions.q: A team adds an automated escalation rule: if a sentiment classifier scores the customer's message below −0.6, the agent immediately routes to a human. Post-launch, escalation volume jumps 40%, but human agents report that 60% of escalated cases involved straightforward, in-policy issues the bot could have resolved. Meanwhile, several calmly worded but truly out-of-policy cases were not escalated. What is the underlying problem?
o: Sentiment is a noisy proxy that correlates with frustration but not with whether the issue is resolvable; escalation should be driven by explicit criteria (human request, policy gap, inability to make progress) rather than emotional tone.
The sentiment threshold is too aggressive at −0.6; lowering to −0.8 will fix the false positives.
The sentiment classifier needs to be fine-tuned on customer-support transcripts to improve precision.
Sentiment-based escalation works in principle but should be combined with a self-reported confidence score from the agent.
questions.e: Sentiment measures emotional tone, which is orthogonal to whether a case is within agent capability. A frustrated customer with an in-policy refund should be served, not escalated; a polite customer asking for a policy exception must be escalated. Robust escalation uses explicit, observable criteria rather than affective signals. **Why B is Wrong:** Tuning the threshold trades one error type for another but does not fix the categorical mismatch between sentiment and resolvability. **Why C is Wrong:** A more accurate sentiment classifier still answers the wrong question. Improving classification of an irrelevant signal does not produce a correct escalation decision. **Why D is Wrong:** Self-reported model confidence is itself unreliable as an escalation gate — models are often confidently wrong and uncertainly right. Layering two unreliable proxies does not produce a reliable trigger.

questions.q: A customer asks the support agent to match a competitor's lower price on a TV. The agent's policy document covers price-matching against the company's own past prices and against authorized resellers, but is silent on third-party competitors. The agent confidently quotes a 12% discount based on what "seems consistent with the spirit of the policy." How should the agent's behavior be corrected?
o: Add the competitor price-match scenario to the policy document so the agent has explicit guidance.
Lower the agent's response temperature to 0 to reduce creative interpretation of policy.

Update the system prompt with explicit escalation criteria, including "if a customer asks about a scenario the policy does not address, escalate to a human agent" plus 2–3 few-shot examples covering policy-gap cases.
Instruct the agent to apply policies "conservatively" when there is uncertainty.
questions.e: The agent's failure was treating a policy gap as an interpretation problem. Explicit escalation criteria for policy gaps — paired with few-shot examples that demonstrate the boundary between covered and uncovered scenarios — give the model a concrete pattern to recognize. **Why A is Wrong:** Expanding the policy is a separate business decision that may take weeks; meanwhile the agent will keep improvising on other gaps. The escalation pattern is the architectural fix and applies to all future gaps. **Why B is Wrong:** Temperature 0 makes the wrong behavior deterministic, not correct. The model still lacks instruction that gaps require escalation rather than interpretation. **Why D is Wrong:** "Conservatively" is vague and the model's notion of conservative may still produce a fabricated discount. Without explicit criteria and examples, the abstract instruction fails predictably.

questions.q: A customer provides only the name "Maria Garcia." The customer-lookup tool returns three matching accounts with different emails and order histories. The agent picks the account with the most recent order and proceeds to discuss it. Which response represents the correct pattern?
o: Use a heuristic — most recent order, highest lifetime value, or closest geographic match — to pick the most likely account, since asking for clarification creates friction.
Pick any of the three accounts and proceed; if the customer corrects, the agent can switch accounts mid-conversation.
Escalate immediately to a human agent because account ambiguity is inherently outside agent capability.
Ask the customer for an additional identifier (email, order number, last 4 of payment method, ZIP code) to disambiguate before discussing any account-specific information.
questions.e: Multiple matches create a real ambiguity that no heuristic can safely resolve, because acting on the wrong account exposes account-specific information to a different customer — a privacy and security failure. The correct pattern is requesting one additional identifier, which costs one turn but eliminates ambiguity deterministically. **Why A is Wrong:** Heuristic selection optimizes for friction at the expense of correctness and privacy. "Most recent order" can easily be the wrong Maria Garcia, and the agent will reveal her details to the wrong person. **Why B is Wrong:** Speaking about one account before disambiguation leaks information about that account to a person who may not be its owner. Mid-conversation correction does not undo the disclosure. **Why C is Wrong:** Disambiguation by asking for one more identifier is well within agent capability and does not require human escalation. Escalating here over-uses scarce human capacity.

questions.q: A research subagent's web-search tool intermittently fails. The subagent currently catches all exceptions and returns the string `"search unavailable"` to the lead agent. Downstream, the lead agent cannot distinguish a transient network blip (worth retrying) from an authentication failure (needs config fix) from a query that simply returned zero results. Reports come back with unexplained gaps. What is the right error contract?
o: Have the subagent suppress the error entirely and return an empty result list, so the lead agent treats failures as "no findings."

Return a structured error object including `failure_type` (timeout / auth / rate_limit / empty_result), `attempted_query`, `partial_results` if any, and `suggested_alternatives`, so the lead agent can decide whether to retry, reroute, or annotate.
Have each subagent independently retry up to 50 times with exponential backoff before reporting any failure.
Replace the search tool with a more reliable provider so error-handling logic becomes unnecessary.
questions.e: Generic error strings collapse meaningfully different failure modes into one opaque signal, destroying information the orchestrator needs to act intelligently. A structured error context — failure type, what was attempted, any partial results, suggested alternatives — lets the lead agent route transient failures to retry, surface configuration failures to operators, and treat genuine empty results as legitimate findings. **Why A is Wrong:** Conflating failures with empty results is a silent-suppression anti-pattern: the report will look complete but is missing data the user assumes was searched. **Why C is Wrong:** Aggressive retry without classification wastes budget on permanent failures (auth, malformed query) and delays the lead agent's ability to adapt. **Why D is Wrong:** No provider is perfectly reliable, so error handling cannot be eliminated. This treats the tool as the root cause when the architectural defect is the error contract itself.

questions.q: A subagent calls a document-retrieval API that has a 2% transient timeout rate. Currently, every timeout is propagated up to the lead agent, which then must decide whether to retry, reroute, or fail. Retries from the lead level cost one full round-trip of LLM reasoning each. How should error handling be redesigned?
o: The subagent should locally retry transient failures (timeouts, 5xx) with exponential backoff up to a small bounded limit, propagating to the lead agent only unrecoverable errors with a description of what was attempted and what failed.
The lead agent should retry every error it receives once, regardless of failure type, since most errors at this scale are transient.
The subagent should treat every timeout as a permanent failure and immediately propagate, since retries hide real problems.
Add a third-tier "retry agent" between subagent and lead whose sole responsibility is retry orchestration.
questions.e: The principle is local recovery for recoverable errors, structured propagation for unrecoverable ones. Subagents are closer to the failure and can retry transient issues cheaply, without consuming lead-agent reasoning tokens. When propagation is necessary, the lead agent receives a structured account of attempts and final failure mode so it can make an informed routing decision. **Why B is Wrong:** Blind lead-level retry of every error wastes LLM budget on permanent failures and conflates retryable with non-retryable. **Why C is Wrong:** Propagating every timeout floods the lead with noise and makes the system brittle to normal network jitter. A 2% transient rate is exactly the case bounded local retry was designed for. **Why D is Wrong:** A separate retry agent adds an LLM-mediated hop for what is a deterministic concern. Retry belongs in the data path as code, not as a third agent.

questions.q: A research orchestrator queries an internal knowledge base via a `kb_search` subagent. For one query, the subagent returns `{"results": []}`. The orchestrator treats this identically to "search failed" and re-issues the query through a different subagent, then a third, accumulating cost without progress. Which design correction addresses the root issue?
o: Configure the orchestrator to never retry searches, since the first answer is usually correct.
Have `kb_search` retry internally until at least one result is returned, then propagate.
Introduce a confidence score on every search result and only re-query when confidence is below 0.7.

Have `kb_search` distinguish in its return value between an access failure (timeout, auth, malformed) and a successful query that returned zero matches, so the orchestrator can treat them differently.
questions.e: Zero results from a successful query is a valid finding ("the KB does not contain this") and should not trigger retry. An access failure is a retryable problem with the channel, not the data. Conflating the two leads to wasted retries on real empty results and missed retries on real failures. The fix is at the contract level — the subagent must report which case occurred. **Why A is Wrong:** Never retrying makes the system fragile to genuine transient failures. The defect is conflation, not retry itself. **Why B is Wrong:** Forcing the subagent to keep searching until it finds something will hallucinate or loosen queries until a result appears, corrupting the research. **Why C is Wrong:** A confidence score on results does not distinguish "no documents matched" from "search service unreachable." It addresses a different problem.

questions.q: A team's subagents wrap all tool calls in `try/except Exception: pass` blocks because "we don't want one bad search to crash the whole research run." After three weeks in production, the team notices reports occasionally cite sources that do not exist, and one report claimed comprehensive coverage of a topic when in fact 4 of 7 subagents had silently failed. What pattern is this and how should it be fixed?
o: The subagents need higher timeout values so fewer exceptions occur.
The lead agent should run a self-review pass after synthesis to catch any inconsistencies.

Silent error suppression is an anti-pattern; subagents should propagate structured error context (failure type, attempted operation, partial results) and the lead agent should annotate the final report with coverage information distinguishing well-supported findings from gap areas.
Switch to a single-agent architecture so there are no subagent failures to suppress.
questions.e: Silently suppressing errors makes failures invisible to the orchestrator and to users, producing reports that overstate coverage. The correct pattern combines structured error propagation with explicit coverage annotations on the final report, so users see what was researched well, what was attempted but failed, and what remains a gap. **Why A is Wrong:** Longer timeouts reduce one failure mode but do not address the structural defect of suppressing whatever errors do occur. **Why B is Wrong:** Self-review by the same model that produced the synthesis is unreliable and cannot detect missing data — the model has no way to know what 4 failed subagents would have found. **Why D is Wrong:** Removing parallelism trades throughput and quality for an avoidable problem. Subagent architectures are correct; suppressing their errors is the defect.

questions.q: A developer is using Claude Code to refactor a 180-file Java service. Around the 90-minute mark, Claude begins giving inconsistent answers about which classes implement a given interface, sometimes referencing "typical Spring patterns" rather than the specific classes it had identified earlier. The developer's first instinct is to upgrade to a model with a 1M-token context window. What is the better remediation?
o: Restart the session from scratch and re-explore the codebase, since context-window upgrades only delay the problem.

Maintain a scratchpad file (e.g., `claude-progress.md`) that records key findings — interface implementers, file paths, conventions discovered — and have Claude reference it for subsequent questions, optionally using `/compact` with custom instructions to preserve those findings.
Increase the temperature so the model relies less on memorized patterns and more on the codebase.
Have the developer manually re-paste the full file list at the start of every prompt.
questions.e: Context degradation in long Claude Code sessions ("context rot") is structural — recall decreases as token count grows even within a window's limits. Persisting key findings to a scratchpad file that survives compactions, and using `/compact` with custom instructions to preserve specific facts, addresses the root cause regardless of window size. **Why A is Wrong:** A blank restart loses all prior exploration work. A scratchpad allows resuming with the high-signal findings already captured, which is far more efficient. **Why C is Wrong:** Temperature does not control reliance on memorized patterns versus context. The model defaulted to "typical patterns" because specific findings degraded, not because of sampling stochasticity. **Why D is Wrong:** Manual re-pasting reintroduces the same volume of low-signal tokens that caused degradation. The fix is condensing key findings, not re-injecting raw content.

questions.q: During a 4-hour Claude Code session migrating a database schema, the IDE crashes and the session is lost. The developer had been tracking progress informally in chat. To make future crashes recoverable, which design is best?
o: Periodically have Claude write a structured state manifest (completed steps, pending steps, modified files, commands run, key decisions, unresolved questions) to a project file; on resume, start a fresh session and have Claude load the manifest as its first action.
Disable auto-save in the IDE so partial state is never persisted in a corrupted form.
Keep one extremely long session open indefinitely and never close the IDE, treating session continuity as the recovery strategy.
On crash, attempt to restore the previous session's exact context window from disk cache and resume mid-thought.
questions.e: Crash recovery for long agent sessions is best implemented as structured state export — a manifest the agent can read into a fresh session to bootstrap. This is more robust than session restoration because manifests are smaller, human-readable, and not subject to corruption of token-level state. **Why B is Wrong:** Disabling auto-save addresses one symptom and prevents the manifest pattern itself, since the manifest needs to be persisted regularly. **Why C is Wrong:** Indefinite sessions accumulate context degradation and are still vulnerable to crashes. Session continuity is not a recovery strategy; it is the absence of one. **Why D is Wrong:** Restoring exact context window state is fragile and ties recovery to internal model state that may not be portable across versions. Manifests are the durable abstraction.

questions.q: A Claude Code agent is asked to "find all callers of `processPayment` and assess whether each handles the new `RetryableException`." Naive execution would have the main agent grep, open dozens of files, read each, and accumulate ~60K tokens of source code in its context before any analysis. Which approach best preserves the main agent's context for the higher-level decision?
o: Run the entire exploration in the main agent but ask it to be terse in its narration.
Use prompt caching on the file reads so the tokens cost less and become acceptable.

Spawn a subagent for the exploration phase whose sole task is to grep, read, and return a structured list of `{file, line, handles_retryable: bool, evidence}`; the main agent receives only that summary, not the raw file contents.
Read all files into the main context first, then ask the agent to summarize them in place to free up tokens.
questions.e: Subagent delegation is Anthropic's core pattern for context isolation: the subagent burns its own context window on verbose exploration and returns a compact, structured result. The main agent's context stays focused on coordination and higher-level reasoning. **Why A is Wrong:** Terseness in narration does not reduce the tokens consumed by file reads themselves — those still enter context. The structural problem is unaddressed. **Why B is Wrong:** Prompt caching reduces cost and latency on repeat reads but does not reduce the in-context token footprint. The main agent still pays the attention cost on cached tokens. **Why D is Wrong:** In-context summarization happens after the tokens have already been read, and the summarization step itself can drop critical evidence. Avoiding the bloat at all (via subagent isolation) is strictly better.

questions.q: A developer's Claude Code session is approaching the auto-compaction threshold. They are mid-way through implementing API changes and want to ensure the compaction preserves the specific endpoints modified, the new request schemas, and the open TODO items, while it is acceptable to discard exploratory tangents and earlier discussion of unrelated files. What is the best action?
o: Run `/clear` to fully reset the context and re-explain the task from memory.
Wait for auto-compaction to trigger with default behavior, since auto-compaction is generally well-tuned.
Run `/compact Focus on the API endpoints modified, new request schemas, and remaining TODO items` before auto-compaction triggers.
Switch to a fresh session and copy the relevant parts manually from the prior session into the new one.
questions.e: `/compact` accepts custom instructions that direct the summarizer toward the specific facts the developer needs preserved. Running it proactively — before auto-compaction's default behavior fires — guarantees the right details survive while exploratory content is discarded. **Why A is Wrong:** `/clear` discards everything, including the API changes still in flight. It is appropriate between unrelated tasks, not mid-implementation. **Why B is Wrong:** Default auto-compaction may discard endpoint-specific details since it has no signal that those particular facts matter more than others. Custom instructions are the available control. **Why D is Wrong:** Manual copy-paste is brittle and time-consuming, and it often misses dependencies (helper functions, decisions). The platform offers `/compact` precisely so this manual work is not necessary.

questions.q: An invoice-extraction system reports 97% overall accuracy on a held-out validation set of 10,000 invoices. The product team is satisfied. A customer using the system for international suppliers later reports widespread errors on VAT-line extraction. Investigation reveals: the validation set was 92% domestic invoices (where accuracy is 98.5%), 8% international (where accuracy on the VAT field is 71%). What measurement change is needed?
o: Increase the validation set size from 10,000 to 50,000 to make the aggregate metric more reliable.

Stratify accuracy measurement by document type (domestic vs international, plus other meaningful segments) and by field, with stratum sample sizes large enough to detect failure modes; route the field-level metrics — not the aggregate — to the production dashboard.
Replace the aggregate accuracy metric with a single F1 score, which handles imbalanced classes better.
Continue using aggregate accuracy but add a customer-feedback channel to surface field-level issues retroactively.
questions.e: A 97% aggregate metric masked a 71% failure rate on a specific field within a specific document subtype. Aggregate metrics weighted by population frequency systematically hide poor performance on minority segments. Stratified measurement — by document type and by field — surfaces these failure modes before customers do. **Why A is Wrong:** Larger samples make the aggregate more precise, not more informative. A 50,000-invoice aggregate of 97% will still hide the 71% international VAT subgroup. **Why C is Wrong:** F1 addresses class imbalance in a single classification task; it does not address segment-level differences across document types and field types. **Why D is Wrong:** Customer feedback is a slow, lagging signal that surfaces failures only after revenue impact. Stratified offline measurement should detect them before deployment.

questions.q: A team monitors extraction error rates in production by reviewing a sample of outputs every week. They currently sample 200 random outputs uniformly. The volume is dominated by one document type (85%), and rare document types are almost never sampled — but rare types are where novel errors typically appear first. What sampling change best supports both error-rate measurement and novel-pattern detection?
o: Use stratified random sampling across document types, with each stratum sampled in proportion that ensures statistical power for that stratum (often oversampling rare types relative to their natural frequency, then reweighting for the global error-rate estimate).
Increase the uniform sample to 2,000 per week so rare types are sampled by chance.
Switch to sampling only the rarest document types, since common types are well understood.
Have Claude self-flag outputs it is uncertain about and review only those.
questions.e: Stratified sampling with per-stratum allocation ensures that every meaningful document segment receives enough samples to compute a reliable per-stratum error rate and to surface novel failure patterns. Reweighting by stratum frequency then recovers an unbiased global estimate. **Why B is Wrong:** Even at 2,000 samples, a document type at 0.5% frequency would only contribute ~10 samples — too few for reliable per-stratum estimates and still likely to miss novel patterns. **Why C is Wrong:** Sampling only rare types loses error-rate visibility on the common types that drive most volume and revenue. Both ends matter; stratification covers both. **Why D is Wrong:** Self-flagged uncertainty is an unreliable proxy — models are often confidently wrong on novel patterns precisely because the model has no internal signal that the pattern is novel.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline outputs values for 12 fields per document. Stakeholders need a human review workflow that catches likely errors without reviewing every document. The team has labeled validation data per field and observes that field-level confidence scores from the model, after calibration on the validation set, correlate well with field-level error rates. What is the right human-review design?
o: Send every document to human review, since extraction is too important to trust.
Send a fixed 10% of documents to human review, randomly sampled.
Send documents whose overall (document-level) confidence score falls below 0.85 to review.

Compute calibrated confidence per field; route any extraction to review if any field falls below its field-specific threshold or if multiple sources within the document contradict each other; document-level confidence is not used as the routing signal.
questions.e: Field-level confidence calibrated against labeled data lets thresholds be set per field according to that field's risk profile. Document-level scores average over fields and mask one bad field among eleven good ones — the same masking pathology as aggregate accuracy. Adding contradiction detection catches errors confidence alone misses. **Why A is Wrong:** 100% review eliminates the value of automation. The point is to spend human attention where it provides the most marginal value. **Why B is Wrong:** Random sampling treats every document equally regardless of likely error, missing the bulk of high-risk extractions while wasting reviewer time on obvious low-risk ones. **Why C is Wrong:** Document-level confidence at 0.85 hides field-specific risk. A document where 11 fields are highly confident and 1 critical field is uncertain may still score above 0.85 overall, escaping review.

questions.q: A multi-agent research system synthesizes findings from five subagents into a final report. Each subagent currently returns a free-text prose summary. The final report frequently states claims without traceable sources, and post-hoc citation attempts often hallucinate URLs. What change to subagent output most directly preserves provenance through synthesis?
o: Add a final "citation agent" that reads the report and re-derives citations from web search.
Have each subagent return a free-text summary plus a list of URLs it consulted, appended at the end.

Have each subagent return structured `claim → source` mappings (claim text, source URL, document name, supporting excerpt) that are preserved through the synthesis prompt and rendered into citations in the final report.
Have the lead agent ask the user to verify each claim manually after the report is produced.
questions.e: Provenance is preserved by carrying claim-source bindings as structured data through every stage, not by attempting to recover them after synthesis. When each subagent returns explicit `(claim, source, excerpt)` tuples and the synthesis prompt is designed to retain those bindings, the final report can render grounded citations. **Why A is Wrong:** Post-hoc citation re-derivation is exactly what produces hallucinated URLs — the citation agent has no ground truth for which source actually supported a claim and must guess. **Why B is Wrong:** A bare URL list at the end of a prose summary loses the binding between specific claims and specific sources. The synthesizer cannot tell which URL backs which sentence. **Why D is Wrong:** Pushing verification to the user destroys the value of the system and does not address the architectural defect; provenance should be machine-tracked.

questions.q: Two subagents return conflicting statistics on the same question: the World Bank reports 7.2% for 2023, the IMF reports 6.8% for 2023. The synthesis prompt is currently told to "produce a coherent answer." The final report quotes "approximately 7%" without attribution to either source. A reviewer flags this as misleading. What is the right pattern?
o: Have the synthesis prompt pick the source with higher historical accuracy and quote only that figure.

Annotate the conflict explicitly in the final report ("World Bank reports 7.2%; IMF reports 6.8%; sources differ on methodology") and surface the divergence to the reader rather than collapsing it into a midpoint.
Average the two figures and present the mean as the consensus value.
Drop both figures from the report and replace with a qualitative phrase like "around 7%."
questions.e: Conflicting credible sources on the same quantity reflect real uncertainty — often methodological — that the user needs visibility into. Annotating the conflict with attribution preserves the information that two reputable bodies disagree, which is itself a finding. Arbitrary selection, averaging, or qualitative softening all fabricate a false consensus and erase real epistemic signal. **Why A is Wrong:** "Higher historical accuracy" is rarely available, often domain-dependent, and silently picks one number over another without showing the user the disagreement exists. **Why C is Wrong:** Averaging two methodologically different estimates produces a number neither source endorses and obscures the disagreement. It manufactures false precision. **Why D is Wrong:** Replacing a precise but contested figure with a vague qualitative phrase reduces information content without resolving the conflict, and still hides the divergence from the reader.

questions.q: A research synthesis report flags a "contradiction" between two sources: Source X says "smartphone penetration is 78%" and Source Y says "smartphone penetration is 91%." Investigation shows Source X is from 2019 and Source Y is from 2024 — both correct for their time. The system has no awareness of this. What design change prevents this misinterpretation?
o: Require each subagent's structured output to include `publication_date` and `data_collection_date` per claim, and instruct the synthesis prompt to treat differing temporal coverage as different facts rather than as contradictions.
Drop the older source whenever two sources disagree numerically, since the newer is presumed correct.
Add a disclaimer at the top of every report stating that all figures may be outdated.
Have the synthesis model use its training-data knowledge of typical timeframes to guess which source is more recent.
questions.e: Temporal metadata is critical for synthesis: two figures from different years are not in contradiction — they describe different points in time. Requiring publication and data-collection dates as structured fields on every claim lets the synthesizer represent "78% in 2019, 91% in 2024" as a time series rather than as a conflict. **Why B is Wrong:** Dropping the older source loses historical trend information and makes assumptions ("newer is correct") that are not always true. **Why C is Wrong:** A blanket disclaimer does not help the user reason about specific figures and does not prevent the system from labeling time-shifted measurements as contradictions. **Why D is Wrong:** Guessing dates from training-data priors is unreliable and can be confidently wrong. Dates are observable metadata that should be captured at extraction, not inferred at synthesis.

questions.q: A reporting system aggregates three content types into a single output: financial figures (12 metrics across 4 quarters), news developments (7 narrative items), and technical specifications (a list of 15 named parameters). The current implementation renders all three as flowing prose, and users complain that financial comparisons are hard to follow and technical specs are easy to misread. What is the best fix?
o: Render everything as a single flat bulleted list with one bullet per item.
Apply heavier prose with more transition sentences so the financial and technical sections feel less abrupt.
Use a single Markdown table for the entire report with three columns (financial / news / technical).

Render each content type in the structure that fits it: financial figures as a table (quarters as columns, metrics as rows), news developments as prose paragraphs, and technical specifications as a structured list with parameter names bolded.
questions.e: Different content types have different optimal renderings: tabular data is read best as tables, narrative news is read best as prose, and named-parameter lists are read best as structured lists. Content-type-appropriate rendering is a final-stage formatting decision driven by the data, not a single uniform style. **Why A is Wrong:** Flat bullets destroy the row/column structure of financial data and the narrative flow of news. Uniform rendering is what the question is critiquing, not solving. **Why B is Wrong:** Heavier prose worsens the financial-comparison problem (numbers get harder to scan when buried in sentences) and adds noise to technical specs. **Why C is Wrong:** A three-column shared table forces incompatible content types into the same grid; news paragraphs do not align row-wise with financial metrics or technical parameters.

questions.q: Your support agent requests `lookup_order`, your application executes it and receives the order data, but on the next API call the model requests the identical `lookup_order` call again — and keeps doing so until the process is killed. What is the most likely defect in the agentic loop?
o: The system prompt lacks an instruction telling the model not to repeat tool calls it has already made
The loop is missing an iteration cap, which would have detected the repetition and terminated cleanly
The tool result is never appended to the conversation history, so the model never sees that the call succeeded
The `lookup_order` description is too vague, causing the model to select it repeatedly over other tools
questions.e: The model has no memory between API calls; if an executed tool's result never enters the conversation history, the model cannot learn what happened and typically re-issues the same call — this is the documented symptom of a skipped append step. A is the wrong layer: no prompt wording can compensate for a result the model literally never sees. B is the named anti-pattern of treating a cap as a control mechanism — it would mask the bug, not fix it. D misdiagnoses a loop-plumbing defect as a tool-selection problem; the model is choosing the right tool, it just never receives the result.

questions.q: In your research system, an engineer proposes ending the coordinator's agentic loop whenever the model's response text contains the phrase "research complete." During review you're asked to recommend the correct termination mechanism. What should drive loop exit?
o: Exit the loop when the API response's `stop_reason` field is `"end_turn"` rather than `"tool_use"`
Keep the text check but expand it to a list of completion phrases so paraphrases are also caught
Cap the loop at fifteen iterations, the maximum any research task has needed in testing
Instruct the model to emit a dedicated `DONE` token as its final word and check for that token each turn
questions.e: The `stop_reason` field is the single signal that drives loop control flow: `"end_turn"` means the model is finished, `"tool_use"` means it wants another tool executed. B and D are both variants of the named anti-pattern of parsing natural-language output for termination — the model can say "research complete for phase one" mid-task, and a magic token is still probabilistic text the model may forget or emit early. C is the other named anti-pattern: an iteration cap is only a runaway fail-safe, never the primary stop mechanism.

questions.q: Your Agent SDK productivity assistant is asked to find all callers of a deprecated function. The app sends the request, prints the assistant's opening text ("I'll search the codebase..."), and then exits — the model had requested a Grep call that was never run, and the task never completes. What fix repairs the loop?
o: Raise `max_tokens` so the model can complete the entire search analysis within a single response
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to keep working until the task is fully done
Replace the loop with a decision tree that maps "find callers" queries to a fixed Grep-then-Read tool sequence
Check `stop_reason` after each response and, on `"tool_use"`, run the tool, append the result, and re-call the API
questions.e: The app is skipping the inspect step — it treats every response as final, so the loop goes silent after the model's first tool request; checking `stop_reason` and continuing the cycle (execute, append, re-call) is exactly the missing lifecycle step. A misunderstands the architecture: the model cannot execute Grep itself no matter how many tokens it has. B is a prompt-layer fix for a code-layer defect — the model already wants to continue; the app hangs up on it. C abandons model-driven decision-making for a hardcoded route, which is the documented anti-pattern, not a repair.

questions.q: To hit the 80% first-contact-resolution target more predictably, a teammate proposes classifying each incoming ticket in application code, then programmatically executing a fixed `get_customer` → `lookup_order` → `process_refund` sequence, calling Claude only to word the final reply. What is the key architectural cost of this design?
o: Nothing significant is lost, provided an iteration cap is added as a safety net around the fixed sequence
The system is no longer agentic — hardcoded routing, not model reasoning over accumulated results, chooses each next action
It violates the SDK requirement that every tool invocation must originate from a `stop_reason` of `"tool_use"` in a model response
Tool results can no longer be appended to the conversation history once tools are called from application code
questions.e: Model-driven decision-making over the updated conversation is the defining property of an agentic loop; a pre-configured decision tree handles only the cases its author anticipated, which is precisely what caps first-contact resolution on messy real tickets. A is irrelevant reassurance — a cap is a runaway fail-safe, not a substitute for adaptive reasoning. C invents a nonexistent rule; applications are free to call their own functions, it just isn't agentic. D is false mechanically — nothing stops you from appending results to history; the problem is the model no longer decides what happens next.

questions.q: A bug once caused your research coordinator to loop indefinitely, and the postmortem asks what role a maximum-iteration limit should play going forward. The team is split between "make it the stop mechanism" and "delete it entirely." What is the correct position?
o: Keep `stop_reason: "end_turn"` as the loop's control mechanism, with a generous iteration cap purely as a fail-safe
Tune the cap to the typical number of iterations a research task needs, so it doubles as the primary termination signal
Keep the cap but add a backup check that scans the model's text for completion phrases before the cap is reached
Remove the cap entirely, since a correctly implemented loop always receives `"end_turn"` eventually
questions.e: The documented position is exactly this split role: `end_turn` drives control flow, while a hard cap is acceptable only as a fail-safe against runaway loops — never the primary stop. B converts the fail-safe into the control mechanism, the named anti-pattern, and would truncate legitimately long investigations. C layers on a second anti-pattern, parsing natural-language text for termination. D is too absolute: bugs, adversarial inputs, and pathological states are why the fail-safe exists, as this team's own postmortem demonstrates.

questions.q: Your support coordinator verified a customer's identity with `get_customer` early in the conversation, then spawned a billing-investigation subagent. The subagent immediately tries to re-verify the customer because it has no idea who the customer is. Why?
o: A bug in the Task tool is preventing the SDK's shared-memory layer from replicating to the subagent
