o: Write the schema into the system prompt with detailed formatting instructions, then parse the response text as JSON.
Ask Claude to write a Python script that generates the JSON.
Define a tool whose `input_schema` matches the target schema and have Claude call it with the extracted data as arguments.
Use extended thinking so Claude reasons carefully about the schema before emitting JSON in a code block.
questions.e: "Guarantee schema conformance" disqualifies anything depending on the model following instructions. A tool whose `input_schema` mirrors the target schema makes the extraction a tool call, enforced by the calling mechanism. **A** leaves the schema as prose. **D** makes the model reason harder about the same prose. **B** adds indirection without forcing the script's output to match either.

questions.q: A developer is debugging a failing integration test. They need to (1) search a large codebase for all usages of a deprecated `AuthClient` method, (2) read the relevant test fixtures, and (3) propose a fix. The search returns hundreds of matches across dozens of files, most irrelevant. What best manages the main conversation's context?
o: Run the search directly in the main conversation, then read each matching file there before proposing a fix.
Delegate the entire task to a sub-agent with the prompt "debug the failing integration test."
Increase the context window size and run everything in the main conversation.

Delegate the search to a sub-agent with a prompt specifying the exact method name, the codebase area, and the expected output format, then use the returned summary to decide which files to read directly.
questions.e: The problem is not difficulty; it is that one step produces high-volume, mostly-noise output that would permanently occupy the main context. D isolates the noisy step with a specific brief and keeps the judgment. **B** delegates everything with a vague prompt: the sub-agent starts blank and rediscovers what you know, and you get an opaque answer. **A** keeps the mess. **C** makes room for the mess.

questions.q: A financial services company deploys a customer service agent that can issue refunds. Policy requires any refund over $500 to be escalated to a human; the model must not make that call itself. Testing shows prompt-based instructions produce compliance about 97% of the time. Which implementation satisfies the requirement?
o: Add the policy to `CLAUDE.md` and reinforce it in the system prompt.
Implement a `PreToolUse` hook that inspects the `process_refund` call and blocks it when the amount exceeds $500, routing to the escalation path.
Add the rule to the `process_refund` tool's description, stating that amounts over $500 require human approval.
Strengthen the system prompt with emphatic language: "CRITICAL POLICY: you MUST NEVER issue a refund over $500 without human approval."
questions.e: "97% of the time" is the disqualifier, handed to you deliberately. Three violations per hundred refunds. Every option leaving the decision with the model inherits that 3%. **D** is the emotional trap; capitals change nothing structural. **A** is the same shelf in a different file. **C** is the hard one, because tool descriptions really do beat `CLAUDE.md`. Still an instruction. Nothing physically prevents `process_refund(amount=750)`. C is the best answer on the wrong shelf.

questions.q: A developer needs to add one validation condition (a date-range check) to an existing validator in a single file. The requirement is unambiguous. What is the best approach?
o: Use plan mode to explore the codebase before editing.
Write a test suite first, then implement.
Use extended thinking to reason about edge cases before editing.
questions.e: Small and unambiguous means direct execution. B, C, and D apply real techniques to a two-line change. Over-engineering is punished as hard as under-engineering.

questions.q: A team runs a custom MCP server that exposes prompts named `deploy_checklist` and `incident_response`. How do developers use them in Claude Code?
o: They are automatically prepended to every message sent to the model.
They are registered as tools and invoked by the model when relevant.
questions.e: MCP prompts surface as slash commands, namespaced `/mcp____`. **B** is what resources do, **D** is what tools do, **C** describes the `CLAUDE.md` model.

questions.q: An agent integrates with an MCP server that returns `"Operation failed"` for every error. The agent cannot distinguish transient network issues from permission problems or invalid inputs, so it retries indiscriminately. What is the best fix?
o: Add a retry counter that caps attempts at three.
Instruct the agent in the system prompt to retry only twice before escalating.
Return structured error metadata including `errorCategory`, `isRetryable`, and a human-readable `description`.
Wrap every MCP call in a try/except that escalates to a human on any failure.
questions.e: The agent cannot reason about failures it cannot distinguish. Structured metadata gives it a category to branch on, a retryability flag, and a description it can relay. The wrong answers each fix one dimension. **A** caps waste but leaves the agent unable to explain anything. **B** puts a retry policy in prose with no information to apply it to. **D** escalates every transient blip to a human.

questions.q: During a multi-turn verification flow, an agent asks for the customer's name in turn 1, then asks for it again by turn 3. What is the most likely cause?
o: The conversation history is not being included in subsequent API requests.
The model's context window was exceeded.
The temperature setting is too high.
questions.e: Three turns is nowhere near any limit, so B dies on arithmetic. The model has no memory; it knows only what is in the message list. If your code is not re-sending the full list, every request arrives as a fresh conversation.

questions.q: An API endpoint began returning 500 errors after last night's deploy. The team's documented investigation procedure is always the same: check the error logs, diff the deploy against the previous release, examine the endpoint's handler, then check dependency health. What is the best approach?
o: Give an orchestrator the goal "find out why the endpoint is failing" and let it decide which subtasks to run.
Run all four steps as parallel sub-agents and synthesize the results.
Ask the model to propose its own investigation plan, then approve it before execution.
Specify the four steps as a fixed sequence for the agent to execute in order.
questions.e: The steps are the same every time regardless of what the logs say. That is a fixed plan, and specifying it up front is correct. **A** is the tempting one. An orchestrator will probably get there and will spend tokens rediscovering a procedure the team already wrote down. Adaptive machinery earns its cost only when the path is genuinely unknown. **B** breaks the diagnostic ordering, where each step informs the next. **C** re-derives a plan that already exists. Signal words: *"the standard procedure," "the team always," "in this order."*

questions.q: A developer has spent considerable time having Claude analyze a legacy module, reading the code, mapping dependencies, and identifying tight coupling. They now want to explore two competing refactoring strategies (extract-interface and strangler-fig) and compare the results, without either attempt's reasoning influencing the other. What is the best approach?
o: Run the first approach to completion, then use `/clear` and start the second fresh.
Spawn two sub-agents, one per approach, each prompted with the strategy name.
Use `fork_session` to branch the current session twice, exploring one approach in each branch.
Explore both approaches sequentially in the same conversation, then ask Claude to compare them at the end.
questions.e: Two constraints, each killing a different option. The analysis was expensive, so nothing may discard it. The attempts must not influence each other, so nothing may share one context. **A** satisfies isolation and destroys the analysis. **B** satisfies isolation but a sub-agent starts blank, so a strategy name alone gives it none of the dependency mapping. **D** violates isolation precisely: A's exploration sits in context while B is reasoned about, so the model is anchored and the final comparison is not neutral.

questions.q: A team is adding a real-time notification feature and must choose between WebSockets, server-sent events, and polling. The trade-offs depend on infrastructure constraints and the team wants to weigh in before implementation. What is the best approach?
o: Use plan mode to explore the options and present a recommendation for the team to approve.
Implement WebSockets, as the most capable option, and refactor if needed.
Implement all three behind a feature flag and benchmark them.
Ask Claude to pick one and proceed directly.
questions.e: Architectural trade-off plus a team that wants to weigh in. **B** commits to the most complex option before evaluating constraints. **C** builds all three to answer a question a short investigation settles. **D** removes the human decision the question asked for.

questions.q: A support agent must guarantee that every customer interaction ends either resolved or handed to a human, regardless of how the agent loop terminates. What achieves this?
o: Instruct the agent in the system prompt to always escalate when it cannot resolve an issue.
Have the orchestration layer check the outcome after the loop terminates and programmatically call `escalate_to_human` when the issue is unresolved, passing the accumulated context.
Add a maximum iteration count so the loop cannot run forever.
Give the model an `escalate_to_human` tool and describe carefully when to use it.
questions.e: Hooks fire on tool calls. Guaranteeing how a whole interaction *ends* needs the orchestration layer, which also survives terminations the model did not choose: `max_tokens`, an iteration cap, a crash. **A** and **D** are prose. **C** prevents a runaway loop and says nothing about the outcome; stopping is not resolving.

questions.q: Logs show an agent calling `process_refund` with an `order_id` that was never returned by any prior tool call and does not exist in the system. What is the best fix?
o: Add a line to `CLAUDE.md` instructing Claude never to fabricate parameters.
Update the `process_refund` tool description to state that `order_id` must come from a prior `lookup_order` call and must never be assumed or invented.
questions.e: Fabrication is fixed where the value is produced. The tool description is what the model reads at the moment it decides how to fill the parameter. **C makes it worse.** `required` forces the model to supply a value; without a real one, being required is what pushes it to invent one. `required` constrains shape, not provenance. **A** is a general instruction competing with everything else. **B** misdiagnoses the mechanism.

questions.q: An agent has spent 25 minutes exploring a game engine's rendering subsystem, reading shader code, buffer management, and frame synchronization. An engineer now asks it to understand how the physics engine integrates with rendering for collision debug overlays. You notice recent responses reference "typical rendering patterns" rather than the specific `VulkanPipeline` and `FrameGraph` classes it discovered earlier. What is the most effective approach?
o: Use `/clear` to reset context completely, then start fresh with physics exploration using file paths from the project's `CLAUDE.md`.
Spawn a sub-agent to explore physics independently, then manually synthesize its findings with the rendering knowledge accumulated in the main conversation.
Summarize the key rendering findings, then spawn a sub-agent for physics exploration with that summary in its initial context.
Continue in the current context with more targeted prompts referencing the specific classes by name.
questions.e: Two facts are load-bearing and most people catch only one. Generic language replacing named classes means context has degraded, *and* the new task "integrates with" rendering, so it requires the knowledge being lost. C summarizes while the findings are still partly present, then delegates with that summary in the sub-agent's initial context. **B** is the near-miss: it plans to synthesize against the very knowledge that is degrading, and sends the sub-agent to explore physics *independently* for an *integration* task. **A** deletes 25 minutes of discovery for a task that needs it; file paths are addresses, not findings. **D** treats a symptom as a preference.

questions.q: An agent calls `lookup_order` and receives the order data. How does it determine what to do next?
o: A predefined workflow specifies which tool follows `lookup_order`.
The tool result is appended to the conversation and the model reasons over the full context to choose the next action.
An orchestration layer inspects the tool result and routes to the appropriate next tool.
The tool's own definition declares which tool should be called next.
questions.e: This asks whether you know what makes an agent an agent. The result is appended, the API is called again, and the model chooses over the full context. Nobody wrote those branches. **A** and **D** describe a fixed path, which is a pipeline; D also invents a "next tool" field that does not exist. **C** is the sophisticated trap: if your code picks the next tool, your code is doing the reasoning and the model is a formatter.

questions.q: A developer needs Claude to follow an integration pattern that is documented on the team wiki and used in three existing modules. This is a one-time integration; the pattern is not a general convention. What is the best approach?
o: Add the pattern to `CLAUDE.md` so Claude always knows it.
Create a skill in `.claude/skills/` documenting the pattern.
Use `@` references in the prompt to point Claude at the three existing modules.
Paste the entire wiki page into the system prompt.
questions.e: Durability test: would an unrelated session six months from now benefit from this? No. **A** turns a one-time integration into a permanent convention. **B** is heavier still. **D** adds a volume problem to the durability problem.

questions.q: A generated PDF report has three formatting problems: column widths are wrong, dates render in the wrong format, and page breaks fall in bad places. Column width affects how dates wrap, and page breaks depend on the resulting content height. What is the best approach?
o: Fix one problem at a time, testing the rendered output after each change.
Provide all three specifications in a single prompt so Claude can fix them together and account for the interactions.
Fix the page breaks first, since they depend on everything else.
Rewrite the PDF generation layer from scratch.
questions.e: The three problems interact: column width affects how dates wrap, and page breaks depend on the resulting content height. Interacting problems should be described together in one message so Claude can account for the interactions; sequential fixing is for independent problems. A fixes them in isolation and invites rework when one change undoes another. C starts with the most dependent problem. D is disproportionate.

questions.q: An analyst must digest 12 industry reports of roughly 40 pages each and cite about 6 figures in a client proposal. Which approach is best?
o: One sub-agent reads all 12 reports and returns a summary of the important findings.
Read all 12 reports in the main conversation to retain full detail.

Fan out one sub-agent per report, each briefed with the proposal's argument and instructed to return verbatim figures with the source sentence, report name, and page number; select and write in the main conversation.
Delegate the entire proposal, including the writing, to a single sub-agent.
questions.e: Two seams. Reading 480 pages is volume; choosing the 6 figures and writing is judgment. **A** gets the seam right and chokes the sub-agent, which degrades on its own desk exactly as your context would. It is also under-briefed: an agent that does not know the argument cannot know what "important" means. C also fixes the subtler failure — if output will be quoted downstream, demand verbatim text with provenance, because a paraphrase cited as a source is fabrication in a new outfit, and unverifiable once the sub-agent's context is destroyed.

questions.q: A refund request falls outside the 30-day policy window. The MCP tool rejects it, and the agent retries the call repeatedly, consuming turns without progress. What is the best fix?
o: Return a structured error with `isRetryable: false` and a customer-friendly explanation of why the refund cannot be processed.
Reduce the retry limit to one attempt.
Remove the refund tool from the agent's tool set.
questions.e: A permanent failure must be labelled permanent, and the customer needs to know why. The flag stops the retry loop; the description lets the agent respond usefully. **B** reduces waste and leaves the agent unable to distinguish permanent from transient, so it will under-retry genuine timeouts. **C** removes a capability legitimately needed. **D** paces pointless retries more politely.

questions.q: Which statement about a tool's `input_schema` is accurate?
o: It guarantees the arguments are structurally valid, but not that their values are correct.
It guarantees both the structure and the factual accuracy of the arguments.
It is documentation for developers; the model does not use it.
It replaces the need for a tool description.
questions.e: The schema constrains the shape of the move, not its quality. It guarantees `start_time` is a string, not that it is the right time. **C** is wrong twice: the model does read the schema, and the mechanism enforces it. **D** confuses the two fields.

questions.q: An engineer stores case state as JSON on disk, updating it after every turn, but does not include it in the `messages` array. What does the agent know about the stored state?
o: Nothing. The model only sees what is in the request.
Everything, since the file is in the working directory.
Only the most recently written fields.
It depends on whether the file is referenced in `CLAUDE.md`.
questions.e: The model has no filesystem access. A JSON file on disk is, from its point of view, identical to a file that does not exist. Writing state is half the job; injecting it is what makes it real.

questions.q: A regulated team must retain an audit record of every file the agent modifies, including timestamp and the diff. The record must be complete; a missing entry is an audit finding. What is the best implementation?
o: Instruct the agent in `CLAUDE.md` to log each modification to an audit file after editing.
Give the agent a `write_audit_log` tool and describe in its system prompt when to call it.
Review the conversation transcript at the end of each session and extract the modifications.
A `PostToolUse` hook on file-editing tools that writes the audit record automatically.
questions.e: "Complete; a missing entry is an audit finding" is the disqualifier. Anything relying on the agent remembering to log inherits a failure rate. A `PostToolUse` hook fires automatically after every matching tool call, so the record cannot be skipped. **B** and **A** both leave it to the model. **C** reconstructs after the fact from a transcript that may itself have been compacted, and produces nothing in real time.

questions.q: An authentication library is being upgraded from v2 to v3. The change is breaking and affects roughly 45 files. What is the best approach?
o: Edit files one at a time in the main conversation until the build passes.
Use plan mode to map the affected call sites and the nature of each change before editing.
Delegate the whole upgrade to a sub-agent.
Ask Claude to write a codemod script without inspecting the call sites first.
questions.e: Breaking change across 45 files means map the blast radius first. The risk is missing a call site, not writing the code. **A** discovers problems one compile error at a time and piles every file into context. **C** delegates a judgment-heavy, verification-heavy task. **D** writes a transformation before knowing what needs transforming.

questions.q: A developer's loop terminates as soon as the response contains any text. Users report the agent frequently stops mid-task, acknowledging a request without completing it. What is the cause?
o: The model's `max_tokens` is set too low.
A single response can contain both a text block and a `tool_use` block, so the loop exits before executing the tool.
Conversation history is not being passed correctly.
questions.e: Same mechanism as Q2 seen as a bug report. **A** would truncate mid-sentence, not produce a coherent acknowledgement then stop. **C** causes wrong tool selection. **D** causes amnesia, which is Q11.

questions.q: A team is migrating components from React to Vue and has standardised the procedure. They want it invocable as `/migrate-component` by every developer, and they want improvements to propagate as the team refines it. Where should it live?
o: `.claude/skills/migrate-component/SKILL.md` at the project root, committed to version control.
A shared document on the team wiki that developers paste in when needed.
questions.e: Team scope means project scope means version control. **A** is the personal machine-local location, which contradicts "every developer." **B** loses the `/migrate-component` invocation. **D** drifts immediately.

questions.q: A developer asks an agent to "write comprehensive tests for the payment module." Nobody has yet examined what the module contains, how many units it has, or which paths are already covered. What is the best decomposition?
o: Write the subtask list up front based on the module name, for example tests for the parser, the validator, and the formatter.
Issue it as a single prompt and let the model handle the whole thing in one pass.
Run an exploration pass that inventories the module's units and their dependencies, then derive the test-writing subtasks from that inventory.
Write tests for the largest file first and expand outward.
questions.e: You cannot write the plan up front because the subtasks depend on what is in the module. **A** guesses the units before anyone has looked, so half the list will be wrong. **B** produces shallow coverage of whatever the model saw first, and the tokens spent reading crowd out the tokens for writing. **D** uses file size as a proxy for importance.

questions.q: A `lookup_order` tool returns the complete order object, roughly 50 KB of JSON including full item catalogue data and shipping history, on every call. The agent typically needs only the status and delivery date. The context fills quickly across a multi-order conversation. What is the best fix?
o: Instruct the agent in `CLAUDE.md` to ignore the irrelevant fields.
Summarize each tool result with a separate model call before appending it.
Change the tool implementation to return only the fields the agent needs, adding an optional parameter for callers who need the full object.
questions.e: Fix the volume at the source. The tool controls its own return payload, so trim it there and the bloat never enters any context. **A** is prose against a mechanical problem, and the tokens are already in the context whether the model "ignores" them or not — that is the point people miss. **B** buys space and not signal. **C** adds a model call per tool result, paying latency and cost to clean up a mess the tool could have avoided.

questions.q: A developer needs to find every call site of a specific internal function. They know from experience that the codebase contains about five of them. What is the best approach?
o: Run the search directly in the main conversation.
Delegate the search to a sub-agent to keep the main context clean.
Delegate to three sub-agents searching different directories in parallel.
Use `fork_session` so the search does not pollute the main branch.
questions.e: Delegation has a fixed cost: spinning up an agent, plus writing a detailed brief because it starts blank. For five matches that costs more than it saves. Knowing when *not* to delegate is tested as often as knowing when to. **C** compounds the waste. **D** misuses forking, which is for two independent continuations of expensive context.

questions.q: An agent must diagnose a production incident using a 200 MB application log file. What is the best approach?
o: Read the log file into the conversation so the model has full visibility.
Read the first and last 500 lines and infer what happened between them.
Have the agent run filtering commands against the file (time window, error level, request ID) and bring only the matching lines into context.
Increase the context window and load as much of the log as fits.
questions.e: Never read bulk data into context to search it. Filter where the data lives and bring back only matches. **A** is impossible and would be wrong if it were possible. **B** guesses. **D** is the "bigger window" distractor with extra steps.

questions.q: A customer is entitled to a refund. The agent has verified eligibility and can explain the charge, but `process_refund` times out against a failing backend. What should the agent do?
o: Tell the customer the refund has been processed and close the conversation.
Retry indefinitely with exponential backoff, keeping the conversation open.
Apologize generically and end the conversation.
Explain the billing situation, confirm the customer's eligibility, state that a system problem prevented processing, and offer escalation or a later retry.
questions.e: Report the outcome faithfully: what you understand, that they are eligible, that a system problem blocked it, and a route forward. **A** is the designed trap because everything up to the false claim is correct. The customer finds out days later, and a trust failure sits on top of a technical one. **B** hangs the session. **C** discards genuinely useful information.

questions.q: A developer is implementing a complex graph traversal algorithm with well-defined expected outputs and several tricky edge cases. They expect to iterate several times before it is correct. What is the best approach?
o: Write the test suite first, then have Claude implement until the tests pass, using failures to drive refinement.
Use plan mode to design the algorithm before writing any code.
Implement it directly and add tests afterwards.
Delegate the implementation to a sub-agent with a detailed specification.
questions.e: Well-defined behaviour, edge cases, expected iteration. Tests give the refinement loop an objective signal. **B** designs on paper for a problem whose difficulty surfaces in execution. **C** inverts the order; tests written afterwards encode existing bugs. TDD is right when a question pairs iteration with *verifiable* correctness, not merely because a task is hard.

questions.q: An MCP server exposes the team's architecture decision records as resources. How does a developer bring a specific record into a Claude Code conversation?
o: By invoking a slash command named after the resource.
The model calls a tool to fetch it when it judges the record relevant.
Resources are loaded automatically into every conversation on that server.
questions.e: Resources are `@`-mentioned. **B** is prompts, **C** is tools, **D** invents automatic loading. The distinction to hold: prompts and resources are user-initiated, tools are model-initiated.

questions.q: After your code executes a tool that the model requested, what must it append to the message list before calling the API again?
o: The assistant message containing the `tool_use` block, then a user message containing a `tool_result` block whose `tool_use_id` matches.
Only a user message containing the tool's output as plain text.
Only the `tool_result` block; the assistant's turn is reconstructed by the API.
A system message describing what the tool returned.
questions.e: Both turns are required. The assistant turn carrying the `tool_use` block must be present, and the `tool_result` must carry a matching `tool_use_id`, because a response can contain several tool calls and the results have to be paired. **B** discards the structure the API expects. **C** is wrong: nothing is reconstructed for you; the message list is exactly what you send. **D** invents a mechanism. This is also the mechanical answer to why tool results are permanent. You append; nothing removes.

questions.q: A team must ensure that a specific directory of generated protobuf files is never modified by the agent, under any circumstances. Which mechanism fits best?
o: A `PreToolUse` hook that inspects each edit and blocks writes to that directory.
A `CLAUDE.md` note explaining that the directory is generated and must not be edited.
A `PostToolUse` hook that reverts any change made to that directory.
A `permissions.deny` rule scoped to that path.
questions.e: "Never, under any circumstances" plus a specific path is the exact shape `permissions.deny` exists for. It is declarative, scoped, and needs no code. **A** would work and is more machinery than the situation calls for; hooks are for logic a path rule cannot express. **B** is prose for an absolute prohibition. **C** lets the damage happen and then undoes it, which is not prevention and fails if the revert itself fails.

questions.q: A tool parameter accepts exactly one of four ticket priorities. The model occasionally supplies values outside that set, such as `"urgent"` or `"P0"`. What is the most reliable fix?
o: List the four allowed values in the tool's `description`.
Add an `enum` constraint listing the four values in the parameter's schema.
Add a note to `CLAUDE.md` listing the allowed priorities.
Validate the value in the tool implementation and return an error for invalid input.
questions.e: An `enum` in the schema makes an out-of-set value structurally invalid, so it is constrained rather than discouraged. **A** and **C** are prose. **D** catches the problem after the call is made; useful as defence in depth, but the schema prevents it in the first place. Contrast with Q44: `enum` works here because the valid set is small and closed.

questions.q: Midway through a long refactoring session, context compaction fires. The agent's subsequent responses describe the module's structure in general terms rather than referring to the specific classes it mapped earlier. The refactor is half-complete. What is the best next step?
o: Continue, since the agent still has the general shape of the problem.
Use `/clear` and restart the refactor from the beginning.
Re-establish the specifics from durable sources — the actual files and the diff so far — and capture the current state as a compact written artifact before continuing.
Increase the context window and re-run the earlier exploration prompts.
questions.e: The specifics are gone from context; the durable sources are the files themselves and the diff. Re-establish from those, and capture the state as a written artifact so the next compaction does not cost the same again. **A** proceeds on a degraded picture, which is how half-finished refactors go wrong. **B** throws away completed work. **D** re-runs exploration to rebuild what will be evicted again, and the window is not the underlying issue.

questions.q: A researcher needs current information on three unrelated topics: a competitor's pricing model, a regulatory change, and a technology benchmark. Each requires reading many sources. What is the best approach?
o: Research all three sequentially in the main conversation.
Spawn one sub-agent with all three topics in a single prompt.
Use `fork_session` three times, one branch per topic.
Spawn three sub-agents concurrently, each briefed on one topic with the specific question and required output format, then synthesize their returns.
questions.e: Three independent topics, each high-volume, none needing the others. That is the parallel fan-out case: separate contexts, concurrent execution, wall-clock equal to the slowest. **A** serialises and pollutes. **B** puts all three on one desk and produces shallower work on each. **C** misuses forking; the topics are unrelated, so there is no shared context worth duplicating.

questions.q: Before modifying a caching layer, a developer needs to understand how it works. The implementation spans about 15 files. What is the most context-efficient approach?
o: Read all 15 files in the main conversation, then make the change.

Have a sub-agent survey the subsystem and return a structured map (entry points, key scheme, invalidation triggers, file ownership, with file/line references), then read in full only the files that will be edited.
Delegate the whole task, including the modification, to a sub-agent.
Read the two largest files and infer the rest.
questions.e: Survey with a sub-agent, then read in full only what you will edit. **A** is the context pollution failure. **C** over-delegates the judgment step. **D** guesses; file size does not track architectural importance. Brief matters: "summarise the caching layer" returns prose. Ask for entry points, key scheme, invalidation triggers, ownership, with file/line references.

questions.q: Which approach most reliably identifies conversations that genuinely require a human agent?
o: Escalate after three consecutive tool failures.
Run sentiment analysis on the customer's messages and escalate on negative sentiment.
Maintain a rules engine mapping request types to escalation decisions.

Give the model explicit criteria — the customer has asked for a human, the request requires a policy exception, several exchanges have produced no substantive progress, the situation exceeds the available tools — and let it judge.
questions.e: Criteria plus judgment. **A** is rigid in both directions: three transient timeouts do not need a human, and one policy-exception request does with zero failures. **B** is a proxy for distress, not for need, and misses the calm customer with an unresolvable problem. **C** cannot handle what its authors did not anticipate. Hold the distinction against Q15: whether *this case* escalates is judgment, so the model decides. Whether *any* interaction may end unresolved is a guarantee, so code decides.

questions.q: A project's `CLAUDE.md` has grown to 800 lines over a year, accumulating notes from completed migrations, one-off debugging sessions, and superseded conventions. Developers report the agent increasingly ignores rules that used to work. What is the best response?
o: Add a line at the top instructing the agent to read the whole file carefully.
Prune it to the conventions that still apply, and move task-specific material out to skills or `@` references.
Split it into several `CLAUDE.md` files in subdirectories.
Convert the whole file into a `PreToolUse` hook so the rules are enforced.
questions.e: `CLAUDE.md` is always-on context, so everything in it competes for attention with everything else. Stale material does not sit inertly; it dilutes the rules that still matter. Prune, and move task-specific content to skills or `@` references. **A** adds another line to a file already too long to attend to. **C** relocates the volume. **D** misapplies hooks to preferences, which is the Q1 error.

questions.q: A `schedule_meeting` tool has a `duration_minutes` parameter typed as an integer. The model calls it with `duration_minutes: 4000`, which is structurally valid but exceeds any sensible booking. What prevents this?
o: Nothing needed; the `input_schema` already rejects out-of-range values.
Range validation in the tool implementation (or `minimum`/`maximum` in the schema), returning a structured error the agent can act on.
A stronger tool description explaining that meetings are usually under two hours.
questions.e: Range is a value property, not a shape property. `4000` is a perfectly legal integer. Either add `minimum`/`maximum` to the schema or validate in the implementation and return a structured error the agent can act on. **A** is the misconception the question targets: a bare `integer` type accepts any integer. **C** is prose against a value constraint. **D** misdiagnoses. This is the practical face of Q23: schemas guarantee structure, not correctness.

questions.q: An API response returns with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. What does this indicate and how should the loop handle it?
o: The model finished its turn normally; treat it like `end_turn`.
The input exceeded the context window; the conversation must be trimmed.
The model wants to use a tool but ran out of room; execute the partial tool call.
The output hit the token limit and may be truncated mid-content or mid-tool-call; the loop must handle it as an incomplete response rather than a completed turn.
questions.e: `max_tokens` means the response was cut off. It may end mid-sentence or mid-tool-call, so the content cannot be trusted as complete. **A** is the dangerous misread: treating it as `end_turn` ships a truncated answer as final. **B** confuses output limit with input window. **C** is worse than A, because executing a partially-generated tool call means acting on incomplete arguments.

questions.q: A developer has already read a large configuration file in the main conversation and now wants a sub-agent to analyze it. What must they do?
o: Pass the file path or the relevant content in the sub-agent's prompt, because the sub-agent starts with no knowledge of what the main conversation has read.
Nothing; the sub-agent inherits the main conversation's context.
Use `fork_session` instead, since sub-agents cannot read files.
Reference the file in `CLAUDE.md` so all agents can see it.
questions.e: Sub-agents start blank. Nothing is inherited. **B** is the misconception being tested. **C** is false; sub-agents have tools. **D** misunderstands `CLAUDE.md`, which injects its own text, not arbitrary files it names.

questions.q: A developer notices that each successive step of a long agent session takes longer and costs more than the last, even though the individual tasks are comparable in size. What explains this?
o: The model slows down as it approaches its context limit.
Tool execution latency increases with the number of tools registered.
The entire accumulated message list, including every prior tool result, is re-sent on every request, so input size grows monotonically through the session.
questions.e: Every request re-sends the whole accumulated list, so input grows monotonically and each step costs more than the last. **A** attributes it to the model rather than to what you are sending. **B** confuses output budget with input size. **C** is not the dominant effect. Same mechanism as Q3, Q30, and Q36, seen through the billing.

questions.q: A `PreToolUse` hook blocks a tool call the model attempted. What happens from the model's perspective?
o: The model receives the block as a result it can reason about, and can then choose a different action such as escalating or explaining the limitation.
The model never learns the call was attempted and silently continues.
The model automatically retries the same call until the hook allows it.
questions.e: A blocked call comes back as a result the model can reason about, so it can adapt: explain the limitation, escalate, or choose another route. The guarantee holds without the session dying. **B** would leave the model believing an action succeeded, which is worse than blocking. **C** is disproportionate. **D** describes a loop the hook would keep refusing.

questions.q: A developer is extracting a shared utility out of three modules. The behaviour must not change, and the project has a comprehensive test suite covering those modules. What is the best approach?
o: Write new tests for the extracted utility before starting.
Use plan mode to design the extraction, then implement and rely on the existing suite passing unchanged as the correctness gate.
Refactor and manually inspect the diff for behaviour changes.
Delegate the refactor to a sub-agent and review only its summary.
questions.e: Behaviour must not change and a comprehensive suite already covers the modules, so the suite passing unchanged is the strongest available correctness signal. Plan mode handles the multi-module extraction. **A** inverts it: new tests written against your extracted design can pass while behaviour has shifted. The existing tests are the ones that encode the old behaviour. **C** relies on reading a diff for semantic changes. **D** reviews a summary of a change you must verify.

questions.q: A team connects an MCP server exposing 40 tools, most irrelevant to their daily work. Tool-selection accuracy drops noticeably. What is the best response?
o: Accept it; more tools always means more capability.
Add usage examples to all 40 tool descriptions.
Increase the context window to accommodate the larger tool definitions.
Limit the exposed tool set to the subset the team actually uses, so the model chooses among relevant options.
questions.e: Tool-selection accuracy falls as irrelevant options crowd the choice. Exposing the subset actually used removes the noise at the source. **A** is the "more is better" fallacy the question tests. **B** improves each description while the model still chooses among 40. **C** is the window distractor; the problem is selection difficulty, not space.

questions.q: A developer wants to guarantee that a particular request produces a call to `record_calendar_event` rather than a text reply. Which setting achieves this?
o: Listing `record_calendar_event` as the only tool and relying on the description.
questions.e: Only naming a specific tool forces that call. **A** lets the model reply with text instead. **B** forces *some* tool call but not this one, which matters as soon as a second tool exists. **D** relies on the model choosing to call it, which is the thing you wanted to guarantee. `tool_choice` is the most-missed piece of schema-based extraction.

questions.q: Which of the following most clearly justifies breaking a task into multiple explicit phases rather than running it as one pass?
o: The task feels large and important.
An early phase produces high-volume output that later phases will not fully use, or a later phase's content depends on what an earlier phase discovers.
Multiple phases always produce higher-quality output than a single pass.
questions.e: Phases have a real cost: each boundary is a handoff, and handoffs lose information. Volume isolation and genuine dependency are two of the reasons that pay for it. Human approval and parallelisable subtasks are the others. **A** and **C** are preference, not justification. **D** is false; a small task that one pass handles cleanly should be one pass.

questions.q: A sub-agent returns a competitor's headline pricing figure that contradicts a number the developer saw in the source document last week. What is the best response?
o: Trust the sub-agent, since it read the source more recently.
Trust the developer's memory and discard the sub-agent's figure.
Re-run the sub-agent with instructions to return the verbatim sentence and page reference, then check that against the source directly.
questions.e: The disagreement is not resolvable by picking a side, because you cannot audit the sub-agent's reasoning — its context is gone. Re-run demanding the verbatim sentence and page, then check the source. **A** and **B** both guess. **D** invents a number that appears nowhere. This is the practical consequence of Q21: provenance is what makes a delegated finding checkable.

questions.q: Late in a long session, an agent describes the contents of a file it read 40 turns earlier, and the description is subtly wrong in ways it was not at the time. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The earlier tool result has been evicted or compacted out of the context, so the model is reconstructing from general expectation rather than from the text.
The model's training data conflicts with the file.
questions.e: The tool result has been evicted or compacted, so the model reconstructs from general expectation. The tell is the same as Q17: plausible, generic, subtly wrong. **A** is possible but does not explain a description that was accurate 40 turns ago degrading now. **C** does not produce this pattern. **D** misattributes to training data what is a context problem.

questions.q: Which error category most appropriately warrants a retry with exponential backoff?
o: A validation failure caused by a malformed argument.
A permission denial from the upstream system.
A transient failure such as a network timeout or an upstream service returning 503.
A business-rule rejection such as a request falling outside a policy window.
questions.e: Backoff suits failures that may succeed later. **A**, **B**, and **D** are all permanent for the given input: malformed arguments, denied permissions, and policy rejections do not become valid by waiting. Retrying them is the waste Q22 describes.

questions.q: A developer prefers verbose commit messages and a particular terminal workflow. Their team has separate, agreed conventions for the repository's code style. Where should each live?
o: Both in the developer's personal settings.
The personal preferences in the developer's own user-level configuration, the team conventions in project-level configuration committed to the repository.
The personal preferences in project configuration so teammates can adopt them, the team conventions in each developer's user settings.
questions.e: Personal preferences belong in user-level configuration; team agreements belong in project configuration under version control, where they apply to everyone and change through review. **D** inverts both. **A** imposes one developer's habits on the team. **B** leaves team conventions un-shared and drifting.

questions.q: A single API response contains three `tool_use` blocks. How should the loop handle it?
o: Execute the first tool and discard the rest.
Execute all three and send each `tool_result` as its own separate user message.
Reject the response as malformed and retry the request.
Execute all three and append the three `tool_result` blocks in a single user message before calling the API again.
questions.e: Parallel tool use is normal. Execute every block and return all results together in one user message, each keyed to its `tool_use_id`. **A** silently drops work the model is waiting on. **B** breaks the pairing the API expects. **C** treats a documented feature as an error.

questions.q: A team is drawing up requirements for an agent. Which requirement belongs in code rather than in prose instructions?
o: The agent should prefer the team's internal HTTP client over `fetch`.
The agent should write commit messages in the imperative mood.
The agent must never transmit customer records to an endpoint outside the approved allowlist.
The agent should generally explain its reasoning before making large changes.
questions.e: The security boundary is the only one where a violation is unacceptable rather than undesirable. It needs `permissions.deny` or a `PreToolUse` hook. **A**, **B**, and **D** are all preferences: real, worth writing down, and appropriately left to the model's judgment in `CLAUDE.md`. Note that A is *strongly* worded and still a preference; the sorting test is the consequence of a violation, not the force of the phrasing.

questions.q: A bug report describes incorrect output, but the developer has not been able to reproduce it locally. What should the agent be directed to do first?
o: Read the relevant code and propose the most likely fix.
Add defensive error handling around the suspect area.
Rewrite the module to eliminate the class of bug.
Establish a reliable reproduction, a failing test or a concrete input that triggers the behaviour, before attempting any fix.
questions.e: Without a reproduction you cannot confirm the bug exists as described, cannot know whether a change fixed it, and cannot prevent regression. **A** produces a plausible fix for a bug you cannot verify was ever fixed. **B** masks symptoms and can hide the fault. **C** is disproportionate and may reintroduce the bug in new form.

questions.q: An agent must process incoming support emails. Each email falls into one of four known categories — billing, technical, account access, or general enquiry — and each category has a distinct, well-defined handling procedure. Which pattern fits best?
o: A single prompt handling all four categories.
Routing: classify the email, then dispatch to the fixed procedure for that category.
An orchestrator that decides the subtasks at runtime for every email.
A fixed chain running all four procedures in sequence.
questions.e: Four known categories, each with a distinct fixed procedure: classify, then dispatch (routing). The variability is in which path is taken, not in what the path contains. A flattens four distinct procedures into one prompt. C re-derives at runtime a decision the categories already settle, paying orchestration cost for nothing. D runs procedures that do not apply.

questions.q: When the order system is briefly unavailable, the lookup tool returns the text "Operation failed". The agent then either retries many times or tells the customer the order doesn't exist. How should the tool be redesigned?
o: Return a structured error giving the kind of failure, whether a retry makes sense, and a short explanation
Return an empty result whenever the order system is unavailable, so the agent moves on to its next step
Retry inside the tool until the order system responds, so the agent never has to see a failure
Add a line to the system prompt telling the agent to retry three times after any tool failure
questions.e: A. The agent can only respond sensibly if it can tell a temporary outage from "not found". Give it the category and whether to retry. An empty result (B) looks the same as a real "no such order".

questions.q: You need to decide when the agent hands a ticket to a human. Which rule is the most reliable?
o: Escalate when a sentiment score on the customer's messages shows that they are upset or frustrated
Escalate when the customer asks for a person, policy doesn't cover it, or the agent is stuck
Escalate when the agent rates its own confidence in resolving the ticket at below seventy per cent
Escalate any conversation that goes past five turns without the ticket being marked as resolved
questions.e: B. Clear, checkable conditions work best. An upset customer may have a simple problem the agent can fix, and a model's rating of its own confidence (C) isn't a dependable signal.

questions.q: In long conversations the history is summarised to save space. Afterwards, the agent refers to "your recent order" and has lost the order number and the refund amount the customer gave earlier. What is the best fix?
o: Stop summarising altogether, and keep the whole conversation history in every request sent to the model
Have the agent ask the customer to repeat the order number and amount whenever they're needed
Tell the summariser to write longer summaries that try to keep more of the conversation's detail
Keep order numbers, amounts and dates in a separate block that is always sent, never summarised
questions.e: D. Summaries lose exact values. Keep the facts that must stay precise in their own block, outside the part that gets compressed. Keeping everything (A) only delays the problem.

questions.q: When the agent escalates, the human agent can't see the conversation. What should the handoff contain?
o: A structured summary: customer ID, the issue, findings, actions already taken, and a recommended next step
The full raw transcript of the conversation, including every tool call and tool result along the way
A one-line note saying the customer needs help, plus a link to the customer's account page
The customer's sentiment score, the number of turns so far, and the time the conversation started
questions.e: A. The person picking it up needs enough to act without re-asking the customer. A raw transcript (B) makes them dig for it, and one line (C) makes them start again.

questions.q: The coordinator calls the synthesis subagent with the instruction "synthesise the findings". What comes back is generic and ignores what the search and analysis subagents found. What is the most likely cause?
o: The synthesis subagent is running on a model that isn't capable enough to combine findings from several sources
Subagents can't see the coordinator's conversation, so the findings must be passed explicitly in the subagent's instructions
The synthesis subagent's system prompt is too short to explain how findings should be combined into a summary
The search subagent returned its results in a format that the synthesis subagent wasn't able to read
questions.e: B. A subagent starts with only what it's given. Anything it needs (the findings, the goal, the output format) has to be in the task the coordinator hands over.

questions.q: The coordinator sends five independent research questions to the search subagent one after another, waiting for each to finish. A run takes 12 minutes. What is the best way to speed it up?
o: Have the coordinator start all five subagent tasks in the same turn, so that they run in parallel
Put all five questions into a single subagent task, so that only one subagent has to start
Switch the search subagent to a smaller, faster model, so that each of the five searches finishes sooner
Limit each search to its top two results, so that every subagent has less material to read
questions.e: A. Independent tasks can run side by side. One combined task (B) fills a single context with five topics, and the cuts in C and D trade away quality.

questions.q: The final report gives statistics with no sources, and in one place it quietly picks one of two conflicting figures. What change fixes this at the design level?
o: Tell the report writer to add a list of citations at the end of every report it produces
Have subagents return findings as claim-and-source pairs, kept through synthesis, with conflicts flagged and not resolved silently
Use a more capable model for the report writer, so that it attributes statistics to sources more reliably
Run the search step twice for every question, and keep only the figures that match in both runs
questions.e: B. Source details are lost at each handoff unless they're carried as data. The report writer (A) can't cite what it was never given.

questions.q: Every subagent has been given the full set of 18 tools. The document-analysis subagent sometimes wanders off to run web searches, and tool selection has become less accurate across the system. What is the best fix?
o: Add a line to each subagent's prompt that lists the tools it has but shouldn't use
Write longer, more detailed descriptions for all 18 tools, so each subagent can tell them apart
Give each subagent only the tools its own role needs, and remove the rest from its set
Have the coordinator choose the tool for every step, and tell each subagent which one to call
questions.e: C. Fewer, role-specific tools make selection more reliable and keep each subagent on its job. Asking it not to use tools it can see (A) is weaker than not offering them.

questions.q: The CI job needs Claude Code's review findings in a form a script can read, so each finding can be posted as an inline comment on the right file and line. What is the best approach?
o: Run it in interactive mode, and have the script copy the findings from the terminal output afterwards
Run it in non-interactive mode (-p) with JSON output and a defined structure for each finding
Ask for the review as Markdown, and have the script extract each finding with regular expressions
Have Claude Code write its findings into CLAUDE.md, and have the script read them from there
questions.e: B. Automation needs non-interactive mode and structured output it can parse. Scraping free text (C) breaks whenever the wording changes.

questions.q: In the nightly job, the same Claude Code session that writes new tests is then asked to review them. It almost never finds a problem. What is the best change?
o: Ask the same session to review the tests a second time before the job finishes
Add an instruction to the review step that tells the session to be more critical
Run the review in a separate session that doesn't have the writing session's context
Use a more capable model tier for the review step than for the writing step
questions.e: C. A session that made the decisions tends to agree with them. A fresh session judges the result without the reasoning that produced it.

questions.q: The review bot posts many comments about style and minor preferences. Developers have started ignoring all of them, including the real bugs. What is the best fix to the review prompt?
o: Add an instruction to report only the issues that the bot is highly confident about
Add an instruction to be conservative, and to avoid commenting unless it is really necessary
Limit the bot to three comments on each pull request, whatever it finds in the changes
Say what to report (bugs, security problems) and what to skip (style, naming), with examples
questions.e: D. Specific categories and examples change what gets reported. Vague instructions such as "be conservative" (A, B) don't tell the model where the line is.

questions.q: The CI job ignores the team's testing conventions. On one developer's machine Claude Code follows them, because they wrote the conventions into their personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. What is the right fix?
o: Copy that developer's personal CLAUDE.md onto the CI machine, so the job picks it up
Paste the conventions into the CI job's prompt, so they're sent with every review request
Ask every developer to add the same conventions to their own personal CLAUDE.md file
Put the conventions in the project's CLAUDE.md, committed to the repository for CI and every developer
questions.e: D. Personal settings apply to one person's machine. Team conventions belong in the project file, under version control, where every environment picks them up.

questions.q: Before implementing a feature, a developer asks Claude Code to work out how authentication flows through the codebase. The main session fills up with file contents, and the quality of the later coding work drops. What is the best approach?
o: Hand the investigation to a subagent that explores in its own context and returns a short summary
Ask Claude to read every relevant file in the main session first, then clear the conversation before it starts coding
Raise the output token limit for the main session, so it has more room for the files it reads
Tell Claude to read only the first fifty lines of each file, so that less context is used
questions.e: A. A subagent does the reading in a separate context and passes back only the conclusions. Clearing the conversation (B) throws away the findings along with the clutter.

questions.q: Claude has generated a data-transformation function. The developer has described the requirements in prose twice, and it still gets the same edge cases wrong (empty values and mixed date formats). What is the most effective next step?
o: Rewrite the description a third time, with more emphasis on the edge cases that are still being missed
Ask Claude to think harder about the edge cases, and to check its own work before it responds
Switch to a more capable model, and submit the same written description of the requirements once more
Give two or three concrete input and expected-output examples, or failing tests, that cover those edge cases
questions.e: D. When prose has failed twice, concrete examples or tests remove the ambiguity. They also give Claude something to run and check against.

questions.q: The agent needs to find every place the function processRefund is called across the repository. Which approach should it take?
o: Use Glob with a pattern that matches the function name across every source folder in the repository
Use Grep to search file contents for the function name, then Read the files that matter most
Use Read on each source file in turn, and look for the function name in the returned text
Use Bash to print every file to the terminal, and scan the combined output for the name
questions.e: B. Grep searches inside files, and Glob matches file names and paths. Reading every file (C, D) works but fills the context with content that isn't needed.

questions.q: The team shares an MCP server for the issue tracker. Every developer should get it automatically, and each one has their own API token. How should it be configured?
o: Add the server to each developer's user-level configuration, with their own token written into that file
Commit the server to the project's .mcp.json, with every developer's token listed in the same file
Commit the server to the project's .mcp.json, and reference the token through an environment variable
Hard-code one shared team token in the server's source code, and commit that to the repository
questions.e: C. The project file shares the server definition, and the environment variable keeps each person's token out of version control. User-level configuration (A) works but has to be set up by hand for every developer.

questions.q: You're writing the agent's main loop directly against the API. How should the loop decide when the task is finished?
o: Stop when the response's stop_reason is end_turn, and keep going while it is tool_use
Stop when the assistant's text contains a phrase such as "task complete" or "I'm done"
Stop after a fixed number of turns, whatever the response's stop_reason or content says
Stop when a response contains any text block, and keep going while it contains none
questions.e: A. stop_reason is the reliable signal. Claude often writes text alongside a tool call, so D ends too early, and a fixed turn count (C) is only useful as a safety limit on top.

questions.q: During a long session exploring a legacy system, the agent's answers become vague. It talks about "typical patterns" where earlier it named the specific classes it had found. What is the best fix?
o: Have the agent re-read every file it opened earlier, each time the user asks a new question
Have the agent answer from general knowledge of the framework when earlier findings have dropped out of context
Have the user restate the important findings at the start of each new question they ask
Have the agent record key findings in a notes file, and re-read it after context is compacted
questions.e: D. Specific findings are lost when a long history is compressed. A notes file keeps them outside the conversation, where the agent can reload them.

questions.q: Yesterday a developer used the assistant to analyse a module in depth. Today they want to try two different refactoring approaches, both starting from that analysis. What is the best way to set this up?
o: Start two new sessions, and ask each one to redo the analysis before trying its approach
Resume yesterday's session, and try both approaches one after the other in the same conversation
Fork yesterday's session into two branches, so each approach starts from the same analysis
Paste a summary of yesterday's analysis into two new sessions, and try one approach in each
questions.e: C. Forking keeps the full analysis and gives each approach its own branch. Trying both in one conversation (B) lets the first attempt influence the second.

questions.q: Downstream systems need every extraction to match the JSON schema exactly. Which approach gives the strongest guarantee about the structure of the output?
o: Describe the JSON format in detail in the prompt, and ask Claude to follow it exactly
Define the schema as a tool's input schema, and require Claude to call that tool
Give three example outputs in the prompt, and ask Claude to match their structure
Ask for JSON in the prompt, and run a repair step on anything that fails to parse
questions.e: B. Requiring a tool call with a defined input schema constrains the structure of the output. Instructions and examples (A, C) improve the odds but don't guarantee it.

questions.q: Some invoices have no purchase order number. The schema marks that field as required, and Claude sometimes fills it with an invented number. What is the best fix?
o: Add an instruction that tells Claude never to invent values for fields it can't find
Keep the field required, and have reviewers check the purchase order number on every invoice
Make the field nullable in the schema, so Claude can return null when no value exists
Remove the field from the schema, and collect purchase order numbers through a separate manual process
questions.e: C. A required field with no way to say "not present" pushes the model to fill it with something. Allowing null gives it an honest answer to return.

questions.q: An extraction passes schema validation, but its line items don't add up to the invoice total. What is the best way to handle this?
o: Send the document back with the failed extraction and the mismatch, and ask for a correction
Send the same request again unchanged, up to three times, until the totals happen to match
Tighten the JSON schema with stricter types, so that mismatched totals are rejected as invalid
Accept the extraction as it is, and let the downstream finance system catch the mismatch later
questions.e: A. A schema checks structure, not whether the numbers make sense, so this needs a check in code. Retrying with the specific error gives Claude what it needs to correct it, which a blind retry (B) doesn't.

questions.q: Overall extraction accuracy is 97%, and the business wants to cut the amount of human review. What should you do before reducing it?
o: Review a random five per cent of all extractions, and send everything else straight through automatically
Stop human review altogether, since overall accuracy is already above the target the business agreed
Review only the documents where Claude says in its output that it found the task difficult
Check accuracy by document type and field, then send the weaker categories to human review
questions.e: D. An overall figure can hide a document type or field that performs badly. Measure by segment, then keep review where the errors actually are.

questions.q: You send 10,000 archived contracts through the Message Batches API. 300 requests fail because the documents are too long. What is the best way to handle the failures?
o: Resubmit the whole batch of ten thousand, with a higher output token limit set on every request
Find the failed requests by their custom IDs, split those documents into parts, and resubmit only those
Drop the three hundred failed documents, since ninety-seven per cent of the batch came back fine
Move all ten thousand documents to real-time calls, so that failures can be seen as they happen
questions.e: B. The custom ID on each request tells you exactly which documents failed. Fix those and resubmit them alone, without paying again for the 9,700 that worked.

questions.q: The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines covering testing, API style and deployment. All of it applies across the whole repository. The team wants it easier to maintain, without changing what Claude Code loads. What is the best approach?
o: Split it into topic files under .claude/commands, which are loaded alongside CLAUDE.md for the whole project
Split it into a CLAUDE.md in each top-level folder, which are all loaded together when a session starts
Split it into topic files under .claude/rules, which are loaded alongside CLAUDE.md for the whole project
Split it into skills under .claude/skills, which are loaded in full alongside CLAUDE.md for the whole project
questions.e: C. Rule files with no path pattern load for the whole project, the same as CLAUDE.md. Commands and skills load only when they're used, and a nested CLAUDE.md loads only when Claude works in that folder.

questions.q: A team skill, /audit-deps, runs a long analysis that prints hundreds of lines. After it runs, the main conversation is crowded with its output and later answers get worse. What is the best change to the skill?
o: Add context: fork to its frontmatter, so it runs in a subagent and returns a summary
Add allowed-tools to its frontmatter, so it runs with fewer tools and prints less output
Move its instructions into CLAUDE.md, so they're loaded once and the output stays shorter
Add an argument-hint to its frontmatter, so developers can ask it for a shorter report
questions.e: A. Forking runs the skill in its own context, so the long output stays out of the main conversation. Limiting tools changes what the skill is allowed to do, not how much it prints.

questions.q: A developer is about to ask Claude Code to build a caching layer. They don't know the area well, and the requirements are vague. What is the most effective way to begin?
o: Ask Claude to implement its best guess first, and correct the design through several rounds of review comments
Ask Claude to interview them about requirements and edge cases first, and implement once the answers are agreed
Ask Claude to implement three different designs in parallel, and keep whichever one passes the most tests
Ask Claude to copy the caching approach from another service, and adjust it wherever the tests fail
questions.e: B. When requirements are unclear, having Claude ask questions first brings out decisions the developer hadn't thought about. Guessing and then correcting spends several rounds undoing the wrong design.

questions.q: A developer resumes a Claude Code session from two days ago. Since then, a teammate has changed several of the files that Claude analysed in that session. What should the developer do?
o: Resume the session and carry on, since the earlier analysis is still held in the conversation history
Resume the session and ask Claude to re-read every file in the repository before it continues
Resume the session and ask Claude to rely on its earlier tool results wherever the files differ
Resume the session and tell Claude which files changed, so that it re-reads those before it continues
questions.e: D. A resumed session still holds the old file contents, which are now out of date for the changed files. Pointing Claude at what changed is much cheaper than re-reading everything.

questions.q: You've defined three extraction tools, one each for invoices, contracts and receipts. The document type isn't known in advance. Claude usually calls the right tool, but sometimes replies in plain text. What is the best fix?
o: Set tool_choice to auto, so Claude decides whether to call a tool or reply in text
Set tool_choice to any, so Claude must call a tool but can choose which one fits
Set tool_choice to the invoice tool, so Claude must call it for every document it receives
Set tool_choice to none, so Claude replies in text that follows the schema in the prompt
questions.e: B. any forces a tool call and leaves the choice of tool to Claude. auto still allows a text reply, and naming one tool forces the invoice schema onto contracts and receipts.

questions.q: The schema has a category field with a fixed list of allowed values. Some documents have a category that isn't on the list, and Claude picks a poor match. What is the best change to the schema?
o: Remove the fixed list from the schema, and accept any free-text value for the category
Keep the list as it is, and tell Claude to choose whichever value is closest
Add an "other" value to the list, with a separate text field for the detail
Keep the list as it is, and reject any document whose category isn't on it
questions.e: C. An escape value stops the model forcing a poor fit, and the detail field keeps the real information. Dropping the list loses the consistency that downstream systems rely on.

questions.q: Extraction works well on standard invoices. It fails on unusual layouts, such as totals given in a footnote or amounts in two currencies. What is the most effective improvement?
o: Add a few worked examples to the prompt that cover the unusual layouts and their correct extractions
Add detailed written rules to the prompt that describe each of the unusual layouts seen so far
Add a second extraction pass over every document, and keep whichever result has more fields filled
Add a pre-processing step that converts every document into one standard layout before extraction
questions.e: A. Worked examples show Claude how to handle varied layouts, and it generalises from them better than from a growing list of written rules.

questions.q: You want to send only the doubtful extractions to human review. Which approach gives the most dependable signal for deciding what to send?
o: Have Claude give a confidence score per document, and trust any document scored above ninety per cent
Have Claude extract each document twice, and trust the result whenever both extractions are identical
Have Claude give a written reason per field, and trust any field that comes with a detailed reason
Have Claude give a confidence score per field, and check those scores against a labelled sample first
questions.e: D. A model's confidence scores are only useful once they've been checked against known answers. Scores per field also show which part of a document needs a look. Two identical extractions can both be wrong in the same way.

questions.q: A validation step sends failed extractions back to Claude with the error. For some invoices it keeps failing on the supplier's tax ID, however many times it retries. Those invoices don't show a tax ID anywhere. What should you change?
o: Increase the number of retries from three to ten, with the validation error included each time
Retry with a more capable model, and include the validation errors from the earlier attempts
Stop retrying when the value isn't in the document, and return null or send it for review
Retry with a stricter prompt, which says that the tax ID field must always be filled in
questions.e: C. Retrying helps with format and structure errors. It can't produce information the document doesn't contain, and pushing harder invites an invented value.

questions.q: The coordinator sends every query through all four subagents, including simple factual questions. Simple queries are slow and cost as much as complex ones. What is the best change?
o: Have the coordinator assess each query, and call only the subagents that the query actually needs
Have the coordinator call every subagent each time, and discard the results it doesn't need
Have the coordinator call every subagent each time, but on a smaller and cheaper model
Have users choose which subagents to run, with a set of checkboxes on the query form
questions.e: A. Not every query needs every specialist. Letting the coordinator choose saves time and cost on simple queries without lowering quality on complex ones.

questions.q: In the current design, subagents send messages directly to one another. Failures are hard to trace, and each subagent handles errors in its own way. What is the best redesign?
o: Keep direct messaging, and add logging inside each subagent for every message that it sends
Route all communication through the coordinator, so there is one place for control and error handling
Keep direct messaging, and add a shared memory file that every subagent reads and writes
Route all communication through the report writer, so the final step sees everything first
questions.e: B. With one hub, every handoff is visible and errors are handled the same way each time. Logging lets you see the tangle but doesn't remove it.

questions.q: The search subagent returns about 15,000 tokens of raw page content and its own reasoning. The coordinator passes all of it to the synthesis subagent, whose output has become less focused. What should the search subagent return?
o: Everything it gathered, with the synthesis subagent moved to a model with a larger context
A one-sentence conclusion for each question, leaving out the sources and the supporting detail
Everything it gathered, with the coordinator cutting it down to a fixed length afterwards
Structured key findings with their sources, leaving out the raw pages and its own reasoning
questions.e: D. The next agent needs the findings and where they came from, not the raw pages. A single sentence loses the sources that the report has to cite.

questions.q: The search subagent has one general fetch tool. Flags on it switch between searching, loading a page and reading a PDF, and the subagent often sets the wrong flags. What is the best fix?
o: Keep the single tool, and add a longer description that explains every flag in detail
Keep the single tool, and add examples of each flag combination to the system prompt
Split it into separate tools for searching, loading pages and reading PDFs, each clearly described
Split the work across three separate subagents, and give each of them the same single tool
questions.e: C. One tool per job, with a clear name and description, is easier for the model to choose correctly than one tool with many flags. Extra subagents add overhead without fixing the tool.

questions.q: For one of five subtopics the search subagent found no usable sources. The final report simply leaves that subtopic out, and readers assume the report is complete. What is the best change?
o: Have the report state which subtopics lacked sources, so readers know where its coverage is thin
Have the report leave the subtopic out, so that every statement in it is fully sourced
Have the report cover the subtopic from the model's general knowledge, in the same style
Have the system re-run the whole research task until every subtopic has at least one source
questions.e: A. Saying where coverage is thin lets readers judge the report. Leaving the subtopic out hides the gap, and unsourced general knowledge looks the same as researched findings.

questions.q: On every new ticket, the agent should look the customer up before it does anything else. Sometimes it starts with an order lookup or a text reply. Which tool_choice setup is best?
o: Set it to any on every request, so that the agent always calls one of its tools
Set it to the get_customer tool on the first request, then return it to auto for later turns
Set it to auto on every request, and say in the prompt to look the customer up first
Set it to none on the first request, so that the agent asks the customer for their details
questions.e: B. Naming a tool forces that exact call, which suits a fixed first step. After that, auto lets the agent choose. any forces a tool call but doesn't say which one.

questions.q: A customer's message contains three separate requests: a refund, a change of address and a delivery question. The agent deals with the first one and closes the ticket. What is the best change?
o: Have the agent answer the first request, and ask the customer to raise the others as new tickets
Have the agent pass any message with more than one request straight to a human agent
Have the agent choose the most urgent request, resolve it fully, and close the ticket afterwards
Have the agent list each separate request first, work through them all, then send one combined reply
questions.e: D. Customers often raise several things at once. Listing them first makes sure none is dropped, and a single reply saves the customer from chasing the rest.

questions.q: The order tool draws on three back-end systems. Each one returns dates and status codes in its own format, and the agent sometimes misreads them. What is the most reliable fix?
o: Add a hook that runs after each tool call and converts the results into one consistent format
Add a section to the system prompt that explains each back-end system's date and status formats
