Add a second model call after each tool call that rewrites the results into plain English
Add few-shot examples to the prompt that show the agent reading each of the three formats
questions.e: A. A hook is code, so the conversion happens the same way every time, before the model sees the result. Explaining the formats in the prompt leaves the model to convert them, and it will sometimes slip.

questions.q: Each order lookup returns more than 40 fields, and the agent uses about five of them. After several lookups the conversation is crowded and the agent's answers get worse. What is the best fix?
o: Summarise the whole conversation after each tool call, so that earlier results take up less room
Move the agent to a model with a larger context window, so that all the results fit
Trim each tool result to the fields the task needs before it is added to the conversation
Limit the agent to two order lookups per ticket, so that fewer results are ever added
questions.e: C. Most of each result is never used. Cutting it down at the source keeps the context for what matters and loses nothing the task needs.

questions.q: A customer gives their name as John Smith, and the customer lookup returns three matching accounts. The agent currently carries on with the first one. What should it do?
o: Have the agent choose the match with the most recent order, since that customer is most likely
Have the agent ask the customer for another identifier, such as their email address or postcode
Have the agent choose the first match returned, and confirm the name with the customer afterwards
Have the agent run the lookup again with the same name, in case the results come back different
questions.e: B. Guessing between people with the same name risks showing or changing the wrong account. One more identifier settles it.

questions.q: An MCP server offers a code_search tool that understands symbols and references. Its description reads "Searches code". The agent keeps using the built-in Grep and gets poorer results. What is the best fix?
o: Remove the built-in Grep tool from the agent, so the MCP tool is the only way to search
Add a line to the system prompt saying the agent must never use Grep for code searches
Rename the MCP tool to something longer, so that it sorts above Grep in the tool list
Expand the MCP tool's description to say what it searches, what it returns and when to prefer it
questions.e: D. The description is what the model uses to choose a tool, and "Searches code" gives it no reason to prefer this one. Removing Grep takes away a tool that is still right for simple text searches.

questions.q: The assistant needs to read and comment on issues in the team's issue tracker. The tracker's vendor publishes a maintained MCP server that covers this. A developer proposes writing a custom MCP server for it. What is the best decision?
o: Use the vendor's server, and build a custom one only for needs that it doesn't cover
Build a custom server from the start, so the team controls every tool and its description
Skip MCP for this, and have the agent call the tracker's API through Bash commands
Use both servers side by side, so the agent can choose whichever tool works best
questions.e: A. A maintained server saves the team from building and looking after its own. Keep custom work for the gaps. Two servers with overlapping tools make it harder for the agent to pick the right one.

questions.q: You've defined three subagents for the assistant. The coordinator never hands work to them and does everything itself, even when the user asks it to delegate. What is the most likely cause?
o: The subagents' descriptions are too short, so the coordinator can't tell which of them to choose
The subagents' allowed tools include too many entries, so the coordinator refuses to start any of them
The coordinator's allowed tools don't include the tool that starts subagents, so it can't delegate
The coordinator's system prompt doesn't name the subagents, so they were never loaded into the session
questions.e: C. An agent can only use the tools it has been allowed. Without the tool that starts subagents it can't delegate, whatever the prompt or the user says.

questions.q: A developer wants to try an experimental MCP server in all of their own projects. Teammates shouldn't get it. How should they add it?
o: Add it at user level, so it is available in their own projects and not shared
Add it to each project's .mcp.json, and ask teammates not to use it until it's ready
Add it to each project's .mcp.json, and leave that change uncommitted in every repository
Add it to each project's CLAUDE.md, with a note explaining how the server should be started
questions.e: A. A user-level server follows the developer across projects and stays out of the repository. An uncommitted project file has to be repeated in every repository and is easy to commit by mistake.

questions.q: An engineer asks the assistant how billing works in a large legacy codebase. It reads files more or less at random and runs out of context before it can answer. What is a better strategy?
o: Read every file in the billing folder from top to bottom, then summarise what was found
Read the largest files in the repository first, since they hold most of the logic
Search for the word "billing", then read every file in which that word appears
Search for the entry points first, then follow the calls and read only those files
questions.e: D. Following the path from the entry point reads what matters, in the order it runs. Reading whole folders or every match fills the context before the picture is clear.

questions.q: Each time a developer pushes a new commit to a pull request, the review bot posts all of its earlier comments again. What is the best fix?
o: Delete all the earlier comments before each run, so the pull request shows only one set
Pass in the earlier findings, and ask Claude to report only new or unfixed issues
Run the review on the first commit only, and skip every later push to the branch
Limit each run to the three most serious findings, so that fewer comments are repeated
questions.e: B. With the earlier findings in hand, Claude can tell what is new and what has been fixed. Deleting the old comments hides the history without stopping the repeats.

questions.q: The CI job has to run with nobody there to approve actions, but it shouldn't be able to do anything it likes on the build machine. How should permissions be set?
o: Skip all permission checks for the job, since it runs inside a pipeline with nobody watching
Leave the default prompts on, and have the pipeline answer yes to each one automatically
Give the job full permissions, and tell Claude in the prompt which commands to avoid
Allow only the specific tools and commands the job needs, and deny everything else in settings
questions.e: D. A pipeline can't answer prompts, so permissions have to be set in advance. Allowing only what is needed keeps the job working and limits the damage from a mistake or a malicious pull request.

questions.q: The review bot's severity labels are inconsistent. The same kind of issue is marked "critical" on one pull request and "minor" on another. What is the best fix?
o: Define each severity level in the prompt, with a concrete code example of each
Ask Claude in the prompt to apply severity levels carefully, and to be consistent between runs
Remove severity levels from the output, and list every finding with the same weight
Run each review three times, and use whichever severity level appears most often
questions.e: A. Concrete examples show where each level starts and ends. Asking for consistency doesn't tell the model what the levels mean.

questions.q: One category of review comment, unused imports, is wrong most of the time. Developers have started to distrust the bot's other comments, which are accurate. What should you do?
o: Turn the whole review bot off until every category is accurate, then switch it back on
Keep every category running, and add a note to each comment saying it may be wrong
Turn that one category off while its prompt is improved, and keep the accurate categories running
Keep every category running, and ask developers to mark each wrong comment as resolved
questions.e: C. One noisy category makes people distrust all the comments. Pausing only that one protects trust in the rest while it is fixed.

questions.q: tool_choice is fixed on the invoice extraction tool. When a document turns out not to be an invoice, Claude still fills in the invoice fields with invented values. The pipeline needs a machine-readable result for every document. What is the best fix?
o: Set tool_choice to auto, so Claude extracts invoices and replies in text for anything else
Keep the extraction tool forced, and add an instruction to leave every field empty for non-invoices
Add a second tool for rejecting a document, and set tool_choice to any for every request
Set tool_choice to none, and ask Claude to return the extraction as JSON in its text reply
questions.e: C. The pipeline needs a structured result for every document, including "this isn't an invoice". Two tools with any gives Claude an honest way to say that. Forcing the extraction tool makes it describe an invoice that isn't there, and auto allows plain text the pipeline can't read.

questions.q: The schema has a contract end date field. Some contracts give no date, only wording such as "twelve months from signing". Claude works out a date, and it is sometimes wrong. What is the best schema change?
o: Add a field for the wording as written, beside a date field that may be null
Keep the single date field, and tell Claude to work the date out as carefully as possible
Keep the single date field, and reject any contract that doesn't state an exact end date
Change the date field to free text, and let downstream systems interpret whatever was written
questions.e: A. Keeping the original wording preserves what the contract actually says. A date that can be null stops a calculated guess being stored as a fact.

questions.q: On contracts of more than a hundred pages, a single extraction pass regularly misses clauses in the middle of the document. What is the best redesign?
o: Extract from the whole document twice, then keep the result that has more fields filled
Extract from the first and last twenty pages only, since key terms usually appear there
Extract from the whole document once, with an instruction to pay attention to the middle
Extract from each section separately, then merge the results and check them for conflicts
questions.e: D. Attention thins out over a very long document, most of all in the middle. Section-by-section passes give each part full attention, and the merge step catches conflicts between them.

questions.q: Human reviewers spend most of their time hunting through each document to confirm the extracted values. Which change to the output would speed them up the most?
o: Return each value with a confidence score from one to ten, set by Claude itself
Return each value with the page number and the exact wording that it was taken from
Return each value twice, from two separate runs, so that reviewers can compare them
Return each value with a short explanation of why Claude believes that it is right
questions.e: B. A page number and a quote let a reviewer confirm a value in seconds. A confidence score or an explanation still leaves them searching the document.

questions.q: You're about to send 100,000 archived documents through the Message Batches API with a new extraction prompt. What should you do first?
o: Run a sample of a few hundred first, fix what fails, then submit the full set
Submit the full set at once, then resubmit whichever documents come back with errors
Split the full set into ten equal batches, then submit all of them at the same time
Submit the full set through real-time calls, then watch the first results as they arrive
questions.e: A. A sample run finds prompt and schema problems while they are cheap to fix. Finding them after the full run means paying for it twice.

questions.q: A set of rules about database migrations matters only when someone works in the migrations folder. The team wants those rules to use no context at any other time. Where should they go?
o: In the root CLAUDE.md, under a heading that names the migrations folder
In a rule file with no path pattern, alongside the team's other rule files
In each developer's personal CLAUDE.md, under a heading for this project only
In a rule file whose path pattern matches the migrations folder only
questions.e: D. A rule with a path pattern loads only when Claude works on matching files. A rule with no pattern is loaded in every session, the same as CLAUDE.md.

questions.q: One developer wants a local build command to run without an approval prompt, on their own machine and in this project only. Where should that permission go?
o: In .claude/settings.json, which applies to everyone on the project and is committed
In .claude/settings.local.json, which applies to them in this project and isn't committed
In the project's CLAUDE.md, as an instruction saying the command needs no approval
In the managed settings file, which applies to everyone in the organisation
questions.e: B. settings.local.json is personal to that developer in that project and stays out of version control. The shared settings file would change the permission for the whole team.

questions.q: The team's code formatter has to run after every file edit that Claude makes, with no exceptions. Which mechanism should enforce that?
o: A line in CLAUDE.md that tells Claude to run the formatter after every edit
A skill that developers invoke to run the formatter whenever they remember to
A hook that runs the formatter automatically after every file edit that Claude makes
A rule file that reminds Claude about formatting whenever it opens a source file
questions.e: C. Something that must happen every time belongs in a hook, which runs as code. Instructions and rules are followed most of the time, not every time.

questions.q: A developer keeps one Claude Code session open all day and works through several unrelated tasks in it. By the afternoon, Claude is mixing up details from earlier tasks. What is the best habit to change?
o: Start a fresh session for each unrelated task, and carry over only what the next one needs
Keep one session for the whole day, and remind Claude of the current task every few turns
Keep one session for the whole day, and ask Claude to ignore everything from earlier tasks
Start a fresh session only when Claude makes an error, and continue in it until the next
questions.e: A. Leftover context from earlier tasks competes with the current one. A fresh session keeps the context for the task in hand.

questions.q: A developer wants Claude Code to work on two independent features at the same time, without one piece of work overwriting the other's files. What is the best setup?
o: Run two sessions in the same folder, and tell each one which files to leave alone
Run one session, and ask Claude to switch between the two features after each change
Run two sessions in separate git worktrees, so each has its own copy of the files
Run two sessions in the same folder, and commit after every edit to avoid any clashes
questions.e: C. Separate worktrees give each session its own files, so neither can overwrite the other. Sharing one folder relies on both sessions staying out of each other's way.

questions.q: You're deciding what the coordinator should put in the brief it gives each subagent. Which contents lead to the most useful results?
o: The full conversation so far, so the subagent can work out for itself what is needed
The goal, what is already known, the format to return, and where the task should stop
A one-line topic, so the subagent is free to decide the scope and the format
The coordinator's system prompt, so the subagent follows exactly the same rules and role
questions.e: B. A subagent starts with nothing but its brief. It needs the goal, the starting point, the format and the limits. The whole conversation buries those in noise.

questions.q: The system runs each stage once: search, analyse, combine, write. Reports often miss an angle that a human researcher would have gone back to look for. What is the best change?
o: Have the coordinator accept the first set of findings, and note in the report that it may be incomplete
Have the coordinator run every search twice at the start, so that gaps are less likely to appear
Have the report writer fill any gaps from general knowledge, in the same style as the rest
Have the coordinator check the combined findings for gaps, and send follow-up tasks for what is missing
questions.e: D. A single pass can't know what it missed. Checking the result and sending follow-up tasks is how the coordinator closes the gaps.

questions.q: Two sources give different figures for the same statistic. On inspection, the figures come from different years. How should the system handle cases like this?
o: Record the date of each figure with its source, so differences over time can be told apart
Keep the figure from the more recent source, and drop the older one from the findings
Keep the average of the two figures, and cite both of the sources next to it
Record the figure that appears in more sources, and treat the other one as an error
questions.e: A. Two figures from different years may both be right. Recording the date lets the report show a change over time and not a false contradiction.

questions.q: The document-analysis subagent needs to work with a store of several hundred internal reports. It currently spends many tool calls finding out what exists. How should the store be offered to it?
o: Expose one tool that returns every report in full, so the agent has everything at once
Expose one tool for each report, so the agent can call the one it needs by name
Expose the report catalogue as MCP resources, so the agent can see what exists before fetching
Expose the store through Bash commands, so the agent can list and open the files itself
questions.e: C. Resources let the agent see what is available without spending tool calls to find out. One tool per report doesn't scale, and returning everything fills the context.

questions.q: A full research run takes about two hours. When something crashes part-way through, all the work so far is lost and the run starts again. What is the best design change?
o: Have the coordinator restart the whole run from the beginning, with a longer time limit set
Have each agent save its progress to a file, and have the coordinator resume from those files
Have the coordinator keep all progress in its own conversation, and summarise it more often
Have each agent work on a smaller, faster model, so runs finish before a crash can happen
questions.e: B. Progress saved outside the conversation survives a crash. Progress held only in the coordinator's context is lost along with it.

questions.q: Research questions arrive as four to six sub-questions. The sub-questions don't depend on one another, but the report can't be written until all of them are answered and any conflicts between them are settled. Today a single agent works through everything in one context. A run takes 25 minutes, and the later sub-questions get thinner treatment as the context fills. You need to cut the run time, keep the treatment even, and keep one place that decides whether coverage is good enough. Which structure fits best?
o: Use a coordinator that sends each sub-question to its own subagent one after another, collects the findings, checks coverage itself, and only then passes the combined findings on to the synthesis step.
Use a chain in which each sub-question's subagent passes its findings directly to the next subagent, with the last one in the chain checking coverage and then writing the synthesis itself.
Use a coordinator that sends each sub-question to its own subagent in parallel, collects the findings, checks coverage itself, and only then passes the combined findings on to the synthesis step.
Use parallel subagents for the sub-questions with no coordinator, have each one write its own section of the report, and join the sections in the order the sub-questions were asked.
questions.e: C. Independent sub-questions can run in parallel, which cuts the run time and gives each one a clean context. The coordinator stays the single place that judges coverage. Running them one after another keeps the control but not the speed, and dropping the coordinator loses the coverage check and the settling of conflicts.

questions.q: The coordinator briefs the document-analysis subagent with a step list: open each PDF, extract every table, and list every figure above ten per cent. This works on standard reports. On unusual ones, where the key data sits in the narrative text and there are no tables, the subagent returns almost nothing. The coordinator also needs to compare results across documents, so it must be able to line them up. Which change to the brief best addresses both needs?
o: State what the analysis is for and what a good result contains, let the subagent decide how to find it in each document, and require every result in the same fixed structure.
State what the analysis is for and what a good result contains, let the subagent decide how to find it in each document, and let it choose whichever structure suits each result.
Keep the step list, add further steps that cover narrative text and documents with no tables, and require every result in the same fixed structure so that documents can be compared.
Keep the step list, add a closing step telling the subagent to use its judgement when a document doesn't fit, and let it choose whichever structure suits each result.
questions.e: A. A goal with success criteria lets the subagent adapt to documents the step list never anticipated. A fixed return structure keeps the results comparable, so the coordinator keeps its view. Adding steps only covers the cases someone thought of in advance.

questions.q: All four subagents were given the full set of 14 tools "for flexibility". Logs show the report writer occasionally running new web searches and adding claims that never went through analysis or synthesis, and the search subagent sometimes writing files. A teammate points out that it is occasionally handy for the report writer to look something up. You want every claim in a report to have passed through the same checks. What is the best design?
o: Give each subagent only the tools for its own role, except for the report writer, which keeps the search tools so that it can fill small gaps without a round trip.
Keep all the tools on every subagent, and add a section to each system prompt that lists which tools belong to its role and which ones it should leave alone.
Keep all the tools on every subagent, and have the coordinator inspect each subagent's tool calls afterwards and discard any output that came from a tool outside its role.
Give each subagent only the tools for its own role, and send any need outside that role back through the coordinator, so that new material always passes through analysis and synthesis.
questions.e: D. Tools that aren't offered can't be misused, and fewer tools make each subagent's choices more reliable. Sending out-of-role needs back through the coordinator keeps every claim on the same path. Leaving the report writer its search tools keeps the exact problem you are trying to remove.

questions.q: The coordinator calls the synthesis subagent with a prose summary of what the search and analysis subagents found. The synthesis comes back with claims that have no sources, and the subagent often has to ask the coordinator for details that were left out, which costs extra round trips. What should the coordinator pass in so that the synthesis subagent can finish the task in one go?
o: The findings themselves as structured data, each with its source, date and supporting quote, but without the research question, so that the synthesis is not steered towards one particular answer.
The findings themselves as structured data, each with its source, date and supporting quote, together with the research question and the output format that the report writer expects to receive.
A longer prose summary of the findings that mentions the main sources by name, together with the research question and the output format that the report writer expects to receive.
The identifiers of the earlier subagent runs, together with the research question, so that the synthesis subagent can ask the coordinator for the particular findings it decides that it needs.
questions.e: B. A subagent has only what its brief contains. To finish in one go it needs the findings with their source details, the question they answer and the format wanted. A summary, however long, has already thrown the source details away.

questions.q: One kind of request asks the system to compare how three countries regulate a product, then assess which approach would suit a fourth country. The three country studies don't depend on one another. The assessment depends on all three. Today the coordinator starts all four tasks at once, and the assessment comes back generic because its subagent started with nothing to assess. How should the coordinator order the work?
o: Run the three country studies in parallel, wait until all three have returned, and then start the assessment with their findings included in the brief that its subagent is given.
Run all four tasks in parallel as now, and have the assessment subagent ask the coordinator for the country findings when it reaches the point where it needs them.
Run all four tasks one after another with the assessment last, so that each subagent can be given the findings of every task that finished before it started.
Run the three country studies in parallel, start the assessment at the same moment, and combine the assessment with the country findings afterwards in the synthesis step.
questions.e: A. Run independent work in parallel and dependent work after the things it depends on. Running everything in sequence would also work, but it gives up the time saved on the three studies.

questions.q: The team has four kinds of guidance to set up. First, coding conventions that apply to every file. Second, rules for API handlers that matter only for files under src/api. Third, a forty-step release procedure that is used about once a fortnight. Fourth, a requirement that the linter runs after every edit, with no exceptions. Which arrangement puts each one in the right place?
o: Conventions in the project CLAUDE.md, the API rules in a rule file with a path pattern for src/api, the release procedure as a hook, and the linter as a skill.
Conventions in the project CLAUDE.md, the API rules in that same file under their own heading, the release procedure as a skill, and the linter as an instruction in a rule file.
Conventions in a rule file with a path pattern for src/api, the API rules in the project CLAUDE.md, the release procedure as a skill, and the linter as a hook.
Conventions in the project CLAUDE.md, the API rules in a rule file with a path pattern for src/api, the release procedure as a skill, and the linter as a hook.
questions.e: D. Match each mechanism to when the guidance should apply: CLAUDE.md for always, a path-scoped rule for certain files, a skill for an occasional procedure loaded on demand, and a hook for something that must run every time.

questions.q: Security policy says Claude Code must never read files in the secrets folder and must never run terraform apply. The restriction has to apply to everyone who works in the repository, and it must not depend on Claude choosing to comply. Where should it be defined?
o: As deny rules in the permissions of .claude/settings.local.json, which is kept out of version control and applies on the machine where it was written.
As deny rules in the permissions of the project's .claude/settings.json, which is committed and applies to everyone who works in the repository.
As a security section in the project's CLAUDE.md, which is committed and is loaded into every session for everyone who works in the repository.
As a rule file with a path pattern for the secrets folder, which is committed and is loaded whenever Claude works on a matching file.
questions.e: B. Permission rules in settings are enforced by Claude Code itself, so they don't rely on the model complying. The project settings file is shared through the repository. CLAUDE.md and rule files are guidance, which is followed most of the time, not always.

questions.q: Yesterday a developer spent a long Claude Code session mapping a module of about forty files and agreeing a refactoring plan. Overnight a teammate merged changes to three of those files. Today the developer wants to carry on and implement the plan. They want to keep the analysis and the agreed plan, avoid acting on file contents that are out of date, and avoid repeating yesterday's work. What should they do?
o: Resume yesterday's session, and ask Claude to re-read all forty files and rebuild its analysis before it goes any further, so that nothing in the conversation is out of date.
Start a new session, and ask Claude to map the module again from the beginning, so that both the analysis and the plan are based on the files as they are now.
Resume yesterday's session, tell Claude which three files have changed, and ask it to re-read those and confirm that the plan still holds before it goes any further.
Resume yesterday's session and carry on with the plan as agreed, since the earlier file contents are still in the conversation and only three of the files were touched.
questions.e: C. Resuming keeps the analysis and the plan. Pointing Claude at the three changed files refreshes exactly what is stale. Re-reading everything, or starting again, repeats work that is still valid.

questions.q: Claude Code is tracing a data flow through about two hundred files of a legacy system over a session lasting several hours. Many files are more than two thousand lines long. After the context is compacted, Claude can no longer say which functions it had already confirmed, and it starts re-reading files. What combination of habits best keeps a session like this coherent?
o: Have Claude record confirmed findings in a notes file as it goes, read only the relevant part of each file, and hand broad searches to subagents that return short summaries.
Have Claude record confirmed findings in a notes file as it goes, and keep reading each file in full from top to bottom, so that nothing relevant in a file is missed.
Have Claude rely on the summary that is made when the context is compacted, read only the relevant part of each file, and hand broad searches to subagents that return short summaries.
Have Claude rely on the summary that is made when the context is compacted, and start a fresh session whenever its answers turn vague, repeating the trace from the entry point.
questions.e: A. Three habits work together: a notes file keeps exact findings outside the conversation, targeted reading slows the rate at which context fills, and subagents keep broad searches out of the main context. A compaction summary loses the specifics that a long trace depends on.

questions.q: For one task Claude needs to do four things: find every file in the repository whose name ends in .migration.sql, find every place where the function applyDiscount is called, understand the code of the two most relevant callers, and check which migrations have been applied by running the project's status command. Which choice of built-in tools is best?
o: Grep for the migration files, Glob for the calls to the function, Read for the two callers, and Bash for the project's status command.
Glob for the migration files, Grep for the calls to the function, Bash with cat for the two callers, and Read for the project's status command.
Glob for the migration files, Grep for the calls to the function, Read for the two callers, and Bash for the project's status command.
Bash with find for the migration files, Bash with grep for the calls, Read for the two callers, and Bash for the project's status command.
questions.e: C. Glob matches file names and paths, Grep searches inside files, Read loads a file's contents, and Bash runs commands. Shell commands can do the first two jobs as well, but the dedicated tools are the intended choice and return results in a form Claude handles better.

questions.q: You're setting up the pull request review job. Reviews have to apply the team's standards, the job must not be able to change code or push anything, and a script will post each finding as an inline comment on the right line. Today the job runs with the default tools, the standards were pasted into the job's prompt months ago and have drifted from the repository's own, and the output is prose. Which configuration meets all three needs?
o: Load the standards from the project's CLAUDE.md, leave the default tools in place for simple fixes, and require the findings as JSON with a file, line, severity and message for each one.
Load the standards from the project's CLAUDE.md, limit the job to read-only tools, and require the findings as JSON with a file, line, severity and message for each one.
Keep the standards in the job's own prompt, limit the job to read-only tools, and require the findings as JSON with a file, line, severity and message for each one.
Load the standards from the project's CLAUDE.md, limit the job to read-only tools, and ask for the findings as a Markdown list that the script can then split up into comments.
questions.e: B. Each part answers one need: the project file is the single maintained copy of the standards, read-only tools mean the job can't change or push anything, and structured output is what a script can post reliably.

questions.q: In the nightly job, one Claude Code run generates the missing tests and a second step reviews them. The review step currently resumes the generating session and asks it to review its own changes. It approves almost everything. You want a review that judges the tests on their merits and still applies the team's standards. Which design is best?
o: Run the review as a new session that receives the changes, the project's standards and the generating session's full conversation, so that it understands the reasoning behind every decision.
Run the review by resuming the generating session with the project's standards added and an instruction to be critical, so that it has the full background close to hand.
Run the review by resuming the generating session twice, and keep only the findings that turn up in both passes, so that the result is more dependable than one pass.
Run the review as a new session that receives the changes and the project's standards, without the generating session's conversation, so that it judges the tests on what was actually written.
questions.e: D. A session that made the decisions tends to agree with them, and so does a new session that is handed the same reasoning. A fresh session with only the changes and the standards judges the result on its own.

questions.q: Test conventions live in three places: general ones in the project's CLAUDE.md, a path-scoped rule file for the tests folder, and fixture naming conventions in the lead developer's personal CLAUDE.md. The nightly test job follows the first two but not the fixture naming. The fix has to reach the CI job and every developer, and the conventions only matter when test files are involved. Where should the fixture naming conventions go?
o: Into the path-scoped rule file for the tests folder, which is committed with the repository and is loaded only when test files are involved.
Into the project's CLAUDE.md, which is committed with the repository and is loaded into every session, whichever files are involved.
Onto the CI runner, as a copy of the lead developer's personal CLAUDE.md, so that the job loads the same conventions as that developer's sessions.
Into a skill in the repository, which is committed with it and is loaded when a developer or the job decides to invoke it.
questions.e: A. The conventions must be shared, so they belong in the repository, and they matter only for tests, so a path-scoped rule fits exactly. The project CLAUDE.md would also reach everyone, but it would load them into every session.

questions.q: A pull request touching thirty files has had its first review. The developer then pushes two more commits that change four of those files. The second review should check whether the earlier findings were fixed, review the new changes, avoid repeating findings that are already resolved, and keep the cost down. Which approach is best?
o: Resume the first review's session, and ask it to review all thirty files again from the start, so that the earlier findings and the new changes are covered in a single pass.
Start a new session with the pull request's full set of changes and no record of the first review, so that the second review is not influenced by the first one.
Resume the first review's session, give it the list of files changed since then, and ask it to re-check its earlier findings on those files and review only the new changes.
Start a new session with only the two new commits and no record of the first review, so that just the latest changes are reviewed and the cost stays low.
questions.e: C. The resumed session already knows what it found. Telling it which files changed lets it confirm fixes and look only at what is new. A new session with no record can't tell a fixed finding from one that was never raised.

questions.q: A pull request changes the function calculateTax. Before commenting, the review job needs to understand what else in a large repository could be affected, and it has a limit on the number of turns it can use. Which exploration strategy is best?
o: Grep for the function's name to find its callers, Read each matching file in full from top to bottom, and then Read every file that those files import as well.
Grep for the function's name to find its callers, Read only the calling code around each match, and follow any wrapper functions the same way until no new callers appear.
Glob for every source file in the repository, Read them in alphabetical order until the turn limit is close, and report on whichever callers were found up to that point.
Read the changed file in full, and judge the impact from the function's own code and comments, without spending any turns on a search of the rest of the repository.
questions.e: B. Search first, then read only what the search points to, and follow the trail outwards. Reading whole files and their imports spends the turn limit on code that has nothing to do with the change.

questions.q: Every ticket has to begin with a customer lookup, and a refund must only ever use a customer ID and an order ID that came back from the lookup tools. In testing, the agent sometimes opens with a text reply, and it has twice issued a refund against an order ID that it guessed from the customer's message. Which design closes both gaps?
o: Name get_customer in tool_choice on the first request and return to auto afterwards, and tell the agent in its prompt that refunds must only use IDs returned by the earlier lookups.
Name get_customer in tool_choice on the first request and return to auto afterwards, and have the refund tool refuse any call whose IDs were not returned by the earlier lookups.
Set tool_choice to any on every request so that a tool is always called, and have the refund tool refuse any call whose IDs were not returned by the earlier lookups.
Name get_customer in tool_choice on every request so that the lookup can never be skipped, and tell the agent in its prompt that refunds must only use verified IDs.
questions.e: B. Two separate guarantees are needed. Naming the tool on the first request fixes the opening step, and going back to auto lets the agent carry on. The check on the IDs has to live in the refund tool's own code, because a prompt instruction makes it likely, not certain.

questions.q: Some support conversations run past sixty turns. Cost per ticket is climbing. When the history is summarised, the agent loses order numbers and refund amounts, and each order lookup adds more than forty fields to the conversation, of which about five are ever used. Which approach keeps answers accurate and brings the cost down?
o: Keep the key facts in a structured block that is updated and sent with every request, and keep every turn and every tool result in full so that nothing can be lost.
Summarise the whole conversation every twenty turns, with the key facts written into each summary as it is made, and trim each tool result to the fields the agent actually uses.
Keep the most recent twenty turns in full and drop everything that is older than that from the request, and trim each tool result to the fields the agent actually uses.
Keep the key facts in a structured block that is updated and sent with every request, summarise the older turns, and trim each tool result to the fields the agent actually uses.
questions.e: D. Exact values such as order numbers don't survive summarising, so they need their own block outside the part that gets compressed. With that in place, summarising older turns and trimming tool results cuts the cost safely. Keeping everything in full protects accuracy but does nothing about the cost.

questions.q: A customer asks about two separate orders in one message. To answer, the agent needs the customer record and the details of each order. The three lookups don't depend on one another. Today the agent makes one lookup per response, so there are three round trips before it can reply, and customers notice the delay. What is the best change?
o: Let the agent ask for all three lookups in one response, run them at the same time, and return all three results together in the next message before it replies.
Let the agent ask for all three lookups in one response, run them at the same time, and return each result in a separate message so that it can react to each.
Keep one lookup per response, and cut the delay by moving the agent to a smaller and faster model, so that each of the three round trips finishes sooner.
Merge the lookups into one large tool that always returns the customer record and every order on the account, whichever of them the customer's question needs.
questions.e: A. Independent lookups can be requested in a single response and run side by side, which turns three round trips into one. The results for one response go back together in the next message. A tool that always returns everything fills the context with orders nobody asked about.

questions.q: For billing disputes the agent follows a fixed six-step checklist. It works through every step even after an early lookup has shown the cause, such as a duplicate charge, and it doesn't follow up on things the checklist never mentions, such as a second account under the same email address. Policy does require some checks, identity verification among them, on every dispute. What is the best redesign?
o: Have the agent plan its next steps from what each lookup shows, adding or dropping steps as it learns more, including the checks that policy requires when they look unnecessary.
Keep the fixed checklist, and extend it with further steps for duplicate charges and second accounts, so that the cases seen so far are covered in a set order.
Have the agent plan its next steps from what each lookup shows, adding or dropping steps as it learns more, while the checks that policy requires stay enforced in code.
Keep the fixed checklist, and add a last step in which the agent reviews everything it found and decides whether any of the earlier steps ought to be repeated.
questions.e: C. Letting the plan follow the findings handles cases nobody listed in advance and stops wasted steps. The checks that must always happen are a different kind of requirement, so they stay enforced in code where the agent can't drop them.

questions.q: The agent answers accurately on orders, refunds and delivery. On questions about consumer law and tax it is wrong about a third of the time, and those wrong answers carry real risk. Management wants to keep automation where it performs well. Which change to the prompt and routing is best?
o: State which topics the agent handles and which it must hand over, with examples on both sides of the line, and send the excluded topics to a person.
State which topics the agent handles, leave the others unmentioned so that it can still attempt them, and add a note to those answers that they may be wrong.
Tell the agent to answer only when it is confident, with examples of confident answers, and send anything that it marks as uncertain to a person.
Tell the agent to take special care over consumer law and tax, with examples of careful answers, and keep every topic automated in the way that it is now.
questions.e: A. Where performance is unreliable, draw an explicit boundary: say what is in, say what is out, and show examples of each. Relying on the agent's own sense of confidence doesn't work, because it is often confident when it is wrong.

questions.q: You've defined a test-runner subagent with a description, a prompt and a tool list containing Read and Grep. The coordinator delegates test runs to it correctly. Each time, the subagent reads the test files, explains what the tests would probably do, and reports that it has no way to execute them. What is the cause, and the fix?
o: The coordinator's allowed tools leave out the tool that starts subagents, so the work never reaches the subagent, and that tool needs to be added to the coordinator.
The subagent's description is too brief for the coordinator to match tasks to it, so the wrong work is delegated, and the description needs to be rewritten.
The subagent's definition lists only Read and Grep as its tools, so it has no way to run commands, and Bash needs to be added to that list.
The subagent's prompt doesn't mention running the tests, so it doesn't know that it should, and an instruction to run them needs to be added to it.
questions.e: C. The symptoms locate the fault. Delegation works, so the coordinator and the description are fine. The subagent wants to run the tests and says it can't, which points to its tool list and not its prompt.

questions.q: The team shares an MCP server that searches internal documentation. Every engineer should get it automatically, and each has their own access token. A new engineer reports that the assistant "doesn't have" the documentation tool. Which setup is correct, and how should it be checked?
o: Define the server in the project's .mcp.json with one shared team token written into the file, and have each engineer confirm that the server's tools are listed.
Define the server in each engineer's user-level configuration with their own token written into it, and have each engineer confirm that the server's tools are listed.
Define the server in the project's .mcp.json with the token read from an environment variable, and add a line to the system prompt saying that the documentation tool is available.
Define the server in the project's .mcp.json with the token read from an environment variable, and have each engineer set that variable and confirm that the server's tools are listed.
questions.e: D. The project file shares the server with everyone, and the environment variable keeps each person's token out of the repository. Checking that the tools are actually listed is how you confirm the connection. A line in the prompt can't make a tool exist.

questions.q: Two MCP tools are described as "Search documentation" and "Search code". The first covers the internal wiki and the second covers every repository. Engineers ask how an internal API should be used, and the assistant often picks the wrong tool, or falls back on the built-in Grep in the local checkout. What is the best fix?
o: Rewrite each description to say what it searches and what it returns, and add a rule to the system prompt saying which tool to use for each kind of question.
Rewrite each description to say what it searches, what input it expects, what it returns, and when to choose it over the other tool and over Grep.
Merge the two tools into one search tool with a parameter for the source, and describe the parameter's allowed values briefly in the tool's input schema.
Keep the descriptions as they are, and rename the tools so that each name spells out its source in full and sorts ahead of Grep in the list.
questions.e: B. The description is what the model reads when it chooses a tool, so the boundaries between similar tools belong there, including when to prefer each one. A rule in the system prompt sits apart from the tools and is easier to miss.

questions.q: Before answering questions about the platform, the assistant makes many calls to list_services and get_service_info just to find out which services exist. The catalogue holds about three hundred service descriptions and rarely changes. The same MCP server also offers actions such as restarting a service. How should the server expose these?
o: Expose the service catalogue as MCP resources that the assistant can browse, and keep restart and similar actions as tools, each with a clear description.
Expose the service catalogue and the restart actions as MCP resources, so that everything the server offers can be browsed in one consistent way.
Expose the service catalogue through one tool that returns all three hundred descriptions in a single call, and keep restart and similar actions as tools.
Expose each service's description through a separate tool named after that service, and keep restart and similar actions as tools, each with a clear description.
questions.e: A. Resources are for content the assistant reads, and tools are for actions it takes. A browsable catalogue removes the exploratory calls. Actions can't be resources, and three hundred tools or one enormous result would both overload the context.

questions.q: The assistant automates a migration across eighty modules, with a subagent handling each module. A run was interrupted after fifty. On restart it began again from the first module, and the notes that subagents had made about awkward modules were gone. What is the best design change?
o: Have each subagent save its result and notes to a file when it finishes, and have the coordinator rerun every module on restart so that the results are consistent.
Have the coordinator hold every result and note in its own conversation, summarise them every ten modules, and resume that same conversation when the run is restarted.
Have the coordinator keep a manifest of completed modules, without their results or notes, and have it skip those modules when the run is restarted.
Have each subagent save its result and notes to a file when it finishes, keep a manifest of completed modules, and have the coordinator read both when it restarts.
questions.e: D. Progress has to be saved outside the conversation to survive an interruption. The manifest says what is done, and the saved results and notes keep what was learned. A manifest alone avoids the repeat work but still loses the findings.

questions.q: About three per cent of extractions contain an error. Reviewers currently check a random ten per cent of all extractions and miss most of the errors. Analysis shows that the errors cluster in handwritten documents, in invoices with more than one currency, and in the tax ID field. Which review design is best?
o: Route extractions to review by field-level confidence that has been checked against labelled data, and by document type, and stop the random sample now that routing covers the errors.
Route extractions to review by the document-level confidence that Claude reports, without checking it against labelled data, and keep a small random sample alongside it.
Route extractions to review by field-level confidence that has been checked against labelled data, and by document type, and keep a small random sample to catch what the routing misses.
Raise the random sample from ten per cent to thirty per cent of all extractions, so that about three times as many of the errors are likely to be caught.
questions.e: C. Review effort should go where the errors are: weak fields and weak document types. Confidence scores only earn trust once they have been checked against known answers. The small random sample stays, because it is the only way to notice a new kind of error that the routing doesn't know about.

questions.q: The schema requires a purchase order number, and it requires payment terms chosen from a fixed list: net 30, net 60 or on receipt. Some invoices have no purchase order number, and some state terms such as "45 days from end of month". Claude invents purchase order numbers and files unusual terms under net 30. Which schema change is best?
o: Make the purchase order number nullable, and add an "other" value to the payment terms with a text field for the wording, so that both gaps are recorded honestly.
Make the purchase order number nullable, and keep the payment terms list as it is with an instruction to choose the closest value, so that downstream systems see known values.
Keep the purchase order number required with an instruction to write "unknown" when it is missing, and add an "other" value to the payment terms with a text field.
Keep both fields as they are now, and add an instruction that Claude must never invent a purchase order number or choose a payment term that isn't stated.
questions.e: A. A schema that can't express "missing" or "something else" pushes the model to make something up. A nullable field and an "other" value with the original wording give it an honest answer for each case.

questions.q: Some invoices have more than four hundred line items. The response is cut off part-way through, with a stop reason of max_tokens, and the JSON is invalid. The output limit has already been raised twice, and the largest invoices still fail. What is the best fix?
o: Raise the output limit to the highest value the model allows, and retry any response that is still cut off, checking the total count against the invoice.
Split the document into page ranges, extract the line items from each range in its own call, and merge the lists in code, checking the total count against the invoice.
Split the document into page ranges, extract the line items from each range in its own call, and ask one final call to return all of the lists merged together.
Ask Claude to return the line items in a shorter form with abbreviated field names, so that more of them fit inside the output limit of a single call.
questions.e: B. When the output is too big for one response, make the task smaller instead of the limit bigger. The merge has to happen in code: a final call that returns everything merged would hit the same limit again.

questions.q: The system has two workloads. Accounts staff upload invoices and wait on screen for the extracted fields. Separately, an archive of two hundred thousand documents has to be processed each month, with no deadline shorter than a week. Finance wants the cost brought down. Which processing design is best?
o: Use the Message Batches API for both workloads, since it costs less, and show staff a message that asks them to come back later for their results.
Use the real-time Messages API for both workloads, since one path is simpler to run, and bring the cost down by lowering the output limit on every call.
Use the Message Batches API for the uploads that staff are waiting on, since they are small, and the real-time Messages API for the monthly archive, since it is large.
Use the real-time Messages API for the uploads that staff are waiting on, and the Message Batches API for the monthly archive, since it can wait and costs less.
questions.e: D. Choose by whether someone is waiting. Work that blocks a person needs a real-time call. Work that can wait hours suits batch processing, which costs less. Size isn't the deciding factor.

questions.q: Three teams each use a different way of getting JSON from Claude: a format described in the prompt with an example, a response that is started with an opening brace, and a tool with a JSON schema that Claude is required to call. The nightly load into the finance system rejects anything invalid, and a missing required field stops the whole load. Which approach should the extraction pipeline use?
o: Define the schema as a tool and require the tool call, and remove the validation in code, since a required tool call can no longer return anything that is invalid.
Describe the JSON format in the prompt with a full example, validate the result in code, and retry any response that fails to parse or is missing a field.
Define the schema as a tool and require the tool call, validate the result in code as well, and keep prompt-only formatting for places where an occasional slip is harmless.
Start Claude's response with an opening brace so that it carries on in JSON, validate the result in code, and retry any response that fails to parse.
questions.e: C. A required tool call with a schema gives the strongest guarantee on structure, which is what a strict downstream load needs. Validation in code still earns its place, because a schema can't check that the values make sense.

questions.q: A team's Claude Code agent must never modify files under secrets/. Today that rule lives in CLAUDE.md and was violated once last sprint. Best fix?
o: Rewrite the CLAUDE.md entry in stronger, more explicit language at the top of the file.
Add a PreToolUse hook matching Edit|Write that denies any file path under secrets/.
Add a PostToolUse hook that reverts edits to secrets/ after they happen.
Run all sessions in plan mode so a human approves every change.
questions.e: A: Position and tone don't change the layer's nature: the model reads CLAUDE.md and can drift from it. | B: A 'never' needs a deterministic veto. PreToolUse fires before the edit and can block it — every time. | C: Closer, but wrong event: PostToolUse fires after the damage (the secret may already be exposed in context/logs). Prevention beats cleanup here. | D: Gates every edit in every session to stop one path — disproportionate, and a human approving fast can still miss it.

questions.q: Where should a personal preference like "explain changes verbosely to me" live, for a developer working on a shared team repo?
o: The project CLAUDE.md, so it's versioned with the code.
A PreToolUse hook that injects the preference into each prompt.
questions.e: A: That imposes one developer's taste on the whole team and bloats the shared constitution. | B: Personal preferences belong at user level — they follow the developer across all projects and never pollute the team's shared config. | C: A deterministic mechanism for a matter of taste — the dial turned the wrong way. | D: Settings hold configuration like hooks and permissions, and committing it shares it with everyone — both wrong for a personal preference.

questions.q: S2 · You resume a week-old session to continue a refactor. In the meantime three of the files it analyzed were substantially rewritten. Best move?
o: Resume, but explicitly tell the session which files changed and to re-read them before advising.
Resume and continue — the session already understands the architecture.
Start completely fresh with no context and re-derive everything.
Fork the session so the stale context stays in the original.
questions.e: A: Resumption carries the old tool results forward as if still true. Naming the changed files forces a re-read instead of confident reasoning from a stale snapshot. If most of the context were stale, the better move would be a fresh session plus a structured summary of what was decided. | B: That understanding is built on file contents that no longer exist. A resumed session doesn't know anything changed, and stale specifics are worse than none because they're asserted confidently. | C: Safe but wasteful — it throws away decisions and rationale that are still valid. The decisions didn't go stale; the file contents did. | D: Forking is for exploring divergent branches from a shared baseline. It copies the stale context into the fork rather than refreshing it — the staleness follows you.

questions.q: The team wants a consistent, repeatable code-review prompt that anyone can trigger, which must not edit files and shouldn't fill the main session's context with its long output. What's the right Claude Code mechanism?
o: A skill with allowed-tools restricted to Read/Grep/Glob and context: fork.
A long CLAUDE.md section describing how reviews should be done.
A PostToolUse hook that reviews every edit automatically.
Tell developers to paste a saved review prompt from the wiki.
questions.e: A: Skill = repeatable invocation; allowed-tools = least privilege (read-only); fork = context isolation. Three exam concepts in one file. | B: Always-loaded context cost in every session, and nothing repeatable to invoke. | C: Hooks are for must-fire guarantees; an on-demand review workflow isn't one, and reviewing every single edit is noise. | D: Works 'usually' — until paste variance and stale wiki copies creep in. The skill exists precisely to remove that variance.

questions.q: After adding a PostToolUse lint hook, lint errors appear in Claude's context after every edit, and Claude fixes them. A teammate says: "The hook works — so we can delete the 'Lint: ruff check .' line from CLAUDE.md." Is that right?
o: Yes — duplication between layers wastes context budget.
No — the layers serve different purposes: the hook guarantees linting happens; CLAUDE.md tells the model the project's commands and conventions so it can use them proactively.
No — deleting it would disable the hook, since hooks read CLAUDE.md.
Yes — hooks supersede CLAUDE.md in the configuration hierarchy.
questions.e: A: The two layers do different jobs; removing the command line doesn't remove duplication, it removes useful guidance (how to run lint manually, what the project uses). | B: Guidance and guarantee are complements, not redundant copies. Lean CLAUDE.md for context the model should know; hooks for rules that must hold. | C: Hooks are configured in settings.json and fire regardless of CLAUDE.md contents. | D: There's no 'supersede' relationship; they're different mechanisms (guidance file vs. lifecycle scripts), not levels of one hierarchy.

questions.q: Which statement about the configuration hierarchy is correct?
o: Project .claude/settings.json is shared via git; .claude/settings.local.json stays on one machine; user ~/.claude/settings.json applies across all that user's projects.
User-level settings always override project-level settings, so personal config wins.
CLAUDE.md files must be registered in settings.json before Claude Code reads them.
Hooks can only be defined at user level for security reasons.
questions.e: A: That's the hierarchy — and the architectural consequence: team guarantees belong at project level in git, or they don't exist for the team. | B: Backwards for the part that matters: more specific (project/local) refines broader (user). And team-critical rules shouldn't depend on any one user's files. | C: No such registration step — memory files are discovered by location. | D: Project-level hooks are standard — that's exactly how a team ships shared guardrails.

questions.q: An agent has tools search_orders ("search orders"), find_purchases ("find customer purchases") and lookup_history ("look up history"). All three call the same order-history endpoint with the same parameters. It frequently calls the wrong one. The proportionate fix?
o: Add an intent-classification model in front that routes to the correct tool.
Merge them into one well-described tool (they all query order history) with clear parameters.
Add a system-prompt section explaining which of the three tools to use in which case.
Expand each of the three descriptions to spell out what it does, when to use it, and when not to.
questions.e: A: A second AI system to compensate for bad descriptions — now you maintain, monitor, and debug two. | B: They overlap entirely — the model is coin-flipping between synonyms. Fewer, sharper, non-overlapping tools is the root-cause fix. | C: Patches over the real problem (redundant tools) and burns always-loaded context to do it. | D: This is the right FIRST move when tools are genuinely distinct but thinly described. These three aren't distinct — they all query order history. Beautifully describing a redundant set still leaves the model choosing between synonyms. Remove the redundancy first, then describe well.

questions.q: S4 · Your team's agent needs a GitHub MCP server that every engineer on the repo should get automatically, authenticated with each person's own token. You also want a personal, half-broken experimental server that must not affect teammates. Correct configuration?
o: GitHub server in the project's .mcp.json using ${GITHUB_TOKEN} expansion (committed to git); the experimental server in your own ~/.claude.json.
Both servers in .mcp.json, with the experimental one commented out until it works.
Both in ~/.claude.json, and ask teammates to copy the GitHub block into theirs.
GitHub server in .mcp.json with the token pasted in directly, since the repo is private.
questions.e: A: Project scope = .mcp.json in the repo, shared through version control; user scope = ~/.claude.json, your machine only. Environment-variable expansion keeps the shared file free of anyone's actual credential. Both are active at once, so you lose nothing by splitting them. | B: Commenting things in and out of a committed config is a merge conflict waiting to happen, and it puts your personal experiment in everyone's repo. Scope is about who needs it. | C: Manual propagation of shared config — it drifts the moment one person forgets. That's exactly the problem project scope solves. | D: A private repo is still permanent version-controlled history, across every clone and fork, and it's one visibility change from public. Credentials never go in committed config — expand them from the environment.

questions.q: Your support agent should always have the current return-policy document available, and should be able to look up a customer's orders when it decides it needs them. How do you model these in MCP?
o: Both as tools — the model fetches the policy when needed.
Policy as a resource (application-controlled context), order lookup as a tool (model-controlled action).
Both as resources, refreshed each session.
Policy in the system prompt, orders as a resource.
questions.e: A: The policy isn't an in-flight decision; making it a tool means the model must remember to fetch it (probabilistic) when the app could simply supply it (deterministic). | B: Who decides? App decides every session gets the policy → resource. Model decides when it needs orders → tool. | C: Order lookup is a parameterized action the model takes mid-conversation — that's a tool by definition. | D: Policy-in-prompt is workable, but orders-as-resource breaks: the app can't know in advance which customer's orders the conversation needs.

questions.q: A backend tool call fails and returns the string "Error: operation failed". What's the architectural problem?
o: Nothing — the agent knows the call failed and can apologize to the user.
The error gives the agent no basis for action — it should be structured: category (transient/validation/business/permission), retryability, and a message.
The tool should retry internally until it succeeds, so the agent never sees errors.
Errors should be sent to a logging service for the engineering team to review weekly.
questions.e: A: Failure-blindness: the agent can't choose retry vs. fix-input vs. explain vs. escalate from 'operation failed'. | B: Failure is first-class: an error is data that drives the agent's next decision, not an apology string. | C: Infinite/blind retries hang on permanent failures, and hiding all failure removes the agent's ability to escalate or inform the user. | D: Observability is good but doesn't help the agent act in the moment.

questions.q: The team is adding a 15th tool to the support agent ("check_warehouse_humidity — might be useful someday"). Why does the architect push back?
o: Each tool's definition consumes context budget every turn, and every added tool dilutes selection accuracy across the set — pay those costs only for capabilities the agent actually needs.
More than 10 tools is above the documented hard limit.
The model bills per registered tool.
No pushback needed — more capabilities make a more useful agent.
questions.e: A: Least privilege + context budget + selection quality. Tools are not free even when never called. | B: No such hard limit — invented constraint. | C: Billing is per token, not per registered tool — though definitions do cost tokens, which is the real version of this concern. | D: Ignores selection dilution, context cost, and attack surface. 'Might be useful someday' is how 14-tool mush happens.

questions.q: Which tool description is exam-grade?
o: "update_account — a powerful tool for all account management needs"

"update_account — Update a verified customer's contact fields (email, phone, address). Requires prior get_customer verification. Cannot change tier or billing; use escalate_to_human for those. Returns the updated record."
"update_account — PLEASE be very careful and only use when absolutely necessary!!!"
questions.e: A: Restates the name. Updates what? When? What does it return? What is it not for? | B: Marketing copy. 'All needs' guarantees overlap with every sibling tool. | C: What it does, what it requires, what it can't do, where to go instead, what it returns. The model can place its boundaries exactly. | D: Tone instead of information. Urgency doesn't define scope.

questions.q: An agent harness ends its loop when the model's reply contains the string "DONE". Sessions keep terminating mid-task. Root cause and fix?
o: The completion phrase is too common — switch to a rarer sentinel like "##TASK_FINISHED##".
Loop control is reading probabilistic text; use the structured signal — continue while stop_reason is "tool_use", complete on "end_turn".
Add a system-prompt rule: "Only say DONE when fully complete."
Have a second model classify whether each reply means the task is finished.
questions.e: A: Still parsing prose for a control signal — the model may echo the sentinel while planning or quoting. Same bug, fancier costume. | B: stop_reason is machine-readable protocol metadata, not prose. The only reliable completion signal. | C: Prompting the model to be careful with the magic word is still a probabilistic mechanism for a control-flow guarantee. | D: A probabilistic judge of a probabilistic signal, plus double cost — when a deterministic field already exists.

questions.q: What does stop_reason == "max_tokens" mean, and what should your harness do?
o: The model finished a long answer; process it normally.
The reply was truncated by the output limit — not completion; continue/retry to get the rest, and never parse the truncated fragment as a finished result.
The context window is full; start a new session immediately.
The API is rate-limiting you; apply exponential backoff.
questions.e: A: It means the answer was cut off mid-thought — processing the truncated fragment as complete ships unfinished work. | B: Truncation is an incident with a defined response, not an end state. | C: max_tokens is about the output limit for this reply, not the context window. | D: Rate limiting arrives as an API error, not a stop_reason.

questions.q: The team wants the agent to hand frustrated customers to humans at the right moment. Which design is correct?
o: Run a sentiment model on each message; escalate when negativity exceeds 0.7.
Ask the model to rate its confidence 1–10 each turn and escalate below 6.
Explicit escalation criteria + few-shot examples in the prompt for the judgment call; hard thresholds (like dollar caps) enforced in code.
Escalate every conversation that exceeds five turns.
questions.e: A: Mood ≠ complexity. Angry-but-trivially-fixable and calm-but-impossible both exist; the threshold misroutes both. | B: Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated — a favorite distractor. | C: Judgment where the model is strong, guarantees where stakes are hard. The dial, set per requirement. | D: Turn count is a proxy for neither frustration nor complexity; it floods humans with routine cases.

questions.q: On escalation, what should the human agent receive?
o: The full conversation transcript, so no information is lost.
A structured handoff: customer id, issue, actions taken, recommended action, escalation reason — self-contained.
A one-line note: "Customer needs help, see system."
An AI-generated summary of the customer's emotional state.
questions.e: A: The human must reconstruct the case from a log — they'll skim, then ignore. Raw ≠ informative. | B: The handoff is an interface contract. Extracted facts + a recommendation = a briefing, not a burden. | C: Under-engineered — the human starts from zero with an already-frustrated customer. | D: Mood without facts. The human needs what happened and what to do.

questions.q: Where does max_iterations (a turn cap) correctly fit in an agent loop?
o: As the primary completion mechanism — stop when the cap is hit.
As a safety backstop against runaway loops, while stop_reason remains the completion signal — hitting the cap should be treated as an anomaly worth logging.
It's unnecessary if stop_reason handling is correct.
Set it to 1 so the model can't take autonomous actions.
questions.e: A: A cap detects nothing; it just truncates. Tasks finishing under the cap still need a real signal, and tasks hitting the cap were killed, not completed. | B: Both layers, properly assigned: signal for completion, cap for catastrophe insurance. | C: Failure is first-class: a bug, a pathological task, or a tool that always errors can loop forever. You still want the net. | D: That deletes the agent — tool use requires at least request → result → continuation.

questions.q: A teammate proposes: "The $500 refund cap is in the tool's code already — so we should delete the mention of it from the system prompt to save context." Best response?
o: Agree — redundancy between prompt and code wastes budget.
Keep both: the code enforces the cap; the prompt mention lets the model anticipate it (warn the customer, pre-emptively escalate) instead of discovering it by failing.
Agree, but add a PostToolUse hook that injects the policy after each refusal.
Move the cap entirely into the prompt and simplify the tool.
questions.e: A: One sentence of prompt buys the agent the ability to set expectations and route correctly without burning a failed tool call first. | B: Guarantee + guidance are complements. The gate holds the law; the prompt makes the agent graceful about it. | C: Machinery to re-create what one prompt sentence already does. | D: Backwards — that trades the guarantee away for context savings measured in a few tokens.

questions.q: A coordinator hands a subagent the prompt "Summarize the key risks in the contract" and the subagent responds it has no contract. The team is baffled — "the contract is right there in the coordinator's conversation." What's the fix?
o: Enable context sharing between the coordinator and its subagents.
Pass the contract text (and the goal and output format) explicitly in the delegation — a subagent starts blank and sees only what it's handed.
Tell the subagent in its system prompt to ask the coordinator for missing materials.
Use one agent instead — multi-agent systems can't handle documents.
questions.e: A: No such switch — subagent isolation is structural, not a setting you toggle. | B: The #1 multi-agent fact: no inheritance. The task packet must be self-contained. | C: There's no channel for it to 'ask' through — and even with one, you'd be patching the symptom of an incomplete packet. | D: They handle documents fine when context is passed properly; abandoning the architecture over a briefing bug is overcorrection.

questions.q: Two research subagents keep producing overlapping findings, doubling token cost. Best fix?
o: Add a deduplication pass over the combined findings.
Have the coordinator partition the topic into explicit non-overlapping slices before delegating, and state the boundary in each task packet ("another agent covers X").
Let subagents see each other's progress so they avoid collisions.
Reduce to one subagent so overlap is impossible.
questions.e: A: You already paid for the duplicate work; this pays again to clean it. Symptom, not cause. | B: Root cause is unclear boundaries. Prevent the overlap at assignment time. | C: Cross-agent visibility isn't how isolation works, and even conceptually it adds coordination machinery to dodge a problem partitioning removes outright. | D: Throws away parallelism to avoid writing a clear assignment. Under-engineered disguised as simplicity.

questions.q: The research system's final reports cite sources that don't exist. The proposed fix: add "CRITICAL: only cite real sources" to every subagent prompt. The architect's better answer?
o: The proposal is fine — fabrication is a prompting problem.
Require findings in a schema where every claim carries a source (or explicit null), forbid synthesis from emitting unsourced claims, and verify sources in an independent pass before shipping.
Use a larger model for the synthesis step.
Have the synthesis agent re-read its own report and remove suspicious citations.
questions.e: A: A wish, not a structure. The model can still fabricate; nothing checks. | B: Provenance by structure plus verification: the claim→source mapping travels with the data and gets checked by something other than its author. | C: Capability isn't the issue — attribution is lost structurally during summarization regardless of model size. | D: Self-review: the instance that produced the work defends its own reasoning. Verification must be independent.

questions.q: Why route subagent results through a coordinator instead of letting subagents pass results directly to each other?
o: Direct passing is faster, so actually peer-to-peer is preferred.
The hub gives one place to observe, steer, budget, and merge — peer-to-peer flows are invisible and unsteerable.
Subagents are technically unable to communicate directly.
The coordinator caches results, halving token costs.
questions.e: A: Marginal latency for the loss of any central point of observation and control. | B: Lens 6: hub-and-spoke is chosen for observability and control, not elegance. | C: You could build direct passing; the point is you usually shouldn't. 'Impossible' is the wrong reason. | D: Invented mechanism — routing through a hub doesn't inherently cache or halve anything.

questions.q: A search subagent returns zero results for its slice. The pipeline treats this identically to the time the search service timed out. Why is that wrong?
o: It's not wrong — both are failures and should be retried.
"0 results" is a valid, informative outcome (report it as a finding); a timeout is an access failure (retry with backoff, then annotate as a gap). Different categories, different actions.
Zero results means the query was malformed; the subagent should rewrite it until results appear.
Timeouts should fail the whole run so the report is never incomplete.
questions.e: A: Retrying a genuine empty result wastes turns chasing data that isn't there. | B: Scenario 3's signature error-handling distinction: absence of data ≠ failure to access data. | C: Rewriting-until-nonempty manufactures confirmation.
