Sometimes the truthful answer is 'nothing exists'. | D: Failure-first says the opposite: isolate the failed slice, annotate it, ship the partial with honesty.

questions.q: A team wants to split a simple FAQ-answering bot into five specialized subagents (greeting, lookup, tone, formatting, sign-off). The architect's call?
o: Decline — one agent with a clear prompt and the right tools handles this; multi-agent is a cost paid for context isolation and parallel independent work, which this task lacks.
Approve, but route them all through a coordinator for observability.
Decline, because subagents can't generate text responses.
questions.e: A: Multi-agent adds cost, latency, and coordination failure modes. It's purchased for isolation/parallelism, neither of which an FAQ bot needs. | B: Proportionality. The over-engineered distractor often arrives dressed as 'more agents'. | C: Observability hygiene applied to an architecture that shouldn't exist for this task. | D: They generate text fine — the reason is proportionality, not capability.

questions.q: A prompt says "Flag any concerning clauses in this contract." Reviewers complain results vary wildly run to run. The D4 fix?
o: Raise the temperature down to 0 so outputs are repeatable.
Replace the judgment word with explicit criteria (e.g. auto-renewal > 12 months, indemnification without caps, unilateral termination) plus 2–3 worked examples including an edge case.
Run it three times and majority-vote the flags.
Fine-tune on the firm's past contract reviews.
questions.e: A: Lower variance in wording doesn't define 'concerning' — the criteria are still missing, so runs (and documents) still disagree. Also parameter-fiddling is rarely the exam's answer. | B: 'Concerning' is a mood. Criteria + few-shot turn it into a checkable instruction. | C: Triples cost to average over an ambiguity you could simply remove. | D: Out of scope and massively disproportionate to writing down what 'concerning' means.

questions.q: Your service parses the model's reply as JSON. About 2% of replies arrive wrapped in markdown fences or prefixed with "Here's the JSON you requested:". Best fix?
o: Strengthen the prompt: "Respond with ONLY raw JSON, no other text, no code fences."
Strip fences and preambles with a regex before parsing.
Define the output as a tool's input_schema and force it with tool_choice — the reply is then structurally guaranteed.
Switch to a larger model with better instruction-following.
questions.e: A: Tightens the distribution; doesn't close it. 2% becomes 0.4% — a parser still crashes on schedule. | B: A scraper bolted onto a probabilistic format — new wrapper variants keep arriving. Symptom patch. | C: When a parser waits, shape is a contract: enforce it with the mechanism built for enforcement. | D: Better adherence is still adherence — probabilistic. And costlier.

questions.q: An extraction schema marks every field required. The model fills missing purchase-order numbers with plausible-looking fakes. Why, and what's the fix?
o: The model is hallucinating; add "never fabricate values" to the prompt.
The required field leaves no honest path when data is absent — make genuinely-optional fields nullable (and keep the no-fabrication instruction).
Post-process: detect and remove PO numbers that don't match known formats.
Lower max_tokens so the model has less room to invent.
questions.e: A: Helpful sentence, but the schema still demands a string when none exists — the format itself forces the lie. | B: Required = 'always truly present.' Nullable gives the model a truthful output for missing data; prompt reinforces it. | C: Now you're laundering fabricated data downstream instead of preventing it. | D: Output length doesn't govern fabrication — nonsense fits in few tokens. Invented mechanism.

questions.q: What does a forced tool call (tool_choice: specific tool) guarantee — and not guarantee?
o: Guarantees both valid structure and correct values.
Guarantees syntactically valid output matching the schema's fields and types; does NOT guarantee the values are correct — that needs separate validation.
Guarantees nothing — the model can still reply in prose.
Guarantees the model will pick the most appropriate tool for the request.
questions.e: A: Half right, dangerously: the schema can't know whether 1240.50 is the real total. | B: Shape is guaranteed; truth is checked. The exam loves this exact boundary. | C: Forcing a tool is precisely the mechanism that removes the prose path. | D: Forcing removes the choice entirely — that's its point. Appropriateness was decided by you.

questions.q: Which job belongs on the Batch API?
o: The customer-support agent's replies, to halve token costs.
Overnight classification of 80,000 archived support tickets for a quarterly report.
Validating each invoice extraction immediately after it returns.
An interactive code-review session in Claude Code.
questions.e: A: A customer is waiting; an async window with no guaranteed completion time is categorically wrong for live traffic. | B: Bulk, asynchronous, nobody waiting: the Batch API's exact design case, at ~50% cost. | C: Validation is part of a live pipeline step, not deferred bulk work. | D: Interactive = someone waiting = synchronous by definition.

questions.q: When is adding chain-of-thought ("think step by step before answering") the right call?
o: Always — more reasoning is always more accurate.
For genuinely complex multi-step reasoning where accuracy outweighs latency — e.g. reconciling a total against line items before judging an invoice valid.
Never in production — reasoning text breaks JSON parsers.
Only when using the Batch API, where latency is free.
questions.e: A: It costs latency and tokens; for simple extraction or classification it adds expense without accuracy. | B: Proportionality applied to prompting: pay the thinking cost where reasoning is actually the bottleneck. | C: Reasoning and structured output coexist fine (think first, then emit the tool call / final block). | D: Batch makes latency cheaper but the criterion is task complexity, not API mode.

questions.q: An extraction's validation fails: "total (1480.00) does not equal sum of line items (1240.50)". The pipeline retries with the identical prompt and fails identically, three times. What's wrong?
o: Nothing — three retries is the standard resilience pattern.
The retry must feed back the specific validation error so the model can correct it — and after max attempts, route to human review with the reason.
Switch to a bigger model for retries.
questions.e: A: Blind retries re-roll the same dice. Retry count isn't the issue; retry content is. | B: Validation failures are correctable only when the model learns what failed. Feedback in, structured give-up out. | C: Cost escalation in place of information. The small model with the error message beats the big one without it. | D: That ships wrong financial data to stop an alarm. The alarm was the system working.

questions.q: A tool call times out. Match the correct response.
o: Treat it as permanent: mark the task failed and move on.
Retry immediately in a tight loop until it responds.
Retry with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s…), then if still failing, propagate a structured partial-failure note upward.
Escalate to a human immediately — timeouts may indicate fraud.
questions.e: A: Transient errors are defined by being temporary — giving up instantly wastes recoverable work. | B: Hammering a struggling service makes the outage worse and can run forever. | C: The canonical transient response: spaced retries, then honest propagation — never crash, never hide. | D: Category error: timeouts are temporary infrastructure conditions, not policy violations.

questions.q: The refund tool returns: errorCategory "business", message "Refund exceeds $500 cap". The agent retries the call four times. What's the design flaw?
o: The retry limit should be lower for refund tools.
Business-rule refusals are working-as-intended outcomes: the agent should explain the policy and escalate per criteria, never retry. The error category exists precisely to make that computable.
The cap should return success with a warning so the loop doesn't get stuck.
The tool should block retries by rate-limiting the agent.
questions.e: A: The correct number of retries for a business-rule refusal is zero — it's not a malfunction. | B: Taxonomy → action. Retrying a policy boundary is a category error (and looks like an evasion attempt in an audit log). | C: Disguising refusals as successes is silent failure with extra steps. | D: Infrastructure machinery to compensate for the agent not reading the category it was handed.

questions.q: After /compact in a long Claude Code session, the agent misremembers a deployment port discussed an hour ago. The lesson?
o: Never use compaction; long sessions should just run until the window is full.
Compaction summaries are lossy and shed exact values first — preserve critical facts deterministically (a notes file, CLAUDE.md, structured store) before relying on a summary.
Increase the context window so compaction never triggers.
Add 'remember the port number' to the compaction instruction.
questions.e: A: A full window degrades too (middle-loss, truncation). Compaction is a tool — the lesson is about what it costs. | B: Transcript = working memory; system of record = somewhere a summary can't erode. | C: You don't escape compaction by sizing up — larger windows still degrade in the middle, and the externalize-state principle stands regardless. | D: Begging the summarizer is the prompt-trap shape; one fact survives, the next one doesn't.

questions.q: Extraction accuracy is 97% overall. A periodic audit finds handwritten invoices fail 40% of the time. What's the right takeaway?
o: 97% aggregate is excellent; handwritten invoices are an acceptable edge case.
Audit by type and field, not just in aggregate — and route the weak stratum (handwritten) to human review until its accuracy is fixed.
Retrain the OCR layer — extraction is fine.
Raise the global confidence threshold to 0.95 for all documents.
questions.e: A: Aggregates hide stratified failure — Cascade's handwritten vendors get systematically wrong records. | B: Calibration is per-segment. Confidence routing + stratified audits catch what the average conceals. | C: Maybe a contributor, but the architectural takeaway is the auditing/routing pattern; 'retrain a component' assumes the root cause uninvestigated. | D: Floods reviewers with fine typed invoices while not specifically addressing the failing stratum.

questions.q: Who should verify a high-stakes extraction before it posts to the ledger?
o: The same model instance: "Review your answer carefully and confirm."
A fresh instance with auditor framing and only the document + extraction — or a human, for the highest stakes.
No verification — the schema already guaranteed the output.
Three parallel extractions with majority voting on every document.
questions.e: A: Self-review — the author defends its own reasoning. The most-tested reliability trap. | B: Independence is the active ingredient: new context, no stake in the original answer. | C: The schema guaranteed the shape. The values — the part the ledger cares about — were never checked. | D: Triple cost on every document, when targeted independent review of high-stakes/low-confidence cases is proportionate.

questions.q: One document in a 50-document batch is unparseable. Rank the three behaviors: (A) the run crashes; (B) the document is silently skipped; (C) 49 process, one is flagged to review with a reason.
o: A is safest — fail fast and loud.
B is most practical — the batch completes and throughput stays high.
C — isolate the failure, keep the good work, flag the gap with a reason attached.
A in production, C only in development.
questions.e: A: Fail-fast is for programmer errors, not data variance: holding 49 good documents hostage to one bad scan is the original disaster. | B: Worse than the crash: invisible data loss that surfaces months later in an audit, untraceable. | C: Partial results + honest annotation: failure as a first-class, visible, routable outcome. | D: Backwards — production, where reruns are most expensive and audits matter most, is exactly where C is required.

questions.q: S4 · An agent must apply the same targeted change to one function in a file — but the exact text it's matching on appears three times. The Edit call fails. Correct next step?
o: Read the file, then Write it back with the change applied.
Retry the Edit with the same match string.
Use Grep to change the matching lines in place.
Use Glob to locate the specific occurrence, then Edit that line number.
questions.e: A: Edit matches on unique text by design — the failure is the tool refusing to guess which of the three you meant. Read + Write is the documented fallback when uniqueness can't be established. | B: Nothing has changed, so it fails identically. Retrying an operation whose precondition is still violated is the blind-retry anti-pattern from EP 06. | C: Grep searches content; it doesn't modify files. This is a capability the tool doesn't have. | D: Glob matches file paths, not content within a file — and Edit targets text, not line numbers. Both halves misread what the tools do.

questions.q: A CI review bot's verdict is consumed by grepping its prose for "LGTM". Last week a review containing "this is NOT LGTM-worthy" auto-passed the gate. The fix?
o: Grep for a stricter phrase and require it at the start of the reply.
Demand structured JSON output (explicit shape in the prompt, --output-format json), validate it in the pipeline, and gate on parsed fields.
Have a second Claude call classify whether the first reply approves the PR.
Make the bot's approval comment trigger the merge via webhook.
questions.e: A: Still parsing prose for a control signal — the same bug that kills agent loops (EP 03), wearing a CI costume. | B: Machine-consumed output is a contract: structured, validated, then gated in code. | C: A probabilistic parser for probabilistic prose, at double cost. | D: Automates the merge without fixing the unreliable signal feeding it.

questions.q: Developers ignore the CI reviewer because it averages 40 comments per PR, mostly style nits. Scenario 5's success metric is trustworthy feedback. Best move?
o: Raise the severity bar in the prompt with explicit criteria and out-of-scope list (style/naming excluded), few-shot examples of qualifying findings, and a valid empty-result path.
Cap output at 5 comments per PR.
Fine-tune a model on the team's past review comments.
Send the comments to team leads instead of developers.
questions.e: A: False-positive volume is a scoping problem. Criteria + exclusions + 'silence is valid' rebuild trust. | B: On a bad PR the 6th finding might be the vulnerability; on a clean PR 5 nits still appear. Quantity cap ≠ quality bar. | C: Out of scope, heavy, and it would faithfully learn to produce… the team's old nitpicks. | D: Re-routes the noise; trust erodes one level up instead.

questions.q: Which tool configuration is right for a headless CI code reviewer?
o: --tools "Read,Grep,Glob" to restrict the surface (Edit/Write/Bash don't exist), paired with --allowedTools so CI doesn't stall on a prompt.
Full tool access, so it can fix the issues it finds.
Read tools plus Bash, so it can run the tests itself.
No tools — paste the diff into the prompt.
questions.e: A: Least privilege with the right flag: --tools restricts what the agent can do at all; --allowedTools only skips the permission prompt (it is NOT a restriction). A reviewer needs eyes, not hands — Edit/Bash are a prompt-injection incident waiting to happen. | B: A reviewer that edits code under nobody's supervision merges its own opinions. Review and write must be separate powers. | C: Bash is arbitrary execution — in unattended CI that's the entire attack surface. Let the pipeline run tests; give the model the results. | D: Workable for tiny diffs but loses the ability to read surrounding context; restricting to read-only tools achieves safety without blinding the reviewer.

questions.q: The sentry script receives unparseable output from the model one night. What should the pipeline do? (The reviewer is advisory only; blocking checks are provided separately by tests and branch protection.)
o: Block the merge — malformed review means the PR wasn't properly checked.
Pass the merge — the reviewer is advisory anyway.
Fail safe: skip the gate for this run, surface a visible warning/alert so the team knows review coverage lapsed.
Retry the review with the same prompt until output parses.
questions.e: A: Now a flaky reviewer randomly blocks unrelated PRs; developers lose trust again — this time angrily. | B: Half right (don't block), but missing the alert: silent reviewer outages become permanent unnoticed coverage gaps. | C: Never act on garbage in either direction — and never fail silently. Failure is first-class even for the reviewer itself. | D: Unbounded retries in CI, with no feedback about what failed — the blind-retry trap on a billable loop.

questions.q: Where does the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY belong in the CI setup?
o: In the CI platform's secrets store, injected as an environment variable at runtime.
In .claude/settings.json, committed so the whole team shares it.
Hardcoded in sentry.sh since the repo is private.
In CLAUDE.md so the agent knows its own key.
questions.e: A: Standard secret hygiene — and the exam's only acceptable answer shape for credentials. | B: A credential in version control is leaked-by-design — settings.json is for config, never secrets. | C: Private repos get cloned, forked, mirrored, and breached. Hardcoded secrets are always wrong. | D: CLAUDE.md is loaded into model context — you'd be feeding the secret to every session and every log.

questions.q: S1 · A support agent must check order status before promising delivery dates. In 8% of conversations it promises dates without checking. The team proposes adding "ALWAYS check order status before promising a date" in bold at the top of the system prompt. Evaluate.
o: Good fix — placement at the top maximizes instruction-following.
Insufficient — make the promise-path depend on the check: the reply tool (or a gate) requires a fresh order-status result before a date can be included.
Replace the agent with a decision tree for delivery questions.
Add few-shot examples of correct check-then-promise behavior.
questions.e: A: Position tunes probability; it cannot reach 'always'. A correctness-critical sequence needs enforcement. | B: Sequence guarantees live in code: the gated path makes the unchecked promise impossible, not just discouraged. | C: Deletes the model's value across all the messy variants of the question — over-rotation to the deterministic end. | D: Better, still probabilistic. Examples narrow the 8%; they don't zero it.

questions.q: S1 · The same agent should decide when a customer's issue is too unusual for self-service and write a handoff. Which division of labor is correct?
o: Code decides escalation via keyword list; model writes the handoff.
Model decides escalation via explicit criteria + examples; the handoff content is forced into a structured schema (id, issue, actions, recommendation, reason).
Model decides via its self-reported confidence; handoff is the transcript.
Code decides via sentiment score; model summarizes feelings for the human.
questions.e: A: Keyword lists are brittle for judgment — 'unusual-ness' is contextual, the model's strength. | B: Judgment to the model with criteria; structure to the schema. Both sides of the dial, correctly assigned. | C: Both halves are the classic traps: uncalibrated confidence as trigger, raw transcript as handoff. | D: Mood ≠ complexity, and the human needs facts and a recommendation, not impressions.

questions.q: S3 · A coordinator spawns three research subagents. Mid-run, subagent B needs a fact subagent A discovered. The team wants A and B to share a memory space. Architect's answer?
o: Enable shared memory between subagents for efficiency.
Route it through the hub: A returns findings to the coordinator, which includes the relevant fact in B's task packet (or re-delegates B after A completes).
Merge A and B into one subagent so the fact is naturally available.
Have B re-research the fact independently to stay decoupled.
questions.e: A: No such toggle — isolation is structural. Distractors love inventing inter-agent memory. | B: Hub-and-spoke exists for exactly this: the coordinator owns information flow — observable, budgeted, explicit. | C: Sometimes valid! But as a reflex it surrenders parallelism/isolation to dodge a sequencing problem the hub already solves. | D: Paying twice for the same fact is the duplication bug as a design principle.

questions.q: S3 · A synthesis agent receives 60 pages of subagent findings and its reports keep missing facts from pages 25–40. What's happening and what helps?
o: The model is lazy; instruct it to "read everything carefully".
Lost in the middle — restructure: key-findings summary at the top, clear section headers, critical constraints repeated at the end; distill subagent outputs before synthesis.
Split synthesis across three agents, one per 20 pages.
Raise max_tokens so the model can attend to more input.
questions.e: A: Lost-in-the-middle is an attention property, not an effort problem; pleading doesn't relocate the weak zone. | B: Place load-bearing content at the high-attention edges and shrink the middle. Structure beats exhortation. | C: Now three partial syntheses must be synthesized — the problem recursed, with more cost. | D: max_tokens caps output length; it has nothing to do with input attention.

questions.q: S4 · An agent exploring an unfamiliar codebase has 22 tools, including six different search variants contributed by different teams. Selection accuracy is poor. First move?
o: Consolidate to a minimal, non-overlapping toolset with boundary-setting descriptions.
Group tools into categories and add a category-picker tool the model calls first.
Log misselections for a month to understand patterns before changing anything.
Set tool_choice to "any" to make selection more decisive.
questions.e: A: Fewer, sharper tools = better selection, smaller context cost, smaller attack surface. The plain answer that's actually right. | B: A routing layer made of tools — sophistication where subtraction was needed. | C: Observation is good, but six overlapping search tools is a root cause you can already see. | D: tool_choice 'any' forces using some tool; it does nothing for choosing among confusable ones.

questions.q: S1 · Which error payload best serves the agent when a customer lookup fails because the CRM is down for maintenance?
o: isError + errorCategory "transient", isRetryable true, message "CRM maintenance window, ends ~10:00", suggestion "retry after, or offer the customer a callback".
Return an empty customer record so the conversation continues smoothly.
questions.e: A: Unactionable — retry? escalate? apologize? The agent can only guess. | B: Category, retryability, and a next-step suggestion: failure as decision-grade data. | C: Status codes are for HTTP clients; the agent needs semantics (is this retryable? what do I tell the customer?). | D: Fabricating an empty success is silent failure — the agent now reasons on false data.

questions.q: S4 · The team wants Claude to always know the repo's build commands, branch conventions, and "never push to main" policy. Sort the three into mechanisms.
o: All three in CLAUDE.md — that's what it's for.
Build commands + conventions in CLAUDE.md (guidance); "never push to main" as a PreToolUse hook blocking the push command (guarantee).
All three as PreToolUse hooks for consistency.
All three in settings.json under a policies key.
questions.e: A: Two of three, yes. 'Never push to main' is a must-hold rule; in CLAUDE.md it's a wish. | B: Each requirement on its certainty layer — D3's entire thesis in one question. | C: Hooking guidance (build commands? conventions?) is meaningless — hooks enforce actions, they don't inform judgment. | D: settings.json has no generic 'policies' interpreter — that's an invented mechanism.

questions.q: S2 · A developer runs Claude Code on a critical payments module. Claude proposes a 9-file refactor in plan mode. The developer doesn't fully understand the plan but it "looks reasonable". Best practice?
o: Approve — plan mode already added the safety gate.
Interrogate the plan first (ask for rationale, risks, alternatives; shrink scope if possible) and approve only what's understood — the human judgment is the gate's entire value.
Reject and write the refactor by hand — payments code shouldn't be AI-touched.
Approve but add a CLAUDE.md line: "be extra careful in payments code".
questions.e: A: A gate nobody actually evaluates is just for show. The approval IS the control; approving without reviewing the plan removes it. | B: Plan mode supplies the checkpoint; the architect supplies the checking. Especially on payments. | C: Over-rotation: with plan review, tests, and hooks, the model is a supervised power tool, not a banned substance. | D: An impression-based safety net under a 9-file change nobody understood.

questions.q: S5 · Security wants the CI reviewer to also auto-commit fixes for the issues it finds, "to save a cycle". Architect's response?
o: Accept — finding and fixing in one pass is efficient.
Keep the reviewer read-only; fixes happen in a separate, human-approved flow (e.g. suggested patches a developer applies).
Allow auto-commit only for "low" severity findings.
Allow it, but add a prompt rule: "never modify files outside the flagged ones".
questions.e: A: An unattended agent with write access whose input is attacker-influencable PR content = prompt-injection-to-commit pipeline. | B: Separation of powers: the unattended path stays read-only; writes stay behind a human. Least privilege is the spine of CI design. | C: Severity is the model's own probabilistic judgment — using it to unlock write access gates the danger with the thing being doubted. | D: A prompt boundary on an unattended write-capable agent is the trap in its purest form.

questions.q: S2 · A team wants every Claude Code session in the repo to start by running their environment-check script. Mechanism?
o: A SessionStart hook that runs the script automatically.
A CLAUDE.md line: "Always run ./check-env.sh before starting work."
A skill /checkenv developers should invoke first.
A cron job running the check every five minutes.
questions.e: A: Lifecycle event + must-happen-every-time = hook. SessionStart exists for exactly this. | B: The model usually will. Usually. The requirement said 'every session'. | C: Skills are on-demand by design — 'should invoke' reintroduces the human forgetting problem. | D: Machinery outside the session lifecycle, checking even when nobody's working.

questions.q: S6 · Legal-document extraction must output a contract_type field that is exactly one of: NDA, MSA, SOW, OTHER. Today the prompt asks for it and the model occasionally returns "Master Services Agreement". Fix?
o: Add to the prompt: "contract_type MUST be exactly one of NDA, MSA, SOW, OTHER".
Define contract_type as an enum in the forced tool's input_schema — the constraint becomes structural.
Post-process with a synonym mapper ("Master Services Agreement" → MSA).
Few-shot examples showing the four valid values.
questions.e: A: Closer, still a request. Parsers downstream need the enum to hold every time. | B: Schema enums make off-vocabulary output impossible, not discouraged. Shape contract = schema mechanism. | C: A growing translation table chasing a distribution you could simply constrain. | D: Helps the judgment, doesn't bind the format — the 0.5% off-vocab case still breaks the parser.

questions.q: S6 · A document analyst asks: "Why not make the model output its reasoning inside the JSON, in a required analysis field, for every extraction?" Best answer?
o: Great idea — reasoning always improves accuracy and the field documents it.
Use reasoning where the task is genuinely complex (e.g. reconciling totals), and don't burden every simple field-grab with it — proportionality applies to prompting too.
Never mix reasoning with structured output — it corrupts the schema.
Reasoning fields are required for the model to use tools correctly.
questions.e: A: For simple extractions it adds cost/latency without accuracy; 'always' is the tell. | B: Chain-of-thought is a paid feature: spend it where reasoning is the bottleneck. | C: They coexist fine (think, then emit the structured block); 'never' is as wrong as 'always'. | D: Invented dependency — tool use doesn't require an in-schema reasoning field.

questions.q: S6 · 120,000 historical contracts need one-time classification by next month; meanwhile the same schema serves a live API where users wait ~2s for single-document results. Architecture?
o: Batch API for the archive; synchronous API for the live endpoint.
Batch API for both — the cost savings are too large to ignore.
Synchronous for both, parallelized heavily for the archive.
Batch for both, with a webhook to make live requests feel responsive.
questions.e: A: Bulk + nobody waiting = batch (~50% cost). Human waiting = sync. The cleanest dial question on the exam. | B: A ~24h async window behind a 2-second user expectation. | C: Pays double for the archive and builds throughput machinery the Batch API already is. | D: A webhook reports when results arrive; it cannot make a 24h window feel like 2 seconds.

questions.q: S6 · After deployment, the extraction pipeline meets its schema 100% of the time, yet the finance team reports wrong totals posting to the ledger. The PM is confused: "we guaranteed the output". What did they actually guarantee?
o: Nothing — schemas don't guarantee anything under load.
Structure only — valid shape, fields, types. Value correctness needs separate validation (cross-checks, independent review, confidence routing).
Structure and values — the wrong totals must come from upstream OCR.
Values only — schemas check content, not formatting.
questions.e: A: They guarantee a lot: structure, fields, types. Just not the part finance cares about. | B: The shape/values boundary is the most reliable single mark on this exam. Guaranteed JSON can be confidently, validly wrong. | C: Possibly a contributor, but claiming the schema validated values is exactly the misunderstanding being tested. | D: Inverted: schemas check shape, not truth.

questions.q: S1 · An agent's context fills with thousands of tokens of raw API responses from order lookups (full JSON dumps per order). Conversations degrade after ~15 turns. Best fix?
o: Have tools return distilled, relevant fields (status, ETA, item) instead of raw dumps; fetch detail on demand.
Compact the conversation every 10 turns automatically.
Route each customer turn to a fresh agent instance with no history.
Instruct the agent to ignore irrelevant parts of tool results.
questions.e: A: Spend the budget on signal: tool results are context purchases — buy only what the conversation needs. | B: Periodic lossy summarization to absorb waste you could simply not generate — and key facts erode each cycle. | C: Cures bloat by amnesia — multi-turn issues need continuity. | D: Attention is influenced by, not exempt from, what's in context; the tokens still crowd the window.

questions.q: S3 · For a due-diligence report, every claim must be traceable to a verifiable source even after three rounds of summarization between subagents and final output. Mechanism?
o: Add "preserve all citations" to each summarization prompt.
Make claim→source pairs the structural unit that flows between stages (schema-enforced), so a claim physically cannot travel without its source; verify sources before shipping.
Skip intermediate summarization so nothing is lost.
Store all sources in a vector database for later retrieval.
questions.e: A: Each lossy hop probabilistically sheds attribution; three hops compound it. | B: Provenance by structure: the mapping is the data format, not a request — plus an independent existence check. | C: Then raw bulk floods every downstream context — provenance preserved, attention destroyed. | D: Out-of-scope tech invoked as a magic provenance fairy — retrieval doesn't reconnect orphaned claims.

questions.q: S5 · A nightly headless Claude Code job summarizes the day's commits. Some nights it hangs indefinitely on a pathological repo state, blocking the pipeline until morning. Smallest robust fix?
o: --max-turns plus a process-level timeout, with the job reporting a structured "did not complete" status the pipeline treats as a visible, non-blocking failure.
Have the on-call engineer check the job each night.
Add "work quickly and never get stuck" to the prompt.
Re-run the job in a retry loop until it completes before sunrise.
questions.e: A: Backstops at both layers + failure as a first-class reported state. Small, complete, observable. | B: A human cron job to compensate for a missing timeout. | C: Pleading with the model about loop mechanics it doesn't control. | D: Retrying a hang spawns serial hangs; nothing reports, nothing bounds.

questions.q: S2 · Two teammates dispute where to put a rule. Alpha: "Use TypeScript strict mode in new files" → PreToolUse hook. Beta: "Block any edit adding eval()" → CLAUDE.md. Who's right?
o: Both are backwards: strict-mode preference is convention guidance (CLAUDE.md); blocking eval() is a security must-hold (hook).
Alpha is right; Beta is wrong.
Beta is right; Alpha is wrong.
questions.e: A: Both are exactly backwards. | B: Sort by certainty needed, not by which mechanism feels more 'serious'. Security 'never' → deterministic; style preference → guidance. | C: Alpha is hooking a style preference — deterministic machinery for a taste call. | D: Beta is wishing a security rule — the most dangerous direction to be wrong in.

questions.q: S1 · Product wants the support agent to "sound warmer" — customers describe it as robotic. The team debates mechanisms. The architect's pick?
o: Tone guidance + 2–3 example exchanges in the system prompt; review samples after deployment.
A PostToolUse hook that rewrites replies through a 'warmth filter' model.
A warmth score threshold each reply must pass before sending.
Schema-constrain replies to include an empathy_statement field.
questions.e: A: Tone is judgment — the dial's left side. Guidance + examples is proportionate; sampling closes the loop. | B: A second model rewriting the first, deterministically invoked, to adjust a vibe. Costume-level sophistication. | C: Quantifying warmth to gate on it inherits all the unreliability of sentiment scoring, now in the critical path. | D: Structurally mandated empathy is how you get 'I understand your frustration' stapled to every message — more robotic, not less.

questions.q: S4 · A productivity agent's MCP server exposes read_file, and a teammate proposes adding execute_shell "for flexibility — we can restrict it later." The architect's call, and the principle?
o: Add it — flexibility now, restrictions when problems appear.
Refuse: grant the narrowest capability the current task needs (least privilege); add specific, described tools when a real need appears.
Add it but instruct the agent in the prompt to use it sparingly.
Add it with logging so misuse is visible afterward.
questions.e: A: Powers are easy to grant and politically hard to revoke; 'later' means 'after the incident'. | B: Every capability is attack surface and context cost. Scope to need, expand on evidence. | C: A prompt leash on arbitrary shell execution. | D: Observability of a capability that shouldn't exist is a well-documented incident.

questions.q: S6 · An extraction pipeline occasionally posts wrong totals to the ledger. The simplest proposed fix: have the same model re-read and confirm its own answer before submitting. Best response? (Careful — the simplest option isn't always the right one.)
o: Good — keep it simple: tell the model to double-check its own answer before submitting.
Add a deterministic cross-check (totals vs. line items) and route mismatched or low-confidence extractions to an independent reviewer — a fresh instance or a human, never the authoring instance.
It already meets the schema 100% of the time, so it's validated — no change needed.
Re-run the extraction twice and ship it if the two runs agree.
questions.e: A: Self-review is the most-tested reliability trap: an instance defends its own reasoning. Here the plainest option is the wrong one. | B: Value-correctness needs a coded cross-check plus an independent pass; the author can't grade itself. The right answer is the more deliberate one. | C: Shape ≠ values: a schema-valid total can be confidently, validly wrong. | D: Two runs of the same model share the same blind spots — agreement isn't independence.

questions.q: S6 · "The simplest way to get reliable JSON is to clearly ask for JSON in the prompt and parse what comes back." Evaluate, for a pipeline whose output is parsed downstream.
o: Correct — a clear "respond only in valid JSON" instruction is the simplest sufficient fix.
Force a tool whose input_schema IS the output format (tool_choice) — the structure is then guaranteed, not requested.
Strip markdown fences with a regex and retry on parse failure.
Switch to a larger model so it follows the format more reliably.
questions.e: A: Still a request: prose can reach 'usually', never 'every time'. For a parsed shape the plain answer under-delivers. | B: A parsed contract needs a structural guarantee, not a polite ask. The right answer is the more deliberate mechanism. | C: Patching the symptom of unconstrained output instead of constraining it at the source. | D: Spends money to make a probabilistic format slightly less probabilistic — the constraint belongs in the schema.
